comment: Fantastic! Best RPG experience in a board game. Your deck is your character, and the fact that you can't massively rework it each scenario (a la Lord of the Rings) means you get to know it really well, flaws and all. You gain experience which can be spent to tweak it and buy better cards, but the small amount you get each adventure means the deck changes gradually. And you can be forced to add bad cards to it due to scenarios. Brilliant.   The bag drawing mechanism is also very clever. Unlike dice, the odds can be changed each scenario by adding new chits, which can very depending upon the results of a game. But what makes the game is the fact that you play a scenario and, win or lose, advance to the next one. That makes each game feel as if it has consequences...cards can be added or not to your decks and chits to the bag depending upon your actions, and choices can come back to haunt or help you later in the campaign.   The biggest criticism is the cost of each adventure. You really need to play each one multiple times to make it worth it, but once you  know the secrets you are less likely to want to do so,  FFG has tried to make sure the replays will be different by including variations of some cards that you randomize when you play, so the game may go differently next time. Good idea.   I hope the quality of the Dunwich Legacy campaign is indicative of those in the future. Right now this is easily the best of the Lovecraft games on the market. A great game solo.

comment: 7 Wonders is a fun card drafting, tableau building game. Probably the biggest selling point is that if everyone knows how to play the game, you can easily play in 30 minutes (even with the full 7 players).  BUT it is not the gateway game I was hoping it to be. It can be a bear to teach because of all the symbols. My friend who plays games at my place and has played complex games like War of the Ring and A Game of Thrones Board Game struggled immensely with 7 Wonders.  But overall 7 Wonders is a fun game that I don't see ever leaving my collection. Every turn is packed with meaningful decisions and it is not as multiplayer solitaire as a game like Dominion; you really need to look at your neighbors and pay attention to what they may pass you, what you don't want to pass to them, and what resources they have.  I highly recommend 7 Wonders, but not as a gateway game. Play Sushi Go! first with non-gamers.

I like the mechanic of choosing which phases are played out and getting a bonus for your chosen phase a la Puerto Rico.  My favorite change from the Puerto Rico formula though is that all phases are chosen and played concurrently instead of each player picking in an order and being the only person who can pick that role/phase so you're not stuck in a position where your board stagnates because other players are locking you out of necessary bonuses and lines of play you need all because of bad board position.  I still love this game but Roll for the Galaxy has completely replaced it.  I like Roll just a little bit more and I don't see the need to keep both.

comment: Ratings updated after each play: 1st play (solo): the first scenario feels pretty cramped, but it shows off the potential of the game in a limited way and helps you get your feet wet. There’s a lot to remember your first time, I gave it an 8 for challenging decisions but a very short plot arc. I lost but really wanted to try again soon.  2nd play (3 players): did the original first again with three players. It took much longer, probably 20 min to set up, 10 for a rushed teach, and then almost 3 hours to play. Despite the thin plot in the first scenario, we had a blast and everyone wanted to play again the next day. Updated rating to 8.5  3rd play (3 players): bumping my rating to a 9.5 and probably a 10 soon. Already my favorite cooperative game and probably just beat 7th continent for my favorite adventure based game, and we’re still on the “lame” base campaign. This scenario was harder and more open ended. Before this session my mom and girlfriend wanted to jump in and not touch the deck building... but after this (2nd) session they were pouring over the deck building options. They’ve NEVER been that into a game, they usually have me build all their decks for them. This game really is something special as a package, despite having few of any truly fresh mechanics of its own. I can’t believe that things allegedly get so much better from here.

comment: Dice are back!! I have had enough of Risk years ago, but games like Yspahan and Stone Age have found a way to use them as an appropriate mechanic for enjoyable game play. I played with my younger group of kids, and they all enjoyed placing their people figures, and did quite decently. I liked that it challenged their math skills as well. I could tell that they were not grasping the civilization cards though, since I smoked them on the final scoring with those cards. They did well with scoring the buildings, but the civilization card scoring was not as apparent to them. So far, very pleased with the game play, even though there is a lot of rolling the dice. The bits are excellent for the theme. There needs to be more gold pieces but I use the gold from Citadels to compensate. The rules presentation is one of the clearest and free of FAQ reference of any new game I have played. UPDATE: Kids are catching on to the strategy and playing more for the points. Very enjoyable family game. And there is a neat element of tension with taking the civ cards to either enhance your own bonuses or block an opponent - but having to sacrifice an opportunity to place a worker on a much needed field or tool space. Great game.

comment: [22 plays] Have really enjoyed this game very much with all numbers of players, from 2 on up to 6. Update 6/4/11: As I cross beyond 20 completed plays, I will modify to say that I don't rate the game a "10" with just 2 or with the full complement of 6 player. I do think it is simply outstanding with 3,4, or 5 players.  This game is an excellent deeper game, and I personally enjoy the mechanics of the power plant market and the resource market of which others have been critical. I don't think they're fiddly, I think they are cool and the unique mechanics make the game.  Power Grid is all about the plant auctions. What to buy and when to buy -- based on the resource market, the current and future demands on resources by the other players, and watching the number rank of the plant if turn order is still of high concern. I absolutely LOVE that mechanic. It wraps me up and makes my gray cells burn in a most delicious way.  Controlling auctions as best you can, controlling your place in the turn order to your best advantage, and calculated grid expansion decisions on the map are all critical. Minute decisions can mean the difference between win and loss when playing with sharp competitors.  Most recent play Aug '17.

comment: What a gem and what a surprise!  Don't let the name Dungeons & Dragons in huge letters plastered across the box fool you--this is NOT Dungeons & Dragons, not even close. It is a bit fiddly putting away, but there is a place for everything and when the box is closed & even transported, and the quality contents stay put.    All really liked this game.  Looking forward to some obvious expansions.  EDIT: I have played a lot of games now with a lot of people.  I haven't begun to tire of it, and everyone has liked it.  Increased the rating.  Increased the rating again.  How appreciative we all are for the simplicity of this game.  There is no question what to do on the board; All the quests and their rewards are clear; The building benefits are obvious; and the Intrigue cards are all unambiguous and easily understood. comment: -a 2012 early Christmas gift for Zack from Julia-  OUR IMPRESSIONS: This is the best teen and adult friendly Euro-styled economic, auction/bidding, and resource management game we have played to date.  My wife Julia's favorite board game has always been Monopoly. She is the most calculating Monopoly player I have ever met.  Now, Power Grid is her favorite board game because it's everything Monopoly wishes it could be.    As an economic gaming heavyweight, Power Grid's mechanics/components not only include cash currency (Elektro)and valued property cards (power plants) but also features painted wooden city tokens for route-building (i.e. Ticket to Ride), real estate auction/bidding/bluffing (i.e. For Sale), and a resource market with fluctuating costs for various energy commodities (painted wooden tokens as coal, oil, garbage, uranium) that require careful resource-management (i.e. Settlers of Catan).  Thematically, the game has an gritty electric aesthetic with crisp graphics that depict a gamut of energy production facilities: from fossil fuels, nuclear materials, and recycled waste, to emerging renewable resources like wind and solar power.  As a hefty Euro styled game with minimal luck involved and a narrative without violent conflict or player elimination, we find Power Grid to be very engaging, quite challenging, and overall more fun and replayable than mainstream 20th century American economic games like Monopoly, Life, Pit, or Pay-Day.  Of the 60+ games in our home, this is THE game that we go out of our way to plan ahead for and play together as husband and wife or with our gamer friends.  It's best played with 3 or more players but with the Power Grid: Robots expansion that adds "AI" 'robot' player(s), we can have the strategic depth and unpredictability of a 4-player game yet are able to play with only 2 human players (my wife and I).    ***  GAMEPLAY: The game is divided in duration by 3 overarching successive STEPS and in gameplay, each round consists of 5 sequential economic PHASES. The winner of the game is the one who succeeds in achieving the game's goal of powering the most cities built into your energy network by simultaneously owning the most efficient combination of power plants and having enough purchased raw materials in your resource supply to meet the economic demand for energy from the linked cities in your energy network. This sounds complex, and it can be at first, but the game flows very well in a consistent and calculating manner.    STEP 1 is the opening step in the game and it's main function is to enforce a rule that a player may only build cities into their network if they are vacant for a cost of 10 elektro + the connection cost (the number value listed between adjacent cities on the map board).    STEP 2 is initiated after a player builds the prescribed number of cities and thus adds more intensity and higher costs/risks/rewards for the players. Instead of building only in vacant cities, now players may build into single occupancy cities to make them double occupancy for an increased cost of 15 elektro + the connection cost.   STEP 3 is the final endgame process that is initiated after the STEP 3 card is drawn from the Power Plant deck in between rounds or during the Phase 2 bidding/auction process. In STEP 3, the auction market from Steps 1-2 with the 4 lowest choices from 8 total plants arranged in descending order on display (the remaining 4 higher cost plants are the future market) is increased to a total of 6 plants available for bidding on the auction market with NO future market. Also at the end of each round in Phase 5, the lowest plant on the auction block is discarded and removed from the game, forcing frugal players to reconsider their strategy if they want to win.   PHASE 1) DETERMINE PLAYER ORDER: First place player is the one who has presently built the most cities in their power plant network.  Note: First place position players do not always win the game after STEP 3 is initiated; some players tactically decide to be in last place during rounds in order to be the first to buy raw materials and build cities.    PHASE 2) BUY POWER PLANT First place begins the Auction/Bidding process for acquiring/upgrading ONE more efficient power plants by spending one's Elektro. (Depending on the number or players, each player may only own and operate a maximum of 3-4 power plants during the game and must discard the least efficient plant from their energy network with each upgrade.) The game begins with each player having 50 Elektro for start-up costs.  The power plants range in minimum bids from 3-50 Elektro and can power from 1-7 cities using single or multiple types of raw materials purchased from the commodities market. Note: In Steps 1-2, there are 8 visible power plants on the market arranged in descending order of cost for a minimum bid. The 4 highest valued power plants are not yet up for auction but   PHASE 3) BUY RAW MATERIALS: Last place is the first to purchase available energy resources from the commodities market using their accrued Elektro currency; each proceeding step in the game effects the surplus supply and costs due to the changing demand for each energy resource. Note: a player may only purchase up to a personal surplus of 200% raw materials of only what their owned power plants require. (i.e. if a player had a power plant that powered 3 cities for 2 coal, then the player can only purchase a maximum of 4 coal from the market.)  PHASE 4) BUILDING: Last place begins the process for building new cities into one's expanding power plant network; these cities are powered by the combination of purchased power plants from phase 2 and raw materials from phase 3.  Note: during the opening round, ALL players must purchase and power 1 or more cities. Also at the start of the game each player will choose to begin building their network in one unoccupied colored region on the map board; the number of players determines how many adjacent regions are accessible for the remainder of the game. In subsequent rounds, the building of one's cities in their own network will spill over into adjacent regions so long as their network is one continuous connection to the origin city selected in the first round of the game. Conflict in the game arises between players in the rare occasions when someone builds from an advantageous location near multiple adjacent cities of other players' regions; so I guess there can be a mechanic of area control in the STEP 1 rounds of gameplay at work.    PHASE 5) BUREAUCRACY: This concluding phase is where risks/costs are rewarded with profits and the market for power plants and raw materials are adjusted accordingly with each succeeding STEP (from 1-3) in the game.    - A) GET MONEY: Here, beginning with first place, each player decides how many cities they want to or are able to effectively power using their acquired power plants and raw materials at hand and thus, are rewarded with Elektro profits allocated according to the number of cities they decide to power. (i.e. if a player who had built 6 cities in their network, but only had a power plant that powered 4 cities for 2 oil, then they could only power 4 cities maximum, and discard 2 oil from their resource supply into the energy surplus pile and receive 54 Elektro in return according to the game's earnings chart.) Note: all used raw materials for powering cities are discarded back into a surplus pile. - B) UPDATE POWER PLANT MARKET according to STEP 1, 2, or 3 that is in effect during the game.  In Steps 1-2 at the end of each round the highest power plant in the market is removed and placed back under the power plant card deck.  In Step 3, at the end of each round, the lowest power plant in the market is discarded and removed for the rest of the game. - C) RESTOCK RAW MATERIALS in the resource marker according to the table listed on the back of the instruction manual (which also lists how many cities need to be built into a player's network to initiate the next STEP).  Each succeeding STEP has different ratios of return for depleting energy resources simulating the market effects of surplus, supply, cost, demand, and inflation/deflation as the raw materials components are placed and displayed on the resource market (see Phase 3) on the bottom/side of the map board.  The Round is now complete and go back to Phase 1 to resume gameplay until the game is complete.        ***  PROS: Power Grid is an excellent game for decision-making and strategic thinking skills. It requires maximum player involvement so that each person gets to work and play through until the its conclusion. It has a back-and-forth momentum from its mixed mechanics that allows a person in last place to have opportunities to gain fresh momentum that can change the pace or trajectory of each game.  The component quality is fantastic with hundreds of colorful painted wood pieces and a great double-sided board.  There are also multiple moderately priced expansion sets available as double-sided map boards of different geographic locations with new power plant cards and special localized rules.  My final pro is that this game seems to be unrivaled among other economic themed games and even among the heavier cult-hit Euro games we have played or heard about; it really stands out on our gameshelf and hasn't had the chance to collect any dust.  CONS: This is not a con from our perspective but it might be for others: there is minimal luck (if any) in this game; there are no dice, but only a shuffled deck of the remaining power plant cards for the auction phase (1 of 5) for each round.  No decision is without consequence and no opportunity can be wasted if you want to win the game. This is what some gamers call a "BRAINBURNER."  It is a mathematical, systematic, sequential reasoning kind of game that takes 2 hours to play. Now for some legitimate cons that we see to be easily reconciled with patience.  For new players or for very analytical over-thinking folks, this game can bring on symptoms of "Analysis Paralysis" where it feels like another players turn seems to take longer than it needs to and thus, the morale of the group playing can diminish. It's not the easiest game to teach without first playing through a game to understand how it fits together and I could see how impatient players or those who avoid conflict in terms of games that have limited number of resources, might not initially enjoy this game until they become more confident with its deep strategic gameplay.    The pros far outweigh the cons in our book.   ***    TEACHING TAKEAWAYS: As a parent and pastor, I like how this game can teach and simulate sound economic principles and reasonable resource stewardship for intentional sequential decision-making. I appreciate how a game like this one can demonstrate how your decisions directly effect the decisions of other players and vice versa. Personally, as a lifelong learner with ADHD, games like these help me to focus and make tactical decisions wisely by following a one-step-at-a-time process while remaining aware of the long-term strategy with an end goal in perspective.  As for my wife, she really likes the mathematical/probability/statistics learning curve this game presents kids and adults who take the time to play this game.  Finally, good map-based games (i.e. "Ticket to Ride") like this can foster basic geography skills with learning city locations in various countries/continents.   GRADE: We rate POWER GRID a 10 out of 10 --- OUTSTANDING!

You can 'win' by leaving everyone else behind, but there are no mechanics to cover it.  How does it follow that you can lose sanity and cause yourself mental problems throughout the game, but leaving everyone you were with to die for no reason is totally fine?  You even apparently have a psychic link with these people, given the game's mechanics.  It's not a problem when they die horrifically?  I think the semi-cooperative aspects could have been thought through better.   Still, the app is great, and the one story we played through was involving enough with some nice little surprises. comment: I really like the way the mechanics work in Concordia. It feels as though the hand management part of the game is about deciding what part of your turn you want to do at what time. I've also noticed that the most successful people in Concordia know what they need and when and don't care if it will help other players.   Essentially, you have cards that each represent a single action. Together, all those cards make up one complete turn. The truly deep strategy comes from deciding what you will do and when. The diplomat card may be one of the best innovations here. It lets you copy a card from another player, but they have to have just played that card last turn. Sometimes you'll sit there waiting and waiting for someone to play a certain card, but you're possibly ruining your own potential in doing that.  The theme would not come across for me had it not included custom wooden pieces.   I would also like to note that the instructions in this game are the most elegant I've yet seen. After playing the game twice I assumed that the rule book would be between 12-20 pages. It is 2 pages front and back. It is the same size as Ticket to Ride instructions. That to me is amazing design.

comment: Mansions of Madness: Second Edition is a scenario-based dungeon-crawler based in H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu mythos.  While there is some combat, the game puts more of an emphasis on exploration and puzzle-solving.  The game is fully cooperative and moderated by a mobile app, that provides information about board setup and what happens when you interact with various features and monsters.  However, the app doesn't track everything--skill checks are still performed with physical dice, and the app doesn't store information about characters' locations, damage, or items.  This is nice as players can still make informed decisions about dice risk, and you don't have to keep fiddling with the app to keep it abreast of everything that's going on.  However, the app does know some things about what's going on, such as which rooms have been explored and which items have been inspected, and clearly presents challenges based on that--the app obscures why some of the events are happening, which can be a little unusual for a boardgamer.  Personally, I was pleasantly surprised by the gameplay of this game, as I found the mystery to be very intriguing, and interacting with the world to find out what happens definitely kept my interest. comment: I have enjoyed each and every playing of Alhambra.  It has become my first dime of 2005 and will only get more and more playings thoughout the year.   I have played multiple games with 2, 3, and 4 players and feel that it scales extremely well.  Alhambra is a game that offers hand management, city building, tile laying and tough choices throughout.  The "invisible" scoring rounds make for difficult decisions when you start getting close.  "Do I take the money, buy another house or should I move this off my reserve to try and score some points?" "Should I buy a garden that will score me immediate points or a tower that could pay off in the long run?"  "Hmmm...  should I buy the piece to extend my wall or to extend my city?"  I feel that it is themed well and if introduced properly, one can bring the players into the games thematic and playing depths very easily.  It is also very easy to learn and play, while leaving many decisions to allow a certain complexity.  I understand why it won Game of the Year over Puerto Rico, I find it to be a much more accessible game.

comment: BSG is one of "those" games people will often either love or hate without a whole lot of in between. But another thing I find is that people often decide whether or not they love or hate it based on one experience. The problem with that is that perhaps not unlike other board games, one round of BSG can differ vastly than the next. I like to describe BSG as a game that has provided some of my favorite gaming experiences, (some of the best) & some of my least favorite experiences, (some the worst)! BSG is a well designed game, but not an easy one. It suffers at times from the fact that many of it's teachers are woefully inadequate at teaching the many rules and intricacies of the game. This is a difficult cooperative game with a hidden betrayer(s), sometimes the "bad guys" can win by simply not helping much and allowing the game to beat the players or by just giving that extra little push towards oblivion at the end. You don't need to be a fan of the mini-series to be a fan of the game, in fact I've never seen a single episode of the show. (But I'm sort of interested now as a result of playing the game).  The game can suffer a little when played with an unbalanced group. I prefer playing with more experienced players but will admit that I am still learning many of the games intricacies. I also think this game suffers when whoever is teaching it takes an hour or more to teach (I've sat through that and thought I would hate the game as a result).

comment: [b]tl;dr[/b] — All the mechanical aspects of a complete RPG adventure in a deck of cards.  Fragile and group-dependent, but deeply satisfying when it works.  [i]Your time pod opens and you greet yourself with a handgun. "Get back in the pod!" you yell. "What?" you ask, confused for like the eleventh time today, "Why?" "Because I can only do this once," you say, putting the gun to your head and pulling the trigger.[/i]  [COLOR=#FF0000]THE FOLLOWING IS CERTIFIED SPOILER-FREE[/COLOR]  "B-Team!  We're sending you in because A-Team went all 'dynamite and fire' on the situation.  You'll be inserted an hour ahead of their arrival—get it right, save some lives.  Dismissed and godspeed!"  [i]One hour later...[/i]  B-Team is vomited from their pods into heaps, snazzy jumpsuits soiled with effluent, sweaty hair pasted in streaks on retching faces.  Someone's crying.  The Time Captain, curled up like a bug, lets out a wheezing croak:  "Need... more... [i]dynamite[/i]..."  [microbadge=36241]  [b]After 4 plays:[/b]  All the mechanical aspects of a complete RPG adventure in a deck of cards.  It's up to you and your friends to actually breathe life into this, but for us, as veteran role-players, it was absolutely perfect.  We banged out "Asylum" across two sessions, with the usually-busy players burning an entire Saturday afternoon (something that NEVER happens) for the final run-through.  I pretty much want everyone I love who also loves RPGs to take a trip through this.  We beat "Asylum" (just barely) and the experience left us with the real treasure of such things:  darkly hilarious emergent narratives that are on track to become Canon Lore in our group.  And only the best adventures do that.  Now, I can totally see how this could fall flat for straight-up board gamers, and even for ardent RPGers—but I really appreciate how it hits somewhere in the middle.  As an RPGer I'm not at all put off by the one-shot nature of the scenarios, seeing this as an elaborate board game-based RPG.  With the lack of Game Master or any required prep (other than sitting down and flipping the first card), this will be our go-to for those RPG nights when we don't have a quorum.*  [size=7]*Of course, this means everyone will always show up so they don't miss out if we're one short, which is another way of saying it'll never get played again...[/size]  I'm down for wherever the system takes me.  [b]After 11 plays:[/b]  Deep into [i]Prophecy of Dragons[/i] it's become clear that this is not just another random adventure scenario, but the third chapter in a much larger, overarching story. I am in awe at the ambitiousness of the project—using a board game as a framing device for serial storytelling—but have no idea if they can stick the landing. But goddamn, [i]the ride[/i]. Such a ride. I'd take it into a brick wall it's so sweet.  [o]The worst thing about Time Patrol is talking to the guy who you know is going to get eaten by the monster for the third time.  The first time you have [i]no idea[/i], and so you're all "Hey, man, how's it goin'?" with honest, fate-ignorant friendliness.  The second time you're startled to see him, and then you're flashing back on the whole monster thing, and like one moment it's him, [i]right there[/i], and the next it's how surprised and terrified and then resigned he looked getting gnashed and slurped and sucked into some kind of otherworldly gullet, and he's startled at your startlement because he doesn't even know you, man, and that look, that awful familiar look, reverberates between your two faces and the one he's going to make like 20 minutes from now when, you know,[i] monster[/i].  But that [i]third[/i] time, that's the really bad one.  Once you convince him to come with—and he shouldn't, what with the way you're utterly failing to sell it:  "Oh, we're not [i]sorcerers[/i], we're [i]time travelers[/i], you know, from the [i]future[/i],"—he's all gung-ho to get to it like [i]right now[/i] and you're all, "Hey, look—a butterfly," and "How's your mom?  Maybe you should write her a note," and "You know this is harder on me, right?" and then you take three steps to the left.[/o] PS.  My Time Patrol callsign is "Clocky"—on account of my penchant for randomly punching people.  "What?  They're already dead where we come from!" comment: Do you like Settlers of Catan, with the fight for control of shared areas that pay out specific resources? Concordia has it.  Do you like Century: Spice Road / Eastern Wonders, or Istanbul, with a physical (but expandable) limit on how many resources you can store? Concordia has it.  Do you like Power Grid, with increasing costs to control the same cities? Concordia has it.  Do you like Orleans, with the need to spend actions to physically move your token along paths to new locations on the map before you can build there? Concordia has it.  Do you like Dominion, where you play cards to take actions to draft new cards into your hand to build a better action deck? Concordia has it.  Do you like Stone Age or Tzolkin, with that thing where the cards are VP multipliers for whatever strategy you're playing, but the good cards are too expensive so you wait for people to buy the cheap cards and your good card will slide down but then somebody else buys it instead? Concordia has it.  Do you like all the best mechanisms from all the best games wrapped up in one gorgeous package? Concordia has it.

comment: Juego ambientado en la serie. Admite hasta seis jugadores. Todos los jugadores deben cooperar para sobrevivir y sobreponerse a los sucesos que van ocurriendo. Cada jugador lleva un personaje que tiene ciertas características. En su turno coge cartas según esas características y escoge una acción (según las cartas o la ubicación que escoja). Al final del turno hay que desvelar una carta de crisis que supone problemas para los humanos. Los retos se resuelven por votación oculta. Cada uno contribuye positiva o negativamente a los test de habilidad que dirimen todos los conflictos. Entre los jugadores hay algún traidor (según el número de jugadores puede  ser 1 o 2 cylon).  Los humanos ganan si consiguen llevar la nave a kobol, después de su octavo salto. Los Cylon ganan si los humanos no lo consiguen, o si la nave es destruida, alguno de los marcadores de los humanos llega a cero, o la nave es invadida. Está entretenido. Gana si conoces la serie. Hay que leer bastante. Lo mejor del juego es la existencia oculta de un traidor, que da lugar a muchas situaciones. Es un buen juego.  Subida la nota de 7.5 a 8 tras mi segunda partida, esta vez, con bastante conocimiento de la serie (a mitad de la tercera temporada). Si eres jugón y te gustó la serie, este es un juego imprescindible.

Ami a legszebb az egészben, hogy nincs egyértelműen legjobb taktika. Bár valószínűleg véges a győzelemhez vezető optimális kombinációk száma, azért nem csekély lehetőségről van szó. comment: I love this game.  My only problem is the length and finding people to play it (this feels like a theme for me).  I think it's a very hard game to score well in during your first couple of plays.  The nice thing about this game, vs. Agricola, is that you don't feel like you're just getting beat up if you're not winning.  The food pressure is much less, and you can always just take loans.  I wish there were multiple strategies in this game besides "ship iron" and constantly work those avenues.  I sort of envision the game as being a little better if someone could realistically deviate from that.  Much more though, I think the game is about who can do that strategy the best and most efficiently.  Either way though, it's an awesome game, and I would recommend this game even at the full MSRP.  Le Grand Hameau adds some nice flavor, and at some level, I wish it added more.  If I can get enough people to play it to the point of understanding the game, I'd like to toy around with removing some more standard buildings and replacing with some more special buildings.  I will say - 5 players, as the box suggests, is not really an option.  2 to 3 is what that game was made for.  4 would get pretty ugly too I think.

comment: Wow. Just played a two player family version. There's a lot to soak in. It was fun but dear lord was it hard to get from the instructions. We watched 2 different youtube videos after reading the instructions and had to read the instructions again afterward. It took us like 1.5 hours from when we had everything out of the wrap and when we finally finished the first move. And there was 14 more to do after that! It was an enjoyable game, but I'm just not as impressed as I should be. It's theme is just so-so, though I really liked the Animeeples for the livestock (just purchased new). For the third rated game on BGG, I was expecting to be blown away, not confused slightly bored. Maybe this will change when I update after playing with the included decks.  Update:  The app made this one a home run for me. Takes care of all the maintanance and I can play the game in a decent amount of time. I think the game plays better online because the game is stressful in person. As of now: Agricola if we are all hardcore gamers that play very fast, but Caverna in any other appropriate circumstance.  Next (and maybe final) update: This game has everything. At first glance from the uninitiated it is complex and has obtuse scoring. With repeated play, it is a masterpiece. No other game offers the same permutations of long term strategies, formed through the in-depth analysis, and preferably drafting, of cards. Tactical decisions and improvisation take over from the initial draft, and the game is a home run. The interaction is perfect, the expansions add infinity to infinity, and the theme is represented as well as can be within the confines of a board game.

Maybe I spend my time gathering mana crystals, and discovering altars in ancient ruins to gain fame points.  I remember opening the box, thinking there weren't a whole lot of artifacts/spells/advanced actions, figuring it would get stale quick.  But I was surprised, you gain cards very methodically, and it makes the decision of what you acquire important, because these special cards really feel special, each one attuned to a particular character build. comment: Designer: Alan R. Moon Artist: Cyrille Daujean, Julien Delval Publisher: 999 Games Player count: 2-5 (best with 4) Weight: light / medium  Mechanics: route/network building,  Setting: turn-of-the-20th century Europe Theme: fair Play time: 45-60 minutes  I've always enjoyed trains and games that involve trains and/or pick-up-and-deliver. So when I discovered Ticket to Ride a few years ago and learned how popular it was, I really wanted to get my hands on a copy.  TtR is a really fun game, easy to explain and easy to play. The game looks very appealing and the rules are quite simple. The game is very suitable for non-gamers as well and can be considered a so called gateway game. You can set up and explain the game in just a few minutes, so that's most welcome when playing with non-gamers.  I've played a dozen games with 2-5 players and all work quite well. As the map is rather large, 4-5 players is probably best, otherwise you will probably stay out of each others' way for the majority of the game. The game really shines when all players are actually competing to finish some central lines in order to complete their tickets. However, if someone beats you to it, you could still use the stations to "borrow" someone elses track, which makes TTR:Europe more forgiving than the original TTR.   Although some people complain they make the game too easy, but I tend to disagree. They can in fact prevent someone from playing a lost game early on, so I think these really add something to the game.  There is a luck factor involved, as you're dependent on the cards you draw, but in the end strategy should pay out. Same goes for the tunnels, which are a unique feature of the European maps. When you want to complete a tunnel, then you have to draw 3 additional cards and if these match the colour of the tunnel, then you need to "pay" additional wagons (or locomotives) otherwise you can't complete the tunnel.  I'm a fan of this game and like to play this again anytime! Next to this version, I also own the TTR 10th Anniversary Edition of the original US map, the Dutch map, the Swiss map and the Indian map. Europe still is one of my favourites though and definitely a keeper in my collection.
name: Ticket to Ride: Europe

comment: This game is tough, mean and not forgiving to those who aren't self seeking. Very true to its source material.  I really like the diplomacy that eventuates from the game's need for temporary alliances. As everyone is jostling to keep one another from reaching a game ending position, it's very bad gameplay not to continually forge and fracture alliances. But we are human, and this is where it gets interesting - can I let the Greyjoys get away with taking two of my territories last turn? Should I simply tell them I will support them and then watch them die a horrible death against the Lannisters? Or should I get over it and play 'the Game of Thrones?'  I like that it isn't 'total conquest' but rather relies on an endgame trigger, however I'm not sure how I feel about that combined with a round limit. Maybe it would have been better to let the game be open ended? I like the combat, the ability to support (although doesn't seem to get played enough), and the way actions are selected. The bidding is tense, and external threats make an interesting mix of co-operative and cutthroat competitive play.

comment: In Le Havre, a player’s turn consists of two parts: First, distribute newly supplied goods onto the offer spaces; then take an action. As an action, players may choose either to take all goods of one type from an offer space or to use one of the available buildings. Building actions allow players to upgrade goods, sell them or use them to build their own buildings and ships. Buildings are both an investment opportunity and a revenue stream, as players must pay an entry fee to use buildings that they do not own. Ships, on the other hand, are primarily used to provide the food that is needed to feed the workers.  After every seven turns, the round ends: players’ cattle and grain may multiply through a Harvest, and players must feed their workers. After a fixed number of rounds, each player may carry out one final action, and then the game ends. Players add the value of their buildings and ships to their cash reserves. The player who has amassed the largest fortune is the winner.

comment: 心得: 煤礦路線似乎很強勢 不過人多時不太可能可以專心只搞自己的 所以還是要觀察場上的互動來決定行動 雖然別人可以卡你 但是就變的目標都是快速朝這個方向前進的樣子 規則: *起始資源   長版玩家有5元一煤   短版玩家有5元2魚2木2土2鐵1牛2煤2皮，單人雙人都起始有一木船 *起始補給板塊洗混蓋著放置，玩家踩到才打開，對應資源格放資源   長版2元2魚2木1土，洗好六張特殊建築放上面   短版3元3魚3木2土1鐵1麥1牛，單人有一木船開著 *挑出對應建築物分三推洗勻，打開按數字牌好放在版圖上，選擇正確的記輪牌疊好 *每輪移動玩家船標記到下一格並補充資源 *玩家每回合可選擇一棟工人到建築物做動作，或是拿某一格資源全部 *此外還可買賣建築物(公有或是建築計畫區最上面那張)不算動作，賣建築物半價，船也可買 *船移動到利息格，有借貸不管幾張都只要付一元 *遊戲任何時候付食物都可用錢取代 *遊戲在每七回合一輪結束付食物並生麥生牛，然後最後一輪結束每位玩家可在執行一個動作(此動作可重複) *工人必須進入建築物才能動作，被買的建築物，上面工人會回擁有者手上，同回合不能同建築物賣又買回來 *建設時，磚可以代替黏土，鋼可以代替鐵 *造船一次只能造一艘

comment: We played with 2 players and enjoyed the game immensely. We played through 2 times before realizing that we were playing wrong; spending more time units than required when exploring a new location. As a game system, we are really excited about playing the next scenarios as they come available. We'll see how they meet expectations. Obviously, with a rating of 9, we really liked the game, but I'll point out a few negatives about the system and this first scenario.  1) The rules just aren't clear enough. They have been intentionally left vague so they fit multiple scenarios, but really need to be tightened up for each scenario. 2) The story is really rambling and while enjoyable, there is no way to know the right path to take. Since the wrong paths are interesting, this isn't so bad. It is like a choose your own adventure book that requires that you read every possible paragraph to make sure you don't miss something. 3) Possible (small, non-specific) SPOILER for Asylum: Having written several professional dinner theater mysteries, I have a complaint that may not bother others. One of the puzzles "breaks the 4th wall" (in a cheap way) which a) made the puzzle confusing and, more important, b) broke the thematic immersion of the players in the game. The clue refers to the game system instead of a story element. Not only was it poorly done, but there was no reason for it. The puzzle could have just as easily referred to a story element and could have been great. Hopefully, this is an early mistake that won't be made in future scenarios.

comment: A game of conflict for 2-5 players (or 6 with certain expansions). Players choose a unique race paired with a special power and over the course of the game a player will put their original race into decline and continue with a brand new race, possibly several times. Points are earned each turn for territories controlled on the always crowded board.  It's a pretty simple game but each race will be paired with different special powers from game to game so you have to re-evaluate and consider new combinations each and every game. Choosing your race/power combo and timing when you go into decline (to pick a new race/power combo) is an essential element to doing well. However, the game is also about territory control and since there is very little luck in the game planning ahead and anticipating (or encouraging) opponents moves pays off.  Some players claim it is obvious what the best move is each turn but it's really not about getting the highest score you can on each turn, it's about consistently scoring. A high score this turn that leaves you exposed and out of position for the next two is not necessarily as good as a moderate score this turn that leaves you in a strong position.   I like the game because it offers new combinations of powers to consider each play and it rewards strategy and thinking ahead while keeping a very simple/streamlined rule set.

In LoW players are simply sending out their workers (agents) to various board locations to get resources (adventurers) to complete goals (quests) and gain victory points or other benefits to help in the game.  One smart addition to the mix are buildings that you can chose to build and open up new worker locations - and when other players use your building, you get a small benefit.  You might notice above that the theme here is a bit thin, but everything looks good and there are bits of D&D lore woven into the quest cards.  So that will satisfy fantasy enthusiasts, while keeping the game accessible enough for anyone that couldn't tell a halfling from a bugbear.

comment: This game has a fantastic theme perfectly integrated with innovative mechanics.  Basically, you place your workers on a number of gears that all move in step with a central gear; the longer the worker stays on the gear, the better the action you'll get when you remove him (generally).  The catch is that, on your turn, you can either place or remove workers--never both and never neither.  Planning becomes essential in this game, as you don't want to get stuck needing resources from removing a worker the same turn you want to place, or run out of workers to place when you need your workers to keep going around.  If you plan it out right, you can truly have some amazing turns though (and conversely, it feels positively suboptimal to only do one thing on your turn sometimes).  This is an excellent planning game that rewards long-term thinking; definitely one of my favorites of the year.  (5+ plays)

comment: [BGCOLOR=#000000][COLOR=#FFFFFF]SoloX.[/COLOR][/BGCOLOR]   Man, sounds really good. This may be the first Kickstarter I really regret not getting in on.  Update: reprint coming to Kickstarter in April 2017. Woot!  Update: backed the second printing on KS, due for [-]August[/-] November 2017 delivery.  Update: holy smokes. Believe the hype. Three of us tackled this over the holidays. Punching out and sorting alone was at least a half hour, and even after watching some videos our first scenario run was easily 2+ hours and we lost. It's not really that complicated though and we played twice more in the same night at around an hour per scenario.  Gloomhaven is "just" a dungeon crawler with a campaign system, but saying so is really a disservice to how terrific the game is. The Euro-y combat mechanics are fantastic, the monster AI and bookkeeping is smooth, the character progression system and campaign are very well done - everything is just excellent and feels polished to the nth degree. Even the fact that the designer made his own world and didn't quite stick to traditional fantasy tropes (no orcs and dwarves, no traditional classes like fighter and cleric - the Scoundrel is the only thing I've seen so far that seems pretty similar to a standard fantasy Rogue) helps set this apart.  Gloomhaven is the best dungeon crawler / pseudo-RPG game out there, hands down. So glad I bit on the second Kickstarter to guarantee myself a copy.

comment: After first try:   We played the intro scenario and one of the two-part level I scenarios.   I've played a lot of roleplaying in my youth (mostly AD&D) so I already knew this would appeal to me, but I expected more game and not only "play".   Even though there was little strategy & tactics involved and mostly move & roll dice I still liked it. You have to see it for what it is. The game has a little more strategy in it and variation than most of the bash-the-zombis that floods the market right now which except for the theme shares a lot with this game, but it's still more an adventure than a game (and more an adventure than the bash-the-zombies games I compare it with).  What makes me like this game appeals to the AD&D-player in me: it's fun to find stuff, buy better weapons and level up.   My friends have made some modifications to the rules to make the monsters a little weaker and also to make it more strategic with more positioning and moving around insted of static headbanging: monsters have one move and one action each turn. With that the intro scenario was easy but the second part of the next scenario we managed by three very lucky dice rolls in a row with only one health left on the guy we were to save.   I surely want to get back to this game and continue our campaign.

comment: Elegant simplicity. The best 2 words I can think to describe this one here. This is definitely the game I would grab for non-gamers who want to do something new and regulars gamers that want to play something for lack of a better word, sophisticated. There is something just relaxing about this game, almost similar to bird watching itself, built into every aspect and detail of this game. The presentation is flawless, filled with very well done art and "fluff" that is interesting and informative, and components that are truly top notch (even for SM games, this is well done). The gameplay is extremely distilled down to basic action choices and card collecting. But that simply carries the meat of the game which is as well-oiled an engine builder that has probably ever existed, the choices presented are at once numerous but not overwhelming or confusing from beginning to end. The variety of gameplay is also fantastic as you have multiple goals/bonuses available in any given game, along with a large stack of individually unique cards. It is in this aspect where the game falters ever so slightly. The slice of variety here means that, quite likely, you might end up "fighting against the tide" so to speak as you are presented with goals or bonuses that simply do not mesh well with the cards you get throughout the game. The way the powers, abilities, and traits on the cards are presented, it is unlikely this will last all game, but some players will definitely find their groove well before others more often than not. This can lead to some frustrating moments for some players if they let it. However, the game is fairly quick and feels even faster than the clock will run most of the time, so if you accept the small chaos, you will be rewarded with a relaxing and informative stroll through nature in board game form.

comment: Terraforming Mars is a card-based engine-building game based on achieving three goals--increasing the planet's temperature, increasing the oxygen level, and placing ocean tiles on Mars. The game has six different resources, and for each of these, you have a bank and an income track. Some of these resources can be traded in directly to impact the three goals, while others just help you pay the costs of cards. The real heart of the game is card play though--the game has hundreds of cards, all different, and each of these manipulates your resources or the planet in various ways. In the end, players add up how much they've contributed to the three goals, along with points from tiles they've placed on the Mars board, points from cards, and various other bonuses to determine a winner. While I'm usually pretty theme-agnostic, I have to admit that this one kind of takes me in. The card play is very engaging, as it's just fun to set up your combos. There is are some take-that elements I didn't enjoy, but those are a minor part of the game. On the whole, this one was a winner.   (5+ plays)

Like most in this genre, falling behind in the tech tree and the arms race is probably a death knell, so even through the game disguises it well, it only takes a turn or two of being knocked around and you're off the pace, so it's as ruthless as any. comment: A very unique and clever game composed of 2 phases. First, players compete to rapidly construct a space ship from parts (tiles) grabbed from a shared supply. The resulting ships are often of questionable quality due to time constraints and having been crafted from a rapidly depleting supply of tiles. Players next send their ships on a voyage where they are mostly helpless as they watch while they may be cleaved in half by laser fire, left adrift by slavers, or perhaps arrive in first place and pristine condition. This process is repeated three times (with the stakes increasing each time) and the person who has done the best at the end of the third round wins.  I especially enjoy the tension of racing to rapidly construct a viable and legal ship while competing for parts with the other players.  It is also quite entertaining to see how the ships that everyone has created perform (or how they get mangled as the case may be). At first glance there appears to be a lot of luck in this game but it is actually quite the opposite. Players with more skill will build better ships and they will do better consistently.  In fact, the only drawback of this game for me is that it can be brutal for new players against experienced players (or even for experienced players playing with a more experienced group). It is definitely a game of skill and if there is much discrepancy in skill levels, those with less skill can really end up getting rapidly left behind or obliterated each round. This can drastically reduce the fun factor for the less experienced player. Fortunately, the expansion offers a way to mitigate this. It contains new rules designed to make the game even more difficult (such as ‘Rough Road Ahead’). To balance the playing field for new players, you can simply apply these rules only to the experienced players. I've tried this with new players several times now and it really helps to keep the game competitive and fun for everyone.

Each round players need to place OR take workers, but not both.  That small rule will cause immense anguish as you try to do all you want to at critical times.  Your workers can "ride" a wheel for only so long, and each space they turn to offers different benefits, so that timing is essential.  And will another player decide to advance the wheel twice in a turn, wrecking all your careful plans?  While I loved all the complexity, I do see some balance issues in the game that are of a concern, but not enough to ruin the overall fun.  Definitely a game worth exploring for all the Euro fans out there.

comment: All the stuff I like in a Euro - no round based stuff, a good tactical decision each turn, a strategy that develops based on the map and card availability that helps drive the tactics, indirect pussage (there being a race for resource generators and cards). It uses the card play/pickup system from Havana / Castle for all Seasons, but I like how when you buy more cards, they add to your hand to keep things going. I also like how you're rewarded for using as many cards as possible before pickup. There's a nice variety of ways to go about scoring points. You want to pay attention to what other people are doing to potentially leech off their card this turn, and also to direct your strategy to alternate ways to score points to minimise direct competition. I was engaged throughout, nice components, nice timeframe, potentially a touch long, and all requiring only 4 pages of rules + setup. An elegant system.

comment: Finally got around to playing this (something I've wanted to do for years now.)  It's mechanically simpler than I was expecting and seems to benefit from having a larger group (although I can imagine 6 or 7 players would really increase the downtime.)  It's interesting and I found myself really drawn to the sheer number of  alien races (50 or so with awesome artwork), which adds a fair bit of replayability.  We played with 2 races each making for interesting mechanic combinations that seemed to add a fair bit to the game.  Of course, because of this nature, it could result in the game being wildly unbalanced, should players clue in alliances should compensate.    The stacking plastic UFOs are pretty cool as well and the overall production value is as high as I would expect from any Fantasy Flight product.  At its core it's a chaotic hand management game (very luck driven), where it seems pertinent to utilize your worst cards effectively.  This is where I found the game would shine, in its devious backstabbing, negotiation or use of flares and powers to help compensate for these cards (who doesn't enjoy a little player interaction and bluffing.)  This leads to the games true nature, the players interactions.  This means that the group you play with is key to your enjoyment of this game, negotiation, diplomacy, betrayal and the ability to analyze your powers strategically are pivotal traits in your group.  .

Player interaction is a little minimal but the gameplay encourages it, and the more players the more interactivity will ensue. For me this game is like a work of art, and decoding it is pure joy. And yet the puzzle is matched with complex possibilities on the board, with players stealing actions, potentially boxing other players into a corner, and mutually benefiting one another through close expansion, which can be both helpful and dangerous.   Personally though, the engine building is where this really shines. Every action and every construction will greatly affect the way your engine functions and what you produce. Sacrifices are encouraged, and will need to be made for efficiency. You really get a sense of it's construction as you go through the game, while at the same time having to make difficult decisions whether to build the engine or go for points. A good Euro forces that decision on you at every turn, and Terra Mystica does just that.

comment: The perfect definition for a filler. Games go for 15-25 minutes maximum.  Jaipur is a set collection game and the rules can be learned in under 10 minutes as each player only has 1 of 2 options per turn and only another couple of options under the taking cards option.   The game is really all about hand management as the 7 card hand limit is very important. The game balances risk versus reward by offering up tokens of diminishing value. So you can go after them quickly but doing so means you won't build up a set in that good type to secure the 3, 4 or 5 card bonus scoring tiles.  It all works really well and lives up to the strong rep that I had heard about.   A great 2-player game that my partner loves. The luck factor is about 60/40 but in a game such as this I have no problem with that.

comment: I've been looking at this game for the past 5 years as it has become one of the most beloved heavier Euro games. I'm glad to have finally had a chance to play it. The rules explanation was long (30+ minutes), and I was not completely grasping how all of the many mechanics fit together. However, after the first turn, it (mostly) all clicked and was a blast. I loved the many choices you had each round in balancing which building you had out (and therefore what resources you got each round) and your power pools while racing the other players for space on the board, bonus tiles, and elemental tracks. I would love to play again with the training wheels off to allow everyone their own choice on one of the 14 species.

comment: Wow.   Great 2P card game.  It is the tensest and most engaging experience that you can have with a deck of cards.  If you play the runner (think computer hacker), you'll have the feeling of being a renegade trying to infiltrate the network of an evil corporation.  If you play the corporation, you'll feel the power of trying to make your servers so well protected that no hacker has a chance of accessing anything.  Despite being so different, both sides of the game offer a great experience.  I only have the base game and that is all I plan to use.  6 plays in we've only used one of the runners and one of the corporations so far....with no deck building.  We'll play all the runners/corps and then we'll start some deck-building (thinning and personalizing the deck).  The base game has enough to keep you engaged for months/years.  All my plays have been with my son Dallin.  We've had a great time with this!  Highly recommended.

comment: [2012-02-19] Tényleg jó, de nem annyira, amekkora őrület most övezi. Talán így lehet a legkönnyebben összefoglalni. Hosszabban nincs sok újdonság benne, de jó elemeket sikerült összegyúrni. Galaxis roncsderbis hajóépítés, tikalos felfedezés. Jól kiegyenlített, mégis különböző fajok, jól kitalált fejlődés, fix kör, emiatt lehet körülbelülire játékidőt is becsülni, több út a győzelemhez. Egyetlen negatívuma van a nagy szerencsefaktor. Legjobban a harcban zavart. Hiába jobb sokkal a cirkálóm, ha 1-eseket dobok, játék dőlhet el rajta. Hiába termelek sok építőanyagot, ha nem jut nekem a fő pontot hozó monolit fejlesztésből. Ha nagyon rosszul húzok a felfedezéseim sem érnek annyit, mint másoké. Legjobban a harci szerencse zavart, meg lehetett volna ez jobban oldani. Kevés játékosnál nem feltétlenül van sok harc és egy-egy nagyon sok mindenről dönthet. Illetve kicsit sok fejlesztés van a hajókhoz, talán felesleges volt bele ennyit tenni. Összességében nem rossz játék, sőt mindenképp élvezetes, sok jó mechanizmussal, bárcsak ezt a szerencsefaktor tudnám feledni. Azt még hozzátenném, hogy a sokak által a hosszabb szabálymagyarázat miatt nem bevállalt Starcraftot nem érzem rosszabb játéknak.  [2013-05-04] Második játékra is tetszett, de nem változott a véleményem, nagyon sok helyen benne van a szerencse és kicsit hosszú. 6-an biztos nem ülnék le hozzá.

comment: Talk about diminishing marginal utility.  For those of you weren't econ majors, diminishing marginal utility is the minimizing of enjoyment with each successive action.  Example.  Butterfingers.  Taste great with the first bite, start feeling sticky teeth with second bite, feel like barfing after wolfing down a movie theater sized serving.  Alas, I must compare the classic game of Munchkin to that Bart Simpson staple confection.  After my first playing at the san diego comic-con, where a grizzled, overweight, under-bathed man whipped out a severely wrinkled, kids-sized Munchkin shirt to start the game and said in Simpson's Comic Guy voice "I can attempt to put it on, but it won't be pretty." I would have rated this game an instant 10.  Indeed I bought the game at the convention and picked up the subsequent expansions.  Sadly, with time, the magic of that comic-con moment has slowly dwindled away and has left me with naught but fond memories of my 1st spiked cod piece.

comment: This came back in stock at Miniature Market after being sold out just about everywhere. I jumped on it and believe I'll be super happy with this game. It feels enough like the recent hit with my family and gaming group, Azul, that I am sure it will go over well. However, it is different enough to justify having both! I have gotten to play it and it is a solid game. It didn't knock my socks off, but I had a lot of fun with it. I love drafting in games, so selecting dice in that way was a hit with me. The puzzle of dice placement in your window is also right in my wheelhouse. I tried to be careful, but still accidentally placed one that made an adjacent location impossible (I used a tool to move it though). There really aren't a ton of ways to get points in this game and it's all done at the end, so no one should feel completely out of it. I must say that the dice are a little smaller than I'd like and can make it hard to place in your window at times without bumping the dice near it. Since the pips matter, you really have to be careful or remember what the number was. It plays fast as well with just 10 rounds. The artwork and colorful nature of this game is amazing! What I really like the most is how it uses the difficulty level of the board you use to assign you more/less tokens. Those tokens are how you are able to use the tools in the game to assist with dice placement (break placement rules, move dice, draw a different dice from the bag, and all sorts of stuff). That helps with the harder boards or just give you points at the end for each one you don't end up using. This would be a nice relaxing filler game for me and for gaming with my family.

comment: I'm not usually a fan of tile-placement or overly abstract games but even though this is heavily in both of those camps I absolutely love everything about Tigris and Euphrates.  The design is just so amazingly elegant.  The interaction of the different leaders, different types of conflicts, need to collect points across all colors evenly because you are scored on the lowest, and so much more offers such a breadth of strategy that this is one of the most thinking games I've ever played and I absolutely love every second of it.  The one sorta criticism I have is that despite the simplicity of this game it is difficult to teach to others.  Certain concepts like that you can put your leader in another kingdom and that a kingdom is never really "your kingdom" are difficult to grasp for new players, it's not the average gaming mindset.  And even when you have a firm grasp on all the rules it is a game that is difficult to master, although that's an attribute of a lot of overly abstract games.

comment: That's right, I'm reviewing chess.  How can one review a game that's older than any of our lifetimes, the answer is: Its not easy.  Chess is timeless, It's infinitely complex, has been redesigned component wise more times than god and the depth is astounding. Truly it is the starting point of strategy games, while at the same time the grandfather to so much more.  The pressure on the win and loss stems from a cerebral exercise making it seem like an accomplishment to win (a key factor to the enjoyment stemming from pure strategy).  However I've always found my big determent to chess is the play time.  Chess really isn't that exciting by modern standards (not that its supposed to be).  The endless struggle of attack and defense will carry through history however and as such that says something as a testiment to the game.  All these things considered there's so many other games I would rather play than a game of chess.  Games have since evolved and arched in so many different flavors and since my 6 yearold self I have since lost a taste for it.  That being said, chess gets a 7.

comment: A really innovative card game that is approaching 20 years old and still going strong.  The players are Bean Farmers and need to plant, harvest and trade their way to a gold haul bigger than anyone elses.   The catch here is that the players must hold their cards in a set order that cannot be altered and beans must be planted in a set order too. But fields are limited and a single field can only hold 1 type of bean at a time.   So the players must negotiate and trade away unwanted beans to try and develop well established fields in order to earn a good gold total at harvest time.   This is a great card game and a good social experience in its own right. It was one of the earliest designer games to accommodate up to 7 players but I prefer 3-5 players.   It also plays with 2 but the rules are modified somewhat to offer a slightly different experience.

comment: Enjoyed this a lot more than I expected to. Having the best cards not just be balanced by money but also by the amount of noise you produce that risks hurting you and possibly eliminating you is great, and adds some drama and uncertainty to the game. And this game breaks a cardinal sin of modern game design by having player elimination, but I think it actually gets away with it.  I'm not usually a big fan of deckbuilders nowadays, but mixing it with a board that you can explore really worked out well, I think. As far as I'm concerned, if all the other deckbuilders never existed and this was the only one around, I think I'd be fine with that.  A couple negative points: Sometimes you've got no choice but to have some really boring or lame turns because of how the cards came up (like stumble and make noise, move one space into an empty space, and spend 3 or 4 skill on a card, boo), but that's true of any deckbuilder (although it is one reason why I'm not so keen on them). Also there didn't seem to be anywhere near as many cards that let you permanently trash your starting cards so these lame turns happened a bit more frequently than in other deckbuilders. This could probably be addressed with a couple good promo cards, or maybe they addressed it in Clank in Space, I don't know, I haven't played that one yet.  But overall, I really liked this and at some point I'll be getting a copy for myself.

comment: T.I.M.E Stories is a cooperative puzzle-solving exploration game that can only be played through once by any given group because you'll remember the solutions. The game takes elements from the movie Groundhog Day (or the game Tragedy Looper) in that the group plays through the same scenario multiple times but can do different things each time. However, after a certain amount of time (actions) each play-through will end and you have to start over again. Many challenges (including combat) are dice-based skill checks that can take multiple turns, chewing up your available time. Some are even red herrings that serve no purpose but to waste your time. This particular scenario presented a good entry point to the system, though the theme was a bit macabre. There was one puzzle in the middle that I felt was too much of a head-scratcher. And winning or losing in the end felt a bit arbitrary. This may be one where I like the system better than the experience that the base game scenario provided.  (played the whole scenario)

comment: Doel van het spel:  Wanneer een speler aan het einde van zijn beurt nog 2 ,1 of  0 treinwagons in zijn voorraad heeft, dan begint de laatste ronde. Iedere speler is nog 1 keer aan de beurt (inclusief de speler die het spel beëindigde). De spelers berekenen hun eindscore en de speler met de meeste punten wint het spel. In geval van gelijkstand, wint de speler met de meeste bestemmingskaarten.   Voorbereiding:  + Iedere speler kiest een kleur en neemt zijn 45 treinwagons en een scoresteen (op veld “1” van het scorespoor).  + Schud de treinwagonkaarten en geef iedere speler 4 kaarten. Leg 5 kaarten open en de overige kaarten vormen een gedekte trekstapel.  + Iedere speler krijgt 3 bestemmingskaarten waarvan hij er minstens 2 moet houden.  + Kies een startspeler.   Speelverloop:  Het spel wordt met de wijzers van de klok gespeeld. De speler aan de beurt kan slechts één van de 3 beschikbare acties uitvoeren:   1/ Treinwagonkaarten nemen   De actieve speler kan 2 open en/of gedekte treinwagonkaarten nemen. Bij het trekken van een open kaart, moet de speler direct een nieuwe kaart uit de gedekte stapel neerleggen. Pas daarna kan hij een tweede kaart nemen (geen locomotief van de open stapel).  Wanneer de speler een open locomotiefkaart neemt dan mag hij geen tweede kaart meer nemen.   2/ Een route claimen   De speler claimt een route tussen twee steden door exact het aantal treinwagonkaarten (met de kleur van de route) uit te spelen. Hij plaatst een treinwagon op ieder vakje van de route. De speler is steeds verplicht om de volledige route te claimen. Hij kan iedere, open route op de kaart claimen (hij moet geen verbinding maken met eerder gelegde routes). Na het bouwen van een route ontvangt hij direct punten:  Lengte van de route – punten:  1 – 1 2 – 2 3 – 4 4 – 7 5 – 10 6 – 15  Alle kaarten die nodig waren om de route te bouwen worden afgelegd.   3/ Bestemmingskaarten nemen   De speler trekt 3 bestemmingskaarten waarvan hij er minstens 1 moet houden. De niet-gekozen kaarten legt hij af.  Eindscore = huidige score van de gemaakte verbindingen + punten van de voltooide bestemmingskaarten + 10 punten voor de speler met de langste aaneengesloten route – punten van alle onvoltooide bestemmingskaarten.  Belangrijke regels:  + Bij 2 à 3 spelers kan slechts één dubbele route gebruikt worden.  + Een locomotief telt als een joker en kan een treinwagonkaart vervangen in het bouwen aan een route.  + Grijze routes = de speler bouwt met een kleur naar keuze.  + Een speler kan niet beide routes van een “dubbele routeverbinding” claimen.  + Liggen er 3 locomotiefkaarten in de open trekstapel, dan wordt de trekstapel afgelegd en 5 nieuwe kaarten getrokken.

An amazing puzzle-like experience that plays best with 2 or 3 and may be my favorite game to play alone with the spouse. It's like a game of basketball in that it's high scoring and scores will typically be pretty close, which may be a turn-off for some. Cons: Setup and take-down time is steep and the insert could have used more small compartments. Player interaction is on the low side, but there's so much to think about that I mind even less than usual.  Pros: Plays in about 30-minutes per player, and gives the perfect blend of dice constraining one's choices while still offering many tactical and even strategic decisions.  The basic rules are very simple with the rules complexity coming from the abilities and uses of the many various tile types.  It feels like a race and you'll never get everything done that you want to in the time that you have. If you like strategic, puzzle-like games with a small dose of dice luck and you don't mind games with only indirect player interaction, I highly recommend it!

There is a small amount of interaction, mainly in deciding whether to keep something to benefit yourself or to go with the lesser card in order to deny it to an opponent who needs it more. You also need to plan with an eye on what resources you can buy from your neighbors, and to be prepared to deal militarily with them as well. The game scales pretty well, with a different challenge depending on how many are playing.   While the expansions add variety, the smoothness of the base game gets messed with just enough that I feel the original is the way to go. I keep the expansions to add as a change of pace. comment: I was a little let down by this game.  That's not to say it's not a good game, I enjoyed myself and look forward to playing again (we have a weekly group set up to run through a campaign).  I'm just saying I had lofty expectations of being blown away by it and I simply wasn't.  Part of it might be because my first (finally!) play of the game was just the introductory encounter.  That said though, I've been playing games long enough that I can usually decipher a lot of what I think about a game from a first play, even if it is a "learning game".  Descent is a very simplified and streamlined dungeon crawl.  A scenario is set up, each player plays a hero against an overlord player who manages all the monsters.  Each side has a win condition and heroes have abilities and equipment they can use to their advantage, as do the monsters plus the overlord has a hand of cards that allow him to use special abilities.  All of this fits into the usual fantasy tropes.  Where I was let down was I felt it was a bit TOO simplified and streamlined for my tastes.  Each hero starts with only 1 or 2 abilities and pieces of equipment and when he levels up the choices are pretty scant.  The maps are a bit claustrophobic and the scenarios (I've read through a few, which isn't cheating by the way, there's always 100% open information) are a bit too simple in their goals and how they're laid out.  I'm also a bit worried that it might suffer in the same way Mansions of Madness does in that while this has more content than Mansions it will still run out and playing through the same capaign repeatedly loses some of its flair.  I guess I'm just spoiled by my tabletop and digital RPG experiences but I just wanted more.  That said it still delivers quite a bit of fun and strategic gameplay and dilutes it down to 2 hours instead of 6.  And watching your character grow delivers a little bit of the same rewarding feeling you would get in those other RPGs.  I'm now currently playing as the Overlord and it is a little less fun because I have yet to win (with my other group, as the heroes, we always won as well).  I'm convinced that this game is not very well balanced for the heroes vs. the Overlord and it has a bad rich get richer problem.  Once heroes in this game realize how powerful the items make them they will strive to get all the treasure counters in each scenario and continue to get stronger while the little bit of advancement the Overlord gets in the form of one time use cards they may or may not see does not even out this experience.  Some of the expansions include a little bit more powerful monsters but it is too little, the game is very one sided.  In the end though the amount of content and the game play keeps bringing me back.  I also enjoy the challenge enough and I've come close to winning a couple times so the motivation and hope that I will win at least one quest is still there.  It's just a much more fun game as the heroes and if this sounds incredibly frustrating to you, you should always stay away from the Overlord role.  I FINALLY won one quest, the second half of Death on the Wing.

comment: Very well-designed system that beautifully conveys the time travel theme.  It takes about 4-6 hours to complete a scenario, over the course of up to 3 plays per case.  Very engrossing -- not quite at the level of Sherlock Holmes Consulting Detective, but close.  It mimics the experience of Myst or King's Quest, but is not able to achieve the same kind of depth.  On the other hand, it transforms these solitary experiences into a face-to-face social activity.  Update:  6/7/19  I still like this game after 25-some plays, but my enthusiasm has declined somewhat.  At its best, it is everything I said above.  Unfortunately, some scenarios don’t deliver, and this just makes it repetitive and tedious.  Worse, some scenarios can break, and result in an un-winnable state  (this happened to us with one adventure).  There is also an overarching plot which is big on teasers and mysteries and low on any meaningful payoff from these.  Favorite adventure:  Under the Mask Least liked:  Lumen Fidei, Estrella Drive

comment: A great alternative to Werewolf.  Werewolf is essentially trying to influence a group-think, mob-mentality and progress is made by player eliminations.  The Resistance has no player elimination and is guided by deduction to determine who amongst us are loyal versus traitors/spies, by voting for missions.  Like Werewolf, it is a social-deduction game not unlike poker.  If you are a Werewolf fan, this is an excellent alternative and I'd gladly play both in appropriate gaming situations.  Also, I know many who do not enjoy Werewolf but like this instead.  I really like both and don't see it as similar games, but view both as having social deduction elements/mechanisms (it's akin to saying that Age of Steam and Ticket To Ride are the same b/c they're railroad games, but in my mind, both are very different).

comment: Mixed feelings about this - Agricola is still one of my favourite games, and I really thought I would enjoy this even more. On the one hand I think it's an interesting redesign and I can see why some feel this is an improvement. But to me it also feels overwrought, too fiddly, and just too much like an optimisation puzzle, losing much of Agricola's tension and charm.  In Agricola, I often get a real sense of achievement, whether it's growing the family, baking bread, building a plough, or even just managing to feed everyone, but in Caverna most things are comparatively easy to come by, so there is no such sense of accomplishment, and the feeding phases of the harvest feel like minor inconveniences instead of important milestones that need to be carefully planned around.  Many of the mechanisms are very similar to Agricola (and even more similar to Agricola: All Creatures Big & Small) but with several extra layers of clutter and fiddliness. I feel it would have been better if Caverna had stood a bit further apart, maybe dropping the grain/vegetables, having fewer animals, and focussing more on the digging/gem mining/expeditions. As it is, it falls foul of my increasing distaste for sameyness in games, and I don't think I'll want to bother with it very often. I have a sense of nostalgia for Agricola, remembering how excited I was to play it when it first came out - Caverna does nothing of the sort for me.  Not sure how to rate it - in terms of game quality it's a 9 or 9.5, but in terms of how enthusiastic I am to play it it's only a 6 or so, so I'm settling on the middle ground of 8.
