comment: Love playing this game.  Finally got bought a copy for Christmas 2011.  Yay!  Ok, so I guess the question is why?  Well this was my introduction to board gaming as the Geek knows it and my first worker placement euro game.  You always remember your first time :) The theme, the mechanics, the quality of the pieces and board, even the start player token blew me away.  The theme is set during the stone age and your tribe is competing for resources to help build huts and cultural objects against other tribes.  You do this by sending them of to cut trees for wood, collect stone, gather gold or hunt for food each year.  We're guessing a year, because the other option you have is to expand your tribe numbers by going to the love shack.  Once your tribe has established a number of resources, you can use these to build huts to live in or expand your culture.  How well you do, is measured in victory points, which are tracked as the years progress with some additional VP's earned at the end of the game. The person with the highest VP's win's the game.  There are worker placement games for any theme you can think of, personally, I still like playing this one because you can introduce it to non-gamer friends and still have fun.  The rules are straight forward to explain and the game length is reasonable.

comment: 7 Wonders lasts three ages. In each age, players receive seven cards from a particular deck, choose one of those cards, then pass the remainder to an adjacent player, as in Fairy Tale or a Magic: the Gathering booster draft. Players reveal their cards simultaneously, paying resources if needed or collecting resources or interacting with other players in various ways. (Players have individual boards with special powers on which to organize their cards, and the boards are double-sided as in Bauza's Ghost Stories.) Each player then chooses another card from the deck they were passed, and the process repeats until players have six cards in play from that age. After three ages, the game ends.  In essence 7 Wonders is a card development game along the lines of Race for the Galaxy or Dominion. Some cards have immediate effects, while others provide bonuses or upgrades later in the game. Some cards provide discounts on future purchases. Some provide military strength to overpower your neighbors and others give nothing but victory points. Unlike Magic or Fairy Tale, however, each card is played immediately after being drafted, so you'll know which cards your neighbor is receiving and how his choices might affect what you've already built up. Cards are passed left-right-left over the three ages, so you need to keep an eye on the neighbors in both directions.  Though the box is listed as being for 3-7 players, there is an official 2-player variant included in the instructions.

comment: I remember playing adventure games like Runebound wishing for a decent experience. I think what always killed them was random encounters. Most of those, if not all, are also lifeless dice chuckers.  MK takes deck building and makes it a central mechanic, yet not the entire game. You move, discover, new creatures are put out and you see them from a distance, making planned encounters. You visit locations, and because movement in the game can be fairly liberal, not to mention locations plentiful, there's little "man it's going to take me 5 turns to get all the way over there", it's more like "I can't wait to see what's over here".  Like any other deck builder you can have some soft turns, but because you can retain cards you can build toward more productive combat or purchasing turns. In the interim there are places you can easily sit for valuable resources or places to go and heal; villages are especially nice for the pillaging, IE extra cards for the next turn.  The game will play in about 45 minutes a player, so it's not short yet you are always looking forward to your next turn. There are some seriously creative ways to combo cards and you really do ave to think about the best way to use your hand each turn. One of the best things about hand management is that even is you cannot use a card for its face function it can still be used as a one value of one of four functions.   It's also wild to see the pacing of the rounds as they are dictated by players. Sometimes you want to burn through your deck to rush other players and harm their progress, other times you'd rather let them end the round (since ending the round means you have to skip a turn).   My initial rating was an 8. After a 3p, 2p, and a solo I now give it a 9.

comment: A beautiful looking game, and after our first play everyone was wondering how we could get hold of a copy. Everyone has a unique 5x4 grid with varied dice requirements on it - this spot can only be yellow, this spot a 2, etc - but no die can be orthogonally adjacent to a die of the same colour or number. The aim is to get as many dice out as possible, and over the 10 rounds you claim 2 dice each turn from a draft, settlers-style. Each round your options diminish as to what dice can validly be placed on your board, and the game feels more and more like Take It Easy - how long can you keep your perfect board going. It's got variable Kingdom Builder type scoring options for inter-game variety, a big plus. The only reason for not rating it higher as that I suspect your score can bust pretty easily on the final rounds, out of your control (again, much like Take It Easy). But it's certainly enjoyable in the playing.

And in any case, it usually short enough that the elimination is not a problem.  Part of me yearns for a bit more control of what happens on a turn. Perhaps a way to give a more steady income of energy points (the game currency) so the cards can get into play? It would also be cool to distinguish the monsters from the outset rather than as they buy powers - is it as simple as giving everyone some cash to spend at the beginning? comment: “Ah," she said, "to come is easy and takes hours; to go is different—and may take centuries.”  ― Robert W. Chambers  I had this game sitting in box untested over two years. Finally, during the COVID-19 lockdown had time try it with online version. We started with Path to Carcosa cycle and some preconstructed decks copied from arkhamdb. What a great experience it has been. Carcosa campaign has shown some great writing and story twists.  Game mechanics with some deckbuilding or more of deck evolving included makes you craft the characters to become more unique with also personal weaknesses and traumas building along the journey. It is swingy and sometimes very hard game, as true Arkham game should be.   If you get hooked and go all in, this game can get very expensive for your wallet. comment: This is the Agricola of cooperative games for me.  I love variety and variability in a game and in that respect, this game is after my heart and has claimed it.  First of all, this game is deceptively less complicated than the rulebook and number of components would have you think.  Also, as a cooperative game you simply need one player who knows the rules well enough to "run the game" so the other players can learn by doing.  The amount of variety and variability in just the base game are staggeringly awesome.  There are 16 different characters for players to choose, 8 different Ancient Ones for the players to fight, huge decks of cards for every situation, many locations with special abilities on them.  The rules system, while like I said not that complicated, is also deep and incredibly thematic.  I would expect nothing less from the King of "Ameritrash".  I will say that you probably need more than 2 players to really have a good chance of tackling this game.  While a lot of things in this game scale with the number of players making it seem balanced across all player numbers (for example the number of successes needed to remove a doom token from the Ancient One and monster limits), one thing that you always get with more players is more opportunity to do stuff,  which means closing more gates, killing more monsters, and more time for players to go shopping.  With just two players you fall behind in both closing gates and killing monsters and are too busy mitigating both of these to really collect stuff for the inevitable fight with the Ancient One (you would have to be really talented/lucky to end a 2-player game without fighting the Ancient One).  I think the magic number of players is 4 as going to 5 puts two monsters in play each turn and to that end if you play with two I would play with each player playing two investigators.  5-8 still wouldn't be too bad since each player still gets to take a turn compared to one gate opening every turn (even with two monsters) and has me wonder why you score more for more players.  I personally think greater player numbers and actions each turn outweighs the monster limit/Ancient One combat number especially since these just seem to attempt to balance as the number of players increase.  3 might also be okay, though challenging but I haven't played with this number yet.  Also, the fight with Yig (suggested for a shorter game) feels just a little too truncated to really experience the game.  I would suggest not playing against this Ancient One if you do have the time for a standard length game (2.5-3 hours) as it might end before you really get to take it all in.  And there's a lot of good stuff to take in here.

comment: My rating is for base game + 1st expansion. Add more things and it gets worse imho. (unless you only add like one thing at time but who does?)  Race for the Galaxy shares lots of mechanism with San Juan. It actually seems to have even less interaction with players than it. You do have to be aware what others are most likely to do so you can benefit from it but beyond that you have very little interaction. There is a good layout and symbols on the cards. So you can see easily (once you learn the symbols) what you can do in each phase of the game. Once you have more games under your belt you'll probably start to remember better what bonuses you get in each phase but I had sometimes hard time to remember those.  It is definitely a very good game but it takes the first game to learn the mechanics and it helps when you have idea what type of cards there are in the deck. I won't think it will be a too big hit with non-gamers as it has a quite steep learning curve. RftG is simply a great game with a lot of replayability and as a bonus game is over in a short time with experienced players.  Update: It's a bit different with two players advanced rules as you can do double-developing or -settling and you're able to play consume/produce-cycle all by yourself. Not sure if this breaks anything in the game but it plays a bit differently being still an excellent game. Two-player game works well with the basic rules too.  Update : Tried to play game after a long time with base + first three expansions mixed in. I did not like it. (ofc I did not know rules for at least 1 expansion) but still, there started to be too many cards and too many icons and too much muchness. I try to play with only 1 expansion, preferably first one as it did not mix too many weird things into game. I'd rate that game I played as 7 instead 9 I rate RftG itself.

comment: One of my favorite small, quick, two-player games.  This game for two players only, has players competing as merchants to make the most rupees in a round and the winner is whoever wins 2 out of 3 rounds.  The game consists of a deck of cards and pile of tokens and the gameplay is really simple.  On a player's turn they can collect or sell goods.  Collecting goods is broken down into either picking up a single good, picking up multiples but having to give up an equal number of goods or camels in your herd (the player with the largest herd at the end of a round gets 5 extra rupees), or picking up all the camels in the market.  The earlier you sell any specific goods the more rupees you will get and selling larger numbers at once gets you a rupee bonus.  A round ends when either the deck of cards is empty or 3 of the five goods tiles are exhausted.  I think this game has endless charm, a lot of interesting decisions to be made, and is quick and simple enough to get it up and running even with new players.  Great option for two players looking for something a little lighter and quicker.

comment: Im a huge fun of Lord of the Rings LCG. And I am also love Lovecraft's prose. I had big expectations for this game. And I was not dissapointed after 7 plays in solo mode. This game is more thematic than Eldritch Horror or Arkham Horror board games. Pictures on cards are also at the very high level. But of course, mechanics is the most important in every game. The game rules are easier than in Lord of the Rings LCG. We have only 4 phases in each round.  Unfortunately, the introduction rules sheet are not explaining many important things, and you must often look to extended rules sheet, which is not enjoyable in first games. The chaos bag system is intersting but very random. Comparing to LotR LCG, in Arkham we have far better card drawing system- you can spend actions (which you have 3 in round) to draw a card. And also you draw one card at the end of the round. So, you won't have problems to have good cards in your hand. The deck is limited to 30 cards (+ few additional cards), so it's easy to draw something good. The decks, that you are able to make with only one core set are quite good, which is untypicall to LCG games. Second great thing is that your equipment is limited to two items in hands, one armor, one ally etc. It makes game very climatic, and there will be no situation that you explore a haunted house with 10 person army. Characters that you have in this set, are interesting and useful. So this core set is probably the best of core sets of LCG games.  In this game you can only play in campaign mode. I don't think that's good idea, because you cannot start a random quest with random deck as in Lotr LCG. You must always start for the beginning. I played only 7 times, so I cannot say if it's better than LotR LCG in which I have huge experience. But I think that Arkham Horror LCG is very,very good card game, and probably one of the best climatic games that were already created.

The card drafting provides good interaction, not so much verbally, but in paying very close attention to what other players are doing.  There is also zero individual down time, which is great.  Finally, if you want to get casual gamers into a deeper drafting game, such as 7 Wonders, this is an excellent way to get them fluent with the drafting mechanism making other games much easier to teach.  I would love to see future mini expansions which add a new sushi type and also bump the player count up to 6 or 7.

comment: I owned and occasionally enjoyed the old version for years, which I had rated an "8". Santorini is a very tactical abstract where players control two pawns, and each turn chooses one to move and build. The first player to have a pawn ascend to the top of a three level tower, before the other player can cap it, wins. The game is about maneuvering your pawns and building in such a way as to block the other player so they cannot prevent you from a winning move.  The base game is quite engaging, but I would describe it as more crafty than deep or strategic. The game comes with optional cards that give each player a unique ability, exponentially increasing the replayability. Every different pair of cards used in a given game creates an entirely different experience. The new production with plastic towers infuses a fundamentally themeless game with lots of character.   When my 9-year-old daughter learned this game, she didn't want to stop playing. My wife is both enamored and challenged by it. Truly a game that appeals to just about everyone who doesn't absolutely hate abstracts. I can't see this ever leaving my collection.

comment: Race for the Galaxy is my most played strategic card game. The theme and artwork are really cool, and I like the idea that Tom Lehmann has tried to create a universe to paste on this abstract game. This game offers endless replayability, especially after adding the expansions. The Gathering Storm increased the possibilities of the rules in the core set, and freshened it up without adding game-changing mechanics. Rebel vs Imperium changed a lot, and not for the better; it added a lot of agression, which doesn't work for me in this game. The Brink of War added an enterely new way of scoring points, which makes the game a lot harder, but definately rewards flexible play. This game plays quickly, it is very deep, and makes games such as Puerto Rico and San Juan redundant for me, because the role selection is the most exciting bit of these games. I mostly play this game as a 2P game, using the double role selection variant. I have yet to try out the drafting variant. I am also very curious to see how the new Alien Artifacts expansion will work out; hopefully it will provide some fresh air in a game that has been played to death by my friend and me. UPDATE: I used to rate this game a 9, but it's starting to decrease to a 7: still a great game, but because it is so low on player interaction, I'm enjoying it less than I used to. Also, I'm getting more convinced that this is a better game when only played with The Gathering Storm expansion.

comment: An innovative cooperative game where players must truly cooperate to win.   Players have the simple task of playing cards of matching colors in the correct numerical order. The twist is that no player can look at their own cards, the cards that they are tasked with playing correctly. So they have to decide what to play and when to play it based on clues from the other players. The type of clues that can be given have certain restrictions and the quantity of clues available to the team is restricted so clues must be given and received very efficiently to get the maximum score.   The game is fun and just the right challenge level to keep you coming back for more. The group gets a 'score' based on how many of the cards were successfully played which, combined with the quick play time and interesting/tough choices, makes for an addictive challenge that keeps you coming back for more.

With the maximum of four it can play in about 30 minutes (a little longer if players are unfamiliar with the cards and their interactions but faster if they are well-versed) and is very simple to teach although because of the variety of cards and different factions isn't so simple that it gets uninteresting too quickly.  The references and art are goofy fun but the game is a bit more simple than I like.  I've decided to be okay with that though, for the purpose it serves simple is good.  The box calls this a "shufflebuilding" game, which is a new term to me but I suppose it fits.  It's essentially a deck-building game where you don't build a deck.  You get 40 cards at the start of the game (consisting of two 20-card factions) and draw randomly from that deck of cards and play them to fill up sites.  When they fill up they score the majority owners points (so there's a bit of an area control element as well).  Because of the different factions which play very differently it feels a bit like Puzzle Strike but simpler and quicker to play (and a lot quicker to set up and break down).  With expansions this could grow to be one of my favorite fillers and simple family games.

Όλες αυτές τις πληροφορίες τις κρατάει κρυφές πίσω από μια οθόνη. Κάθε γύρα δίνει σε κάθε παίκτη μια ή και παραπάνω κάρτες-ονειρα (σκεφτείτε ζωγραφιές στυλ dixit) και ο κάθε παίκτης προσπαθεί να βρει τον δολοφόνο που ανατέθηκε σε αυτόν ανάμεσα σε όλους τους υποπτους στο τραπέζι. Αν το βρει μετά προχωρά στη στην τοποθεσία και μετά στο όπλο. Μέσα σε 7 γύρους το πολύ πρέπει όλοι να τα βρούν όλα αλλιώς χάνουν.   Υπάρχει και η τελική φάση όπου το φάντασμα διαλέγει κρυφά ποιανού παίκτη ο δολοφόνος είναι τελικά ο σωστός δολοφόνος και προσπαθεί με 3 κάρτες όνειρα να δώσει στους παίκτες να το καταλάβουν. Σε αυτή τη φάση η κάθε μια από τις 3 κάρτες δίνει στοιχείο για το πρόσωπο την τοποθεσία και το όπλο αλλά οι ντετεκτιβ δεν ξέρουν ποια κάρτα δείχνει τι. Οπότε το συζητάν και καταλήγουν όλοι μαζί κάπου και είτε κερδίζουν είτε χάνουν.          Υπάρχουν και advanced κανόνες με τον κάθε παίκτη να μαζεύει VP ποντάροντας αν ο συμπαίκτης του κάνει λάθος ή σωστά αλλά τους βρίσκω πραγματικά ανούσιους και είναι εύκολο να τους κάνεις game. comment: 50+ plays. Really fun secret identity game of accusation and counter-accusation, with theories being thrown around with gay abandon on who's the baddies and who the goodies. The start player nominates who goes on the next mission, which is then voted on, and who votes yay or nay tells you something. If the majority says nay, the next player nominates a new team for a mission. Once the majority says yay, then the players on the mission vote secretly for success or failure. Any one failure and the mission's a failure. 3 failed missions and the spies win. So the resistance players are desperately trying to work out who they are and get them and only them on the missions. The spies know who each other are, and they're trying to fool the other players into getting a spy or two onto missions so they can shoot the missions down secretly. The game really shines when clever bluff moves happen at the start which set up turmoil later and people are all over the shop. There comes a point where it'll get down to noting hesitations and changes in behaviour in trying to identify the spies. The time value is excellent, and being able to play with 5-10 players is a big plus as not many games do that well.

The number of actions stays constant, but I think it's slightly less tight than Agricola, making it tense without being frustrating and also avoiding the disappointing feeling you get in Agricola at the end where you feel that you're finally able to get somewhere but too bad the game is over.  I also give it high marks for player interaction, since you use (and block) other players' buildings.  The only downside is that it is a bit on the longer side. comment: Rating after 4 plays.  It's an excellent efficiency engine game, if that's your bag. In some ways, there's even less player interaction than Puerto Rico (which is bad).  However, the multitude of ways you can get your engine working, and the replayability due to the sheer number of cards makes it really stand out.  If you don't like this kind of game, stay far away.  If you do, give it a try.  I'll be re-evaluating my rating after several more plays, to see if it has staying power.  Update 1: It's 4 years after Agricola's release and I still love this game.  It's infinitely replayable, plays in a good timeframe, has an interesting mix of decisions, etc.  Update 2013 July:  Moved to a 10.  I never tire of this game.  I only have about 20-30 plays, so I'm not nearly as burned out as some people may be.  I imagine enjoying this for years to come.

comment: Funkenschlag (2nd ed) was among the heavier and lengthier German games of its time. It does not have particularly complex rules, nor does it offer deep strategic possibilities. However, on a tactical level it really shines. In my first few games Funkenschlag seemed to be mainly about careful turn-by-turn management of resources in order to optimise your position, with some possibility for affecting other players through e.g your decisions on where to build. But with experience, I began to appreciate the more subtle tactical possibilities (which revolve around the mechanics of determining player order, the effect of player order on which power stations you can put up for auction, the mechanics of the fuel market etc). Despite a certain amount of simple number crunching, this game can generally be completed in around 2 hours. Funkenschlag has a great theme, more than adequate components, and the double-sided board adds some variety. Small gripe: electricity grids do not consist of rusting metal pipes (where are the pylons?). UPDATE: It is now 15 years old, and doesn't manage to hold a top spot compared to contemporary games.

comment: GWT offers a circular, rondel-esque action structure that players build with action tiles as the game progresses. While the trail of actions is one way, it always ends in a delivery of cattle and then starts over again. Players cycle through about 5-7 times before the end conditions are met.  The structure of the game is simple and once you get going the game plays fast. However, there are a lot of options and a lot of symbols to learn, so the game may appear a little daunting at first. While there are many ways to get points, there are few key sources where the majority of points will come and how you choose to focus on these areas is the key to doing well. Players are managing and improving a deck of cattle cards that represent their herd. Building your herd and managing your hand to optimize cattle deliveries is one source. Another is advancing your train to better and better stations. Putting out more of your buildings (action spaces) is another possible source. And another source is gaining and playing goal cards. There are a number of other secondary ways to collect points. If you balance your focus between all of the main sources, you are unlikely to do well. As with a lot of these games, the key is optimizing your decisions to primarily support one or two of these sources while keeping an eye on your opponents and hindering them when you can.  While at first glance a mechanical mish-mash, Pfister has done a very good job of melding the various elements into a cohesive whole.  (Reminder to pick up fixed tile when Stronghold makes it available...)

Nagyon jó hangulatot adnak a kártyák címei és szövegei, teljesen bele tudja magát élni a játékos a hidegháborús történelmi helyzetbe. comment: Not a big fan or miniatures or pre-game element selection type stuff, but this played ok and I enjoyed it enough that I'd play again if someone else who was into it set up the scenario. Eerily similar in concept to Ace Of Aces and Wings Of War et al, as you'd expect, in that you secretly plan your maneuver and speed and then reveal / execute. It has a nice twist in that the best pilots move last and shoot fast, giving a double whammy. So a lot of the game is about guessing, double-guessing and then out-guessing where your opponent will go, aiming to have him in your sights and range after all the moves are done. If you did a normal move (as opposed to a high-stress move), you'll get to do an action, either a bonus mini-move or get a dice-manipulator token. The latter of which helps when you fire, which is a straight dice roll looking for hits, up against a defensive dice roll hoping for evades to cancel the hits. Play 'til things are blown up basically, unless you're playing a mission-type scenario. As such it's pretty clean and I'd say an improvement on the other games mentioned before. But the guts of it is out-guessing, which doesn't hold a lot of interest for me. The attraction is obviously how it brings the theme to life (even if it is at 1/50th normal movie speed) which it succeeds at, but not enough for me to invest.

comment: Underrated on BGG due to bias about gamers' childhood experiences with it and misconceptions about best strategies and luck. Dice-rolling combined with the unpredictability of other players' actions does mean that even the best of players will lose often. Tactical tip: never attack 2 armies against 2 unless you're desperate, as that is the only case where the odds favor the defender.  The game is all about maintaining balance while trying to keep yourself in a slightly stronger position. Just blobbing up and taking one arbitrary territory per turn is not a strong strategy. (It's preferable, though, to spreading yourself too thin, which new players tend to do.) If the game becomes unbalanced, one player will handily win, which means poor moves by players can "ruin" a game, but that's just part of the fun (don't take Risk seriously!). You have to wait for the perfect moment to use your card trade-in to wipe out another player, take his or her cards, turn them in again for more armies and start a chain reaction in which you conquer every player in the same turn, moving from weakest to strongest.  Version notes: until 2003, you had to have 6+ cards for a mid-term trade in, but Hasbro revised the rules a decade ago to reduce it to 5+. This shortens the length of the game because it makes it easier to start and maintain the chain reaction (it's also more logical). Hasbro also removed the rule that allows you to put 2 bonus armies on a single territory whose card you turn in. That rule was not part of the original rules when the game came out, and at one point the rules allowed you to put 2 bonus armies on all the territories whose cards you traded in! Removing this rule slightly reduces the significance of luck, which is good.  Parker Brothers.

comment: This is an area majority game in its purest form - have the most caballeros (knights) in a region and score the most points there in one of three scoring rounds.  But it's not so simple - getting your caballeros onto the board and moving them around requires picking the right action cards at the right time.  Timing is determined by playing a "power card" to determine turn order for the round.  Each player selects an available action card and plays it.  Complicating matters is the king - wherever he is, you can't play, but you must enter the board on adjacent provinces.  The very cool twist is the castillo (castle) - there are majority bonuses in this hidden chamber as well.  But before it's scored, players secretly select a region to send their caballeros to after scoring.  That mixes things up when regions are scored!  For a relatively simple game, there's a lot to think about.  Generally I just found it to be fun - something that gets lost in games sometimes.  Definitely looking forward to future plays of this older classic.

comment: Looking for a simple game that all mystery and horror fans can play and enjoy? Probably you are in the right place. Betrayal at house on the Hill is an easy to learn game that offers 50 horror stories to play! Thus, no one can complain about the replayability of the game. Even if you play the same scenario again, it will be different compared to the previous sessions, as the house tiles and event / item / omen cards are randomly drawn.  In my turn I simply move my character from room to room. When I reveal a new room, I place a new house tile and I usually draw a card that matches the room’s symbol (omen, item or event). Then I follow what the card says and that’s it. It is common a card to ask for a check in one or more of my characterer’s traits, which are Might, Speed, Sanity and Knowledge. In such a case, I roll the corresponding number of dice and I see what happens depending on the result. The fun part begins when the haunting of the house is revealed. Every time a player draws an omen card, he have to make a haunt roll. This means that he rolls 6 dice (result 0-2 on each die) and if the sum is less than the total number of omen cards in play, then the haunting is revealed. One player becomes the traitor and his purpose is to kill the others or prevent them from put an end on the haunting, while the other players (survivors) are stuggling to survive and stop the evil plans. There are two books, one for the traitor, one for the survivors, which describe what is the story and what should be done by the players.  In order to enjoy this game, all players have to be in the right mood and like this horror / mystery stuff. I don’t recommend this game for players that want absolute control, as there are too many random elements. Sometimes a scenario is ruined by the game itself due to high randomness. For example, it may end too soon, even in the first or second turn after the haunting. My advice is not to take this game seriously and just play and see what happens like watching a movie but in this case the star is you!  Keep in mind that good knowledge of English is necessary by all players.  (+) Atmospheric gameplay Replayability Easy to learn, even by non-gamers Beautiful tiles and painted miniatures Plays well with any number of players  (-) Simple tokens with no artwork Some scenarios need errata and clarifications
name: Betrayal at House on the Hill

comment: Star Realms really surprised me. I had only heard it in passing in a Rahdo review before someone bringing out their set at Kingdom Con. I love Dominion & deck builders and always am willing to try a new one. I thought that this felt like a lot of games already, like Ascension with its multiple currencies and how you buy new cards from the common pool pulled off the big deck and Legendary with its chaining of hero power activations. The life total and attacking people directly with one of the currencies felt fresh enough that it stood out. The game also has space stations which act as buffers that have to be attacked first or add special abilities. All in all I had a great time and really enjoyed the multiplayer variants. We did 2-headed (2 on 2) and a variant where you only attacked to the right; both lots of fun. The game is also cheap enough (~$16?) that I'll definitely be picking up a copy. My criticisms is that the number of ships available often feel very limiting where there is typically only one or two real choices to be made and later in the game your deck is mostly playing itself as you draw (which is a criticism of any deckbuilder but I felt it here more than most). This automation may be worse with repeated plays, but I definitely had fun while I was playing it.

Around 4-5 hours per play, and we were playing the 'shorter' two day scenarios like Blitz Conquest, with only 3 players.  About the only long games I like are this, Die Macher, and Through the Ages.    The theme is excellent, and all of the game mechanics are exceptional.  I love the mana management, the deckbuilding, the hand management, and the wide variety of options available.  There are also tons of different scenarios, so you can tweak the game to your desires.   I love that you have options to do all sorts of things, even pillaging villages and burning down monasteries, and that these are sometimes or often good decisions, not just automatically terrible.  (Especially village pillaging, I feel is a critical part of strategy).  I ended up loving this game and wanting to repeatedly play it again, in spite of an enormous playtime, and thats extremely rare for me.   Update:  With 3 experienced players I've played Blitz conquest now in 3 hours.  Still too long but not by as much.

comment: Excellent base system that allows for a great variety of thematic action without excess complexity. Instantly vaults to one of my favorite FFG titles. However, the disappointing LCG selling model is really not much better than a CCG.  It builds upon and streamlines some familiar elements from the FFG design book and I won't go into those basics here. There are two primary elements that make this game really sizzle in my opinion. #1 is the race aspect of players trying to meet the objectives of the scenario, called "Acts", before the forces of darkness complete their Agendas. While there is a standard way that both of these clocks advance, scenarios can define their own methods for advancing Acts and Agendas that are appropriately thematic to the story. This race element puts fantastic pressure on the players to fulfill the Acts quickly. The #2 aspect of the game worth highlighting is the location system. The board is an array of cards depicting locations that characters can visit. There are symbols on the cards that show which locations can be reached from other locations. As Acts or Agendas complete, locations can change or disappear while new ones materialize. Locations start face down, so there is an element of exploration when you visit one for the first time.   While we've seen the LCG deck-building before, health and horror trackers, the investigative story-telling, the bag draw for determining chance outcomes - wrapping it together with a thematic game clock and a crafty card-based location system makes this a solid thematic experience where players have real decisions and options to prioritize.

Then a friend mentioned he ALWAYS plays with the following two variants: 1. The center goal card is 1 additional space away (8 instead of 7 - the top and bottom are still 7); 2. If the non-saboteurs win, they only get to share in the gold if they have no remaining broken tools at the end.  Rule 2 is huge -- this causes the good dwarves to turn on each other towards the end and can make it harder to identify the saboteur.  It also keeps people from piling all their attack cards on the suspected saboteur - they want to save some to help get richer.  Much more fun, much better game now.  I also recommend playing with at least 5 to get the potential for 2 saboteurs.

Not necessarily in the sense that everything is happening at once like in Warhammer, but more encapsulates how flanks operate, suppressing fire, and looking for an enemies' weak spot. Certain units may move and fight more than others, based on terrain, or suppressing fire, stamina, morale or choke points. But none of this needs pages of rules to simulate; rather, the gameplay itself brings to life these variables, with card play and tough player decisions. Memoir 44 might seem like a mere gateway war game, but there is so much depth there.

comment: This is a fantastic tableau civilization game with a simple simultaneous card drafting mechanic.  The game's theme is reinforced by the spectacular art of scenes from ancient near eastern and early western empires. I like how each player gets a different wonder with its own distinctive resource production and special wonder-building objectives. Far from a multi-player solitaire, I like that 7 Wonders keeps you on your toes by watching your neighbors tableau on the table closely from which you can purchase resources that you do not own as well as spy on their military strength compared with your own.  My wife and I also appreciate the advanced 2 player variant included in the base game which plays with a 3 player game but with a ghost player.  Best of all, this game plays in 30-45 minutes after the first couple plays and has helpful reference sheets to mitigate the various symbols on each card.  I hope to play the subsequent expansions in the near future.

comment: Fun bluffing game.  You don't assume a role in this game (like The Resistance), you have two cards in front of you which give you two 'special powers.'  Your cards are not known to the other players, so you can claim 'special powers' that you don't actually have.  If someone challenges you and you are bluffing, you have to turn one if your cards face up (if you weren't bluffing, then the challenger needs to turn a card face up).  If both your cards are face up, you lose that round....so don't bluff too much!  Recommended.  Only downside is there is a little bit of a barrier to entry.  It'll take a game or two to get a feel for how to effectively play the game.  But I suppose that is par for an hidden role game.

comment: As with any dice game, there's definitely a randomness to KoT.  However, I think it works well with the fast and chaotic theme.  This isn't a strong strategy game, per se, although there certainly is some decision making.  I tend to really enjoy it because of the fun theme and great art, fairly fast play, and the fact that it plays up to 6 players.  If you like games like Martian Dice or Zombie Dice, I look at this as a much better multi-player implementation of something like that.  You're still just rolling dice and hoping, but there's enough strategy mixed in to keep it engaging.  I do have a hard time with the player-elimination aspect, but it's usually a short enough game that this isn't a notable problem.  Unfortunately, most of the gamers I've played with don't seem to enjoy it as much as me, but as a family game or just something to bring out with a group of casual friends, it seems to go over very well.

comment: It's a neat, light exploration game which goes from "individual" gameplay and shifts into a "team/co-operative" style by rolling into a randomly determined monster scenario (of which there are 50 different types).  This is probably it's best feature, so depending upon which scenario/special monster turns up, and which player becomes the traitor, nearly every game is different with a different set of winning conditions.  The board tiles are modular so the haunted house is also different every time.  There is, with this kind of game, of course, a fair amount of randomness but also some "luck by preparation" as well.  This game reminds me a great deal of another haunted house tile-laying game, Chill Black Morn Manor, but this is much better as it's more balanced, rules are clearer/better and it is a cool "magic fun house" romp creating a fantastical haunted house with lots of fluff.  This may also possibly draw comparisons with Fury of Dracula and Buffy the Vampire Slayer games.  I really enjoy the quick gameplay and especially the theme as light games go.

I still find time monthly to meet up with the same people I originally started playing with and we play a few hands of Magic between board games.  It is basically our permanent go-to filler game.  The one big negative I see with it is the cost... especially if you are seeking some of the older, rarer cards. comment: This game is an area control and faction management game with little splashes of tons of other mechanics added to it.  There is some exploration, combat, and hidden objectives sprinkled in here as well as tons of other stuff.  This game absolutely blew me away.  I had a feeling and actually splurged for the second best edition of the game which included everything except the art book and even not getting that is seeming like a mistake with how beautiful this game is.  While we are on the subject let's talk about the game's art.  It seems like a great place to start because the story I've heard is this game came into being based solely on the beautiful art by Jakub Rozalski.  The designer wanted to use that art in a game and built around it.  On top of which with the Deluxe edition of the game I have a board extension to make the board even larger, nice chunky resource tokens to replace the cardboard, and metal coins.  The game looks absolutely amazing and there is a different piece of artwork on each of the encounter cards.  My personal favorite part is the pairing of this beautiful artwork with humorous satirical descriptions of your options when you draw an encounter card.  Everything from gaining popularity for your long, flowing hair fluttering in the wind to pushing an innocent cow under a marauding mech.  So enough about how the game looks, how does it play?  Incredible.  Which I have to admit when I heard that the game started with art and the gameplay was built around that I was somewhat skeptical.  But the game is almost perfectly designed.  First of all each player has their own faction and player board.  These vary slightly to greatly depending on what portion you look at but they all seem pretty well balanced.  That is not a minor task, being able to offer depth and breadth in play so the game has replayability while also balancing it all.  On top of which with so many of those mechanics sprinkled in there are a ton of ways to approach the game and win.  Something that stood out is in my first game I placed the final achievement star which immediately ends the game.  In theory this meant I did more than my two opponents, my closest competitor still had 2 fewer than me.  I still only came in second however.  There is a popularity track that gives more points based on the tier you are in and I was one tier lower.  Even with "doing less" he got more value out of what he did and beat me.  I lost but I love that the game doesn't have a runaway leader or lock to it that many other, even good, games have.  That is something else  very, very hard to design for.  Between just wanting to stare at this game and all the many ways you can play and the variability and replayability it offers this has immediately become one of my favorite games.

comment: While set in the same universe as The Resistance, and containing deduction and hidden roles, Coup is much closer to a game of BS than a game of Werewolf. Players each receive two hidden roles (out of a possible five). Each role provides a specific powerful action to the player. A player's turn simply consists of taking one of these actions.   The catch is that a player can take any action they choose, regardless of what roles they actually possess. It then becomes incumbent on the other players to decide whether or not to call the bluff. If a bluff is called, either the caller or the call-ee will lose one of their roles. It stays face up on the table for all to see. If a player loses both his roles, he is eliminated from the game.   Games take under 15 minutes to play and provide some wonderful group dynamics. I like the moment that happens when someone takes the perfect action for the situation and no one at the table believes it but no one wants to call them on it either, so they just get to do it while everyone else looks at each other disgustedly. It almost has to be played multiple times in a row as players learn both the interactions of the cards themselves as well as their interactions with each other. This is a great example of a game that plays much "bigger" than the rules or components would suggest; the game is really all about the people playing it.

comment: 規則: *把對應的16個混亂標記丟到袋中，選一張戰役卡，拿對應的場景卡(有對應符號的特定牌組)，把議程卡照數字跟英文字小到大疊起，並根據1a處理劇情，同樣設置設置行動卡，該戰役的場景參考卡放一旁，將書房放入(有鑰匙孔面)，其他會使用的地點卡放一旁，將玩家腳色小卡放在書房旁，書房翻面，幾個玩家就放置左邊線索數幾組，剩下的場景卡全部洗勻 *每個人選擇一個腳色，並選一個人當主導者，根據腳色洗勻起始牌組(使用左上沒有升級標記的牌)，每個人拿五個資源標記，然後抽五張牌，如果抽到弱點牌，先放一旁繼續抽，只後洗進去(每個人可重抽特定張數一次，把最多五張放一旁在抽到五張，放一旁得洗進去) *任何規則處理如果不確定都傾向於對玩家造成最大傷害的選項 *遊戲主要目的是要結算行動卡，並進入下張，如果議程卡被結算通常是負面的，玩家全部死亡也要看參考卡來講述結局 *照順位時由主導玩家開始順時鐘結算，調查員頭像代表該數值要乘上玩家數 *要做技能測試時，從混亂袋中抽一個標記，跟調查員該技能加總，超過或等於就成功，在抽前可棄牌使用左上標記增加該技能數值，測試玩家可用多張，其他同地點玩家一張，或是使用調查員能力，結算完後所有出的牌棄掉，混亂標記丟回袋中 *玩家如果抽到弱點卡就馬上結算 *遊戲進行數輪，每輪有四個階段 1.神話階段(第一輪跳過) >放一個末日標記在議程卡上 >比較末日標記數目跟議程卡左下數字，超過或等於時結算該卡，翻面結算開下一張，末日標記棄掉 >照順位每人抽一張遭遇卡並結算之，敵人卡直接遭遇該腳色(除非有重生點敘述)，叛變卡結算 2.調查階段  玩家自行決定行動順序，每個調成員有三個行動點，行動如下，如果遭遇敵人的話，執行戰鬥逃離跟戰鬥相關能力以外的行動會導致被敵人攻擊 >抽一張牌 >獲得一個資源 >啟動一個花行動的能力，可能在各種卡片上 >遭遇一個同地點的敵人，將敵人放在自己的威脅區(可遭遇在隊友威脅區的) >調查該地點 做一次書本測試，總數值大於該地點左邊數字則成功，拿一個線索標記 *花線索來完成行動卡不算是行動，所有玩家可以一起支付，在任意玩家回合都可以做，行動卡翻面結算後打開下一張 >移動到相鄰的地點 地點相鄰與否看卡牌的下方對應卡牌的左上，到為探索過的地點就翻開，放對應線索標記 *如果移動時有敵人在威脅區，敵人會跟著過去，每個地點只要有未橫置的敵人都會馬上遭遇該地點的調查員，多人則領導者決定 >出一張資產或事件卡 支付卡片左上費用，事件卡結算後棄掉，資產卡放腳色旁，有迅速特性的卡不花行動，腳色除手跟秘笈可裝兩張以外，其他一張，不夠格則棄掉一張 >逃離一個遭遇的敵人 做一次敏捷測試，對應敵人卡最右邊數值，成功敵人卡橫置放到腳色地點卡旁 >跟同地點敵人戰鬥 攻擊同地點的敵人，使用拳頭測試，成功敵人受到一點傷害(敵人卡中間是血量)，傷害超過血量則敵人卡棄掉，有分數的保留一旁，如果失敗且該敵人跟另一位調查員遭遇，則該調查員受一點傷害 3.敵人階段 >未橫置的有獵人特性的敵人往有調查員的地點移動一格，如果遇到調查員馬上遭遇之 >所有在威脅區的敵人做一次攻擊，使用卡片下方的血量跟恐懼值，放到對應腳色上，攻擊完的卡橫置，如果有資產上面有血量也可放傷害，放滿就要棄掉 4.維持階段 >所有調查員卡重置，橫置卡也轉正，所有未遭遇的敵人卡如果地點有調查員就遭遇之 >每個調查員抽一張牌跟獲得一個資源 >手牌超過八張的棄掉 ****組牌規則*** *選腳色，腳色有卡牌張數限制，弱點，調查員專屬卡跟場景卡不再此限 *只能選角色卡後面有的卡單，每種卡最多兩張，戰役模式時只能包含等級0的卡 *基礎弱點卡洗勻抽一張洗進去 *卡片等級從左上數字圓環內的白點個數看 ***戰役規則*** *使用對應的幾張場景卡，根據選擇的難易度放對應的混亂標記到袋中 *根據對應場景設置並進行遊戲，根據戰役內容結算最後結果 *進入下個場景前可用經驗值買道具或能力，要保持牌庫大小，有些卡可升級，花費基本上都是左上白點的差值，買牌也是 *死亡的腳色除非規則特別說 否則就獲得創傷繼續進行到下個場景

comment: Managed to play Clank at PAX West 2016 before its release. It's a really fun game, most similar to Tyrants of the Underdark. A deck builder with dungeon exploration and a very fast learn. The only flaw is that players can be eliminated randomly and quickly, and they have to sit out and watch the entire rest of the game without participation.   What's worse, the press your luck element goes a little bit too far and says that players that die on the bottom half of the map have a score of ZERO at the end of the game, and thus already automatically know they lost, so they don't even have interest in the end result of the game.  I'd like to see a fan-made module to add or an expansion that allows dead players to interact with the game in a meaningful way. I'd also like to see this module provide a path for deceased players to be able to win the game, even if that path is more difficult and unlikely.

comment: Over ten rounds, players draft up to twenty rolled dice (out of 90) of colors chosen randomly from a bag to place on a grid with defined set of requirements and certain restrictive placement rules. The grid sheets are of varying levels of difficulty, requiring colors on some squares and numbers on others. The harder the sheet, the more action tokens a player receives. Action tokens are used to activate three tool cards that allow you to move dice on your grid, sometimes ignoring placement restrictions. After ten rounds, players are scored based on 3 community goal cards and one private goal card.  I enjoy light abstracts on occasion, but because you are drafting rolled dice, the amount of control you have here can feel very limited, even for a light abstract. The biggest constraint is not the requirements sheets, but the fundamental requirement that you cannot place the same number or color orthagonally adjacent. You always need to keep this in mind when placing next to a grid sheet requirement space and in some cases you need to use tool cards to maneuver dice in order to enable a legal placement. In placing the last few dice, it always seems to come down to drawing the right colors and rolling the right numbers. I suspect I'm bumping my score on this a point because of the production. Pure game play would be a point lower.

comment: Battlestar takes the semi-cooperative, "There's a traitor (or two) among us" mystique of Shadows over Camelot and fixes many of the problems with its medieval predecessor. By making the [-]Progression of Evil[/-] Crisis step often a group task, it eliminates the lengthy downtime that can come with games of 5 or more players. By giving Cylons their own section of the board with various powers, it eliminates the often-boring "Add a siege engine, steal a card" revealed-traitor step of SoC. Instead of accusations, people are throwing each other into and out of the Brig left and right, and stripping each other of their titles. The Brig itself is a bit like the Captured! card from Shadows over Camelot: Merlin's Company but without the possibility of throwing a player out of the game for an hour or so by allowing them limited interaction and their own attempts to leave. Making most of the important information on the board (rather than what's in people's hands) makes table-talking much less tempting and necessary-feeling than SoC and keeps people from being mindlessly stuck on the same quest for several turns. Finally, Executive Orders make accomplishing things more possible even when there's five people between you and your next turn. (As an aside, I appreciate that I, someone who has never seen the show, could enjoy this game as much as those who did. Sure, the quotes and flavor text were lost on me, but the game itself was still incredibly fun; I didn't feel left out by my lack of familiarity with the source material at all.)  The game isn't without its flaws. First and foremost, it could've used a few more weeks in playtesting and editing. The rulebook makes finding certain rules a chore, especially since it has one of the most useless indices I've encountered. Some post-publication FAQs REALLY should have been caught before the game came out (how did NO ONE notice the Executive Order loop?). Fighting [-]siege engines[/-] raiders is a bit boring compared to other things you could be doing, and you get sort of stuck out in space--it's not worth spending an entire turn coming back to the ship to do something else. Also, since everything in space disappears whenever you jump and pilots get shunted back into the hangar, it can often feel, as a pilot, like you were just about to blow up some serious Cylon butt when you get teleported back into the ship. And again. And again. So being a pilot's a bit thankless. But overall the flaws are few, and the game is addictive and really well-done. My rating's currently a 9 for it--tied with SoC--but I can see that increasing as I see if I feel the same after more plays.

comment: Arkham Horror Light, best with upto 4 players. This player restriction is in part due to the rumour cards which increase in difficulty based upon the number of players and is one of the weaker aspects of the game.  Having got a few plays under my belt, I can say that I prefer this to Arkham Horror (AH).  My reasoning is that each investigator is potentially equally effective.  What I mean by this is that in AH, players typically become type cast, e.g. magic casters attack magic monsters and melee characters attack melee monsters, in order to use the teams resources efficiently. Within Eldritch, your character starts with stats which mean they are less likely to succeed various skill checks but through items and skill enhancements this evens itself out more. Therefore each person's character is of equal value to the success of the mission and, teaming up is possible and at times a requirement. The turns are also streamlined , although I fear that further expansions from FF may change that. The choosen one who must be defeated also feels unique each time and their effects on the players and the world add flavour to each game.  Finally, the coolest thing is the reckoning.  Players are no longer restricted by money by way of improving their character's belongings.  They can choose to take a debt card for example.  Life goes on for said player, until the reckoning.  At this point, all cards in play with the reckoning icon are resolved. You thought making a deal with those unsavoury characters in order to get that shot gun was a good move.  Well, its pay-back time. If this could be expanded somehow to include skill upgrades, this would make a future expansion even more fun.  In Cthulhu style, where every ability comes with a cost, the path you choose is defined by your actions.  This can lead to some damned if you do and damned later if you don't choices. Making each reckoning unique is  pure genius.  Dark Pact cards being some of the toughest to endure.  For example, with the option of being effectively devoured or given a dark pact card, our hero takes the dark pact.  Only two turns later failing the reckoning roll and having to choose another player to be devoured.

comment: Oh Arkham, I will never stop singing your praises.  So, in the interest of full disclosure: I love co-op games.  If you do not like co-op games, please remove yourself from the vicinity of Arkham Horror.    Okay, now, let's get this out of the way.  There are flaws in Arkham Horror.  Even one who loves it as much as I has to admit this.  The rules are numerous and have strange facets and interactions that could fill a novel with errata and FAQs.  There are seventeen gazillion little fiddly bits, so you will need lots of plastic bags and/or pill cases and/or fishing tackle boxes.  FFG churns out expansions for this at a steady pace, meaning that if you're a completionist or an expansion addict (Hi, that's me), you will be broke and have a closet taken up by this game alone.  Finally, it's lengthy; it often takes 3-4 hours, and can easily exceed that when you're playing with near the maximum number of players.  Now, on to the good stuff.  This game drips with theme and tension.  It can be brutal when you're unlucky, and brutal even when you're lucky (though sometimes, mysteriously, goddesses and gods will smile on you and you will have a smooth game).  There are tons of decisions to be made, and it's often never clear which is the right choice.  This makes it, I think, more enjoyable for newbies than some other co-ops, because there's a lot less of the "Loudest and most analytical person running everyone else's turn" problem.  It's hard to say "You should go here and do this" when, really, anywhere you go could either kill you or give you a great item depending on whether the game hates you or not (Hint: it hates you).  You have to approach it as a fun experience and be ready to lose.  Like a good role-playing game, you leave with lots of funny and exciting memories that you can be discussing for weeks to come (like the time your investigator nearly threw themselves into a well to their death on their FIRST ENCOUNTER, or the time your investigator got beaten up by a monster and woke up in the hospital with.. Tuberculosis?!?).  I love this game so much. :3  COLORBLINDNESS NOTE:  There is some necessary color-distinguishing going on here, but it's a co-op, which makes asking someone or putting someone else in charge of the color-dependent parts fairly easy.  In particular, Arkham location encounter and Other World gate cards are color-coded.  The former I've managed to adapt to by getting good at matching the pictures of the locations on the backs of cards rather than colors--this is a fairly necessary move since the colors are often very similar shades of blue-purple versus straight purple or yellow-green versus sickly yellow.   The Other World cards come in four colors--red, green, blue, and yellow--with no other pictures for distinguishing.  Luckily, I find that they're pretty bright shades that I can tell apart, but people with more advanced red-green colorblindness may have trouble.  UPDATE 3/3/09:  Okay, I finally admitted it.  I downgraded AH from a 10 to a 9.  I have to admit that there are a few problems with the game that are really starting to impede my enjoyment. 1) The difficulty is incredibly inconsistent.  We win some games without breaking a sweat.  Others are long, tense, wonderfully drawn-out battles.  Others are forgone conclusions that manage to still stretch over hours.  It's hard to convince myself to spend the large amount of time to teach, setup, and play the game when I'm not even sure if it will be hard enough to feel climactic and enjoyable.  2.) Fiddliness.  This is FFG at the height of their bizarre obsession with overproduction.  Setup and tear-down take FOREVER.  Digging through billions of chits--and, yes, I'm well-organized, it's not like I have them all in a giant heap--gets annoying.  It's not a game-breaking problem but it's frustrating.  If I had a devoted cat-free room where I could leave the game set up I wouldn't be so bothered, but, y'know.  Not that rich. Yet.  3.) Occasionally stagnant.  This goes with the inconsistent difficulty thing.  There will be times where the game just.. sits.  You're at more or less an impasse--no one has any good options, they're trapped behind monsters and constantly being sent to the hospital or something, and yet the game isn't advancing, no new gates opening.  Maybe it's clear that you're going to lose or win, but it could take another hour to get there, even if only the most wild act of [deity] could change that.  It occasionally goes on far too long in this way.   I still love the game.  It's still a great -experience-, but as a game it has some serious downsides, and some more recent co-ops (particularly Ghost Stories) have hurt my desire to play Arkham as much.

comment: On our 14th box.  Tried sleeving the cards once, but just to hard to shuffle and since we play daily, it's so much faster to shuffle without the sleeves. A beautiful game that is easy on the eyes.Always the game that goes on trips.   I have played almost 10,000 games (each game, 3 hands) since 5/2000.  I do not have that many plays recorded here on BGG because we started playing prior to my recording plays here in 2004, but my husband kept records on paper.  The first decade we played every morning & night.  These last 8 years, just once a day.    (How can I not rate a game a 10 when I have played this many times with my husband--it is one of a dozen games he will play.)  Can't Stop is another he will play regularly.  Once two players are equal in strategy, it becomes more a luck-of-the-draw game, but still addicting.  This is one of the few games my non-gamer family suggests--and since I am game-hungry, I never turn it down.   Highest score after 3 hands, 337 on 1/18/09; Highest score on a single color in one hand, 136 on 12/06; Most games won in a row, 11 on 5/07; The difference of most points in the lead after 3 hands, 227 on 11/05.  I lost the records for the single highest hand.  We lost interest in keeping up on these scores, especially since our playing has evolved so that we rarely get the really high scores any more.  Despite all these games played, I have only played once with four people (combine part of a 2nd deck per rules).

comment: Full Review: http://manualgamer.com/king-of-tokyo-review/  Tokyo smashing goodness!  In King of Tokyo, players get to be giant monsters rampaging through Tokyo, causing as much chaos and mayhem as possible.  It is fast, fun and fantastic for families and casual gamers.  Essentially, it is Yahtzee with giant monsters and super powers.  Fun and light, with different strategies depending on what others are doing, and the cards that are available.  Shall I rush Tokyo and smash down my opponents?  Shall I sit in the background and go for point victory?  Shall I power up my character with various abilities?  King of Tokyo is incredibly easy to learn and teach.  The amount of luck involved means that brand new players have plenty of opportunity to win against seasoned veterans.  Sometimes the interaction between particular power-up cards isn’t clear.  Fortunately this is a rare occurrence, and if players can’t agree then there is a fist full of monster dice to help settle any argument.  Players who have difficulty with being eliminated may need some assistance and coaxing to play (adults or children).  However given the short play time and the amount of luck involved in this game, players shouldn’t take elimination too personally.  While this game does play with 2 players, doing so loses much of the interaction that comes with 3 plus players.

comment: Great game.  Prestige points are almost too much complexity, but they add enough strategy to be worth it.  Military Takeovers are definitely not worth it.  Update Sep 2018: I've enjoyed this game for many years, but my recent plays of it have me wondering, has Roll for the Galaxy replaced it?  The spikey bits of Race are really standing out to me lately. I have the orginal arc of expansions through Vvrnk of War. Takeovers were always rediculous, something I am reminded of every time I need to ignore those icons on a card. Prestige I have learned to cope with, even though it occasionally overwhelms the game. The neceessity of the Search action bugs me though. Its an obvious patch to the self-inflicted dilution problem. I suspect that I should have stopped expanding at Rebel vs. Imperium, as I recall enjoying the game more before adding Brink.  I may take Brink out and see how I like it, but I think I`ve become more inclined to just play Roll instead. I hope I can resist overexpanding that game if the Roll expansions also become problematic.  I`m also temped to try the Xenos arc, as that seems to dispense with most of my annoyances.  I'll miss the goals, but as long as the Xenos module is managable, this may be my optimal solution.

comment: Basically Agricola 2.0 but the games feel pretty different.  The Gric is simpler and at the end of the game your board usually looks similar if you've done well, but the way you get there is different because you have to adapt to cards you were dealt.  With Caverna you can really go in a bunch of different directions and at the end you can have very different boards and still be successful.  I won once doing no expeditions and taking the build a room take a dog space every time.  I had a zillion dogs.  Another time I did a donkey/mine strategy.  It's really cool.  It also lets you run your engine a little longer at the end which I like, compared to the Gric which feels like it ends too quickly.  Comparing the Gric and Caverna has led to some really interesting discussions about game design and what makes them feel different, what one has over the other etc.  To make a long story short, I like Caverna a little better but both are staying in the collection (for now).

comment: Quite simply, the best game I have ever played.  This was my first Eurogame and I am truthfully not sure if I would have become as hooked as I am now playing any other game.  I believe that this remains the best game to introduce nongamers to when trying to convert them to Eurogames.  Further, if the nongamer has a dice game background, such as Monopoly, it makes my argument stronger as they will be comfortable with the dice roll.  The rules are quite simple and after a ten minute quick explanation and quick couple of rounds, most newbies will have things down pat.  Settlers has some randomness to the game as resource production is determined through the roll of dice, but more often then not I find that the person who manages their resources best wins the game.  Trading plays a very important roll in this as people who are able to complete more trades improve their position more often then not.  This game is a lot of fun and very addicting!  A must have for every gamer and a great way to send you down the path of gaming for nongamers.

comment: What a stunner this is. With beautiful visual aesthetics and intuitive, easy to teach rules, T.I.M.E. stories is more or less an old school adventure video game given cardboard flesh and 2-4 player interaction. The mechanics themselves are fairly basic, with a neat die & token system for challenge resolution, but the fact you the insert of the box can also be used as a convenient SAVE STATE for unfinished missions is nothing short of astounding. The one thing it has going against it is that once you've gone through a Mission it won't offer you any surprise, but you can always play dumb so friends can enjoy it and make your own decisions randomly. Also, unlike Pandemic Legacy, you don't destroy the components, so you could lend it out to friends to enjoy while you await future Mission packs (which are a few dollars too pricey, I'll admit). The storytelling in 'Asylum' is quite good, so I can't wait for future scenarios and a possible meta-narrative to emerge.

comment: I played this game when it first came out and I was quite young.  Then, my Magic cards sat in a box for almost 15 years.  When I rediscovered board/card games I knew I didn't want to get back into the CCG thing because I know what kind of a financial stress the addiction can cause.    I considered this game too sloppy, that it depended on the player to put in all the work to organize the cards and the player who had the "best" cards and who spent the most time organizing his deck would almost always win. However, the allure of the Duel Decks was pretty irresistible.  Here were two decks, gorgeously organized, playtested for a perfectly balanced game and it cost as little as a standard cheaper board game.  I picked up Phyrexia vs. The Coalition and loved it.  I thought, here is Magic really shining.  I've also purchased the most recent pair, Elspeth vs. Tezzeret and have found it to be a lot of fun too.  For me, this is the new way to continue enjoying what is a great game. --- More recent explorations in Magic include the DeckBuilder's Toolkit.  I thought I had found my new niche for this game with the duel decks, but I forgot how much fun it is to build a deck.  Even (especially?) with the limited cards from the toolkit, you can build a large variety of decks and if your opponent is working from the same resource, I think it's a fair battle. --- I've rated M:tG a 9 because I do love to play and I love constructing decks (from my modest supply), but Magic is not without its flaws.  In fact, several games have done a lot to fix the problems people have with Magic like getting too many or too few land cards (usually eliminating random mana draws) and card balancing.  However, Magic just has a certain charm to it that no other game captures.

comment: This is officially my favorite dice version of another game.  I typically don't like dice versions of other games, especially games I already adore and I do adore Race for the Galaxy.  I like dice just fine but typically the way dice versions simplify mechanics of games into dice rolls is akin to surgery with a hatchet.  There are some I do enjoy though and this one was so completely well done.  This will feel very familiar if you have played Race for the Galaxy.  Each player has an income track as well as some number of developments or planets in their queue for researching or settling.  Players also have a prep area for dice as well as a dice cup.  Each round players will buy as many dice as they can/want to from their prep area into their cup, roll them, and assign them to actions.  One die each round can select any phase regardless of what side was rolled.  This guarantees that phase will be played.  The other dice have to go under the columns for the side rolled (with some exceptions such as powers from developments and planets).  So some dice may be wasted if they aren't under the phase you selected and no other player selected it either.  The phases are almost identical to normal Race.  Explore will get you new developments or planets into your queues or money.  Research assigns dice to a development, when it is fully researched it goes into your tableau and the dice are released to your prep area.  Same with settle and planets.  There are also produce and ship phases which put dice on planets as resources and sells them for money or points.  Even the end game is the same as normal Race.  12 tiles or all the VP chits are taken.

There are multiple strategies you can take, but it doesn't feel like there is too much going on at the same time. The randomized cards and buildings ensures that each game will be unique. In many Euro games, I feel like I haven't accomplished anything I really wanted before the game is over. I don't feel this way with Stone Age. I always feel like I've built up an engine that is really working for me- then I just sit back and watch the points roll in at the end and see how I fared. I like that you see what cards other players take when they grab them, but then they remain hidden in their hand, so it's hard to know for sure where everyone is at with their scores until the very end. comment: 2-5  Voorbereiding :  + Elke speler neemt een draaischijf, kiest een kleur en de bijhorende cabballero’s en machtkaarten. + Er wordt een regiokaart getrokken voor iedere speler en voor de koning. + De spelers plaatsen hun Grande en 2 cabballero’s in de regio en 1 cabballero op het scorespoor. + 7 cabballero’s liggen in het hof, de overige cabballero’s liggen in de provincie. + De actiekaarten komen naast het speelbord te liggen.  Speelverloop:  Er zijn 9 rondes. Elke ronde bestaat uit de volgende stappen:  1/ De zwarte rondenteller schuift 1 vakje naar beneden. Aan het einde van de 3e, 6e en 9e ronde vindt er een algemene puntentelling plaats.  2/ De 5 actiekaarten worden omgedraaid.  3/ De spelers spelen hun machtkaarten uit.  In de eerste ronde mag de jongste speler als eerste een machtkaart uitspelen. Vanaf de tweede ronde begint altijd de speler die in de voorgaande ronde als laatste aan de beurt was. De overige spelers volgen in de richting van de klok. Alle uitgespeelde machtkaarten moeten een verschillende waarde hebben. De speler die de hoogste machtkaart heeft gespeeld, begint met het kiezen van een actiekaart. Daarna de speler met de op één na hoogste machtkaart, enz. Afhankelijk van de gespeelde machtkaart verplaatst de speler cabballero’s van zijn provincie naar zijn hof.   4/ De machtkaart gaat naar de aflegstapel.  5/ De speler neemt één van de openliggende actiekaarten.  6/ De speler voert de actie uit en plaatst het aantal cabballero’s (afhankelijk van de gekozen actiekaart) op het speelbord. Je mag kiezen of je eerst cabballero’s plaatst of eerst de actie uitvoert. Cabballero’s mogen naar believen geplaatst worden in regio’s naast de koningsregio en/of in El Castillo.  7/ De gekozen actiekaart gaat naar de aflegstapel.  Na ronde 3, 6 en 9 volgt een algemene puntentelling:  1. Draaischijf instellen. 2. Telling van El Castillo. 3. Cabballero’s uit El Castillo  in de (op het draaischijf gekozen) regio plaatsen. 4. Telling van alle regio’s.  Waardetabel:  Bij 2 spelers: 1e cijfer Bij 3 spelers: de 2 eerste cijfers Bij 4 of 5 spelers: de 3 cijfers  In geval van een gelijke stand in een regio, ontvangen de spelers steeds de punten van de lagere lang. In geval van gelijke stand in de koningsregio krijgt niemand de koningsbonus.  Belangrijke regels:  + Er worden alleen maar cabballero’s geplaatst in aangrenzende regio’s van de koningsregio (uitzondering: cabballero’s die in het geheim vanuit El Castillo op het speelbord worden geplaatst). + Er worden nooit cabballero’s geplaatst in de koningsregio (ook niet vanuit El Castillo). + Cabballero’s kunnen vanuit El Castillo slechts in 1 regio worden geplaatst. + De meerderheid halen in de koningsregio = +2 bonuspunten. + De meerderheid halen in de thuisregio (bij een Grande) = +2 bonspunten. + Als je provincie leeg is, mag je cabballero’s van het speelbord halen.

comment: A very cool "atmospheric" game, best played at night by candlelight with one of those haunted house records spinning in the background.  Replay value seems high at first glance (50 different scenarios!) but in reality the card text, while chilling the first time around, gets old with later plays.  My advice:  don't take it seriously (it's far too random for that) and play it as a party game.  Once a year, on Halloween.  In the dark.  [b]After 11 plays:[/b]  As of November 2013, all of them in darkness and firelight, with that goddamn piloerecting spooky soundtrack—[i]A Night in a Haunted House/A Night in a Graveyard[/i] (1992)—whose sound effects invariably, eerily, line up with the action.  Never playing it during the day or in artificial light makes the whole affair rather... [i]mysterious[/i].  Straining to read cards with a candle in the fist really adds a lot to the proceedings.  Even now, in the happy shine of morning, I feel a vague unease upon catching a glimpse of the box...  [q]Highlights from the last couple years:  • Once the traitor was revealed, he didn't want to go into the other room to read his plot synopsis.  He was too freaked out—and we're talking about a grown-ass man here.  • My little dog had worked her way under the table and into the forest of our legs without anyone noticing.  The toll of a bell on the soundtrack made her bark and everyone at the table simultaneously leaped out of their skins and crapped their pants.[/q] UPDATE OCT 2016:  Picked up a copy of 2nd Ed. for component-matching with the upcoming expansion as I have no confidence that the 12-year-old OG printing will line up [i]at all[/i] (cardstock and card sizes will, no doubt, be [url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/image/3066908/hivegod]radically different[/url]).  I've heard they've rejiggered some of the haunts, not that this was ever a problem for us as we're RPGers first and quickly adjudicated any rules weirdness with the wave of a hand.  I do like the severe reduction in tokens, however, and the use of generic markers instead of having to search through a giant pile for the single "eyetooth of a penitent murderer" by candlelight while the narrative tension sags to the floor...  Though it must be said that I miss the Underground Lake in the attic (an accidentally thematic misprint in the original) and the twin "Image in the Mirror" event cards where one had actual mirror-imaged text.  [imageid=3348136 small] [size=7]Fig. 1 — [i]♪ DING DONG ♫[/i][/size]  [filepage=143027]So You're a Traitor! pamphlet[/filepage]  FINAL ANALYSIS:  Parallel-universe me (the one with the evil goatee) would probably give this an unreserved 10!! (with two exclamation points) because 1) he's cool with the excitement graph having both peaks [i]and[/i] valleys on it and 2) because he's slightly stupid when it comes to exclamation points.*  Variability makes or breaks the experience—on the one hand this means no two games are alike; on the other it means sometimes the climax is more denouement.  The question, always, is will [i]this[/i] haunted house configuration make for a thrilling contest, or one that's impossible (or otherwise unfun) for one side?  There's only one way to find out... comment: Dixit consists of a deck of cards featuring some very surreal artwork. Everyone is dealt a hand of six cards. One person starts out as the "storyteller" who picks one card out of their hand and says a sentence related to it. The sentence can be a word or two, a full sentence, a sound, a song line, a movie title - basically anything that can be spoken. Everyone picks a card out of their hand that they think also matches the sentence. The storyteller takes these cards without looking, shuffles them up and lays them out on the table. Players then vote on which card is the storyteller's. The storyteller gets points if some, but not all, players pick his card and other players get points for picking the storyteller's card or by having other players pick their card over the storyteller's. So basically, the sentence needs to be suggestive enough to have some people pick your card, but not all. Good table talk and a bit of creative thinking a good game makes.

comment: Hanabi is a great cooperative deduction game. Players have 4 cards in their hands and they all together need to play numbers of 1-5 in five colors in order to win (well you score points for lesser attempts but ultimately you aim for getting all 5's on table). Easy task except you don't know what cards you have but you know which cards others have. On your turn you either a) play a card b) discard a card c) give a hint to a player. When giving hint you must name all cards with same color/number in somebody's hand. Since there is only a limited number of hints available (discarding gives them back) it is painfully good deduction experience.   The first version (Hanabi & Ikebana) had bad card design. In poor lighting blue and black were too similar and this caused some errors in play way too easily. This would be a non-issue IF cards would differ also in graphical design but no, they are all the same except for colors. Why can't they publish a decent edition of this game? In tin box edition they fixed graphical design by having symbols also but square cards aren't the best possible shape or quality and also it has cludgy lid that won't really hold the game in without rubber band.
