comment: Your turn is to collect cards (6 different colours of various raritude) from the 5 card draft, or sell cards from your hand for VP's. I think the camel idea it implements is clever here - instead of the usual pick 1 card (very staid), you have the option of picking all the camel cards in the draft (they don't get assessed against your hand limit), and then on a later turn exchanging as many as you like with cards in the display, quickly increasing your hand. That leaves a bunch of camel cards in the draft, which the other player may now decide to acquire for later, and the wheel turns. The game also creates pressure to sell which is nice - sell early and you get the best VP's, but hold onto them and trade 3, 4 or 5 at a time and you'll get bonus points, Thurn And Taxis style. The 7 card hand limit also drives the selling. The game is pleasant to play and seemingly spouse friendly. Turns roll along, no big or hard decisions, picking up for a few turns in a row, selling cards for VPs, then back to picking up, but always being aware of what the other player is doing to improve your own decision making on what to pick up and how. Like Fjords, you may want to play only 1 short hand rather than the rules-driven first to win 2 out of 3, but like Lost Cities you probably need to play the extra hands to help balance out the luck of the draft draw. Funnily enough my first playing of this was as a three player where it played similarly and worked fine.

comment: The context of the game is that the players are essentially "time police" who travel to other times and "other realities" in order to prevent time anomalies caused by other time travelers or events. This pretty much leaves the door open for adventures to be set in any theme or time period. Because of this, the pawns and tokens that come with the game are intensely generic as they can represent different things in different adventures. The rule book tries to straddle the line between telling you how to play and not giving anything away. It unfortunately errs on the side of being coy, leaving some basic sections of the game board unexplained! We pretty much just put things out where it seemed to make sense and it was fine. Fortunately, there are not many rules and the flow is fairly intuitive once you get into it.  The heart of the game is in discovering locations, exploring locations, and passing tests - trying to figure out and meet the success conditions before time is up. As you discover locations, four cards representing a map gets updated with new cards. In the most cool and innovative aspect of the game, each location is represented by a panorama of cards depicting people and things in the location. Each card in the panorama can be explored separately or together by each player resulting in different encounters and pieces of information. You can't share your card with players in other parts of the location, but you describe and discuss what you've discovered. Locations also have non-panoramic cards that can be visited or turned over when its requirements are met. The panoramas open a window to the theme and setting nicely and the encounters are basic, but not poorly done.  My main concern at this point is that the game is a bit too much of trial-and-error to succeed. Many times you cannot know that an action is a time-waster until you do it and can only avoid it on the next run after you fail. I don't dislike this aspect of the game, but many of these encounters will lock you in until you succeed in the test and it can make the game feel less about deduction and more about turning over the wrong card. But, that's probably the nature of the beast....

comment: Clank! is what I call a Strategy Deck-Builder in that it uses the mechanism of Deck-Building to drive a larger gaming experience. That experience is dungeon crawling to some degree but really this is neither a Deck-Builder in the true sense of the word, nor is it a Dungeon Crawler in any great way.   What this is though is a fun and silly romp into a dungeon as the players (would-be) thieves try to plunder as much loot and treasure as possible. The trick...well the clock is ticking as a dragon called Nikki awaits in the dark and will go into a rage every so often.   When one player loses their nerve and hightails it back to the surface, the timer is set and the other players must make a mad dash for safety before Nikki loses it completely and tears them all to pieces.   Throw in 'Push-your-luck' done well and this is a really engaging experience.

comment: [b]Best with: 4[/b] [b]3p rating: 8[/b] [b]2p rating: 7 (nile map)[/b]  [b]7/18/13[/b] After debating giving this game a perfect score some things really bother me about it.  -No compensation for late turn order, especially with 4 players.  -The tile draw can be brutal. I appreciate this luck and see it's importance to the game, but the volatility it creates leaves a little to be desired. So it's essential to what this game is, but somehow limits this game from being a top-notch competitive affair. You can only dump tiles so much before you ruin your score. I think this goes away a bit with more competent and familiar play, but I've seen people "stuck" with a hand (and re-filled hand) of blue tiles with no room to start a new kingdom without getting squished. It seems to be a little rougher when you slammed with blue tiles. You can't use them to build a monument paired with the color you really need if the delta is already established. Also, some of the "boom-boom" plays, the situations where a player causes an external conflict and through a scattering of reinforcements players end up with a monochromatic hand and rape you in the following turn. Like mentioned, good play can minimize the tile draw chaos. -The last point, among other factors, results in a game more tactical than I'd like. -The game plays best with 4, but that player count only exacerbates the above 3 problems.  Still it's a game that I'd nearly never turn down. It has a geometric feel to it, almost abstract, that still works well with all the moving parts around it. It's almost elegant and simple enough to give off a "traditional" game vibe- like you could imagine this game having been played for a couple hundred years... well maybe that's a stretch, but compared to modern euro's of the past few years, the game is simple from a structural and mechanical point of view. This was one of the first games I bought back in 2006. Although it didn't hit the table a lot in the beginnings, it's seen fairly heavy table time from about 2010 on and I don't think it's going anywhere. If I could see a log the games played for 2023, I'd be shocked if we weren't still having fun with this one.

comment: This is a fantastic team party game.  The  game is played with two teams trying to find their spies out of a list of random codenames.  Each team has a spymaster that knows which affiliation each of the spies is.  As well as spies for both teams some codenames refer  to civilians that aren't affiliated with either team and one is the assassin which will cause either team to lose immediately if identified.  A team's turn is played much like the classic game show Password.  The team's spymaster will say a single word and a number.  The number refers to how many of that team's codenames on the grid relate to the word said.  So if two of the codenames are "hamburger" and "spaghetti" for example the spymaster could say "food, two".  However, you need to be careful because other words on the grid could relate to that clue.  In one of my games the opponent spymaster said "Asia, one"  trying to get his team to guess "India".  However, "Beijing" was also a codename on the board and it was one of our teams spies so he gave us a point by accident when his team identified that codename.  When a codename not belonging to one of your spies is identified, play passes to the other team.  The game ends when either one team identifies all their spies or the assassin is identified.  This is a clean, clever, and fun game that I will always be up for playing.  I will play either role but I do personally think the spymaster is a lot more fun.

comment: 2-5  Doel van het spel: De speler met de meeste punten (puntenfiches + punten van de gebouwen (bezet/onbezet) + extra punten van bezette grote gebouwen) is de winnaar. Bij gelijke stand wint de speler die de meeste dubloenen en goederen heeft.  Voorbereiding: Iedere speler krijgt een speelbord, geld (zie hieronder) en 1 plantagekaartje (zie spelregels).  3 SPELERS: + 2 dubloenen + geen goudzoekers + 75 puntenfiches + schepen: 4,5 en 6 laadruimte + 4 plantagekaarten open + 55 kolonisten  4 SPELERS: + 3 dubloenen + 1 goudzoeker + 100 puntenfiches + schepen: 5, 6 en 7 laadruimte + 5 plantagekaarten open + 75 kolonisten  5 SPELERS: + 4 dubloenen + alle rollenkaarten + 122 puntenfiches + schepen: 6, 7 en 8 laadruimte + 6 plantagekaarten open + 95 kolonisten  Speelverloop:  De speler met de gouverneurkaart begint. Hij neemt 1 van de rollenkaarten en voert de bijhorende actie uit. Daarna voeren ook alle andere spelers met de klok mee deze actie uit. De speler die de rol koos heeft recht op een privilege. Wanneer elke speler een rol heeft gekozen, eindigt de ronde. Aan het einde van een ronde wordt er op elke niet-gekozen rol een dubloen gelegd. De gouverneurkaart schuift door naar de volgende speler.  De 7 verschillende rollen:  1/ Landbouwer:  Actie: neem een plantagekaartje (na deze fase worden alle niet-gekozen plantages verwijderd en komen er nieuwe plantages open te liggen).   Privilege: neem een steengroeve in plaats van een plantagekaartje.   2/ Burgemeester:  Actie: Verdeel de kolonisten van het schip (beginnend bij de actieve speler) en plaats de kolonisten op je gebouwen/plantages. Bezette gebouwen/plantages vervullen hun functie, onbezette niet. Aan het einde van deze fase komen er minstens zoveel kolonisten op het schip als de som van alle onbezette velden bij de spelers (niet van de plantages en steengroeves). Opgelet: Er worden steeds minstens zoveel kolonisten op het schip geplaatst als er spelers zijn.  Privilege: De burgemeester krijgt 1 extra kolonist uit de algemene voorraad.   3/ Bouwmeester:  Actie: gebouw bouwen (nooit 2x hetzelfde gebouw bouwen).  Privilege: 1 dubloen korting bij de aankoop van een gebouw.  4/ Opzichter:  Actie: De spelers nemen om beurt hun geproduceerde goederen (bezette plantages leveren grondstoffen op).   Privilege: De opzichter krijgt één goederensteen extra van een product naar keuze, dat hij net heeft geproduceerd.  5/ Handelaar:  Actie: Volgens beurtvolgorde kunnen spelers maximaal 1 goederensteen aan het handelshuis verkopen. Men ontvangt daarvoor de aangegeven prijs. De handelaarsfase eindigt wanneer elke speler 1 keer aan de beurt is geweest of wanneer het handelshuis vol zit. Als laatste handeling wordt het handelshuis leeggemaakt indien er 4 stenen liggen. Liggen er slechts 1, 2 of 3 stenen, dan blijven alle stenen liggen.  Privilege: 1 extra dubloen bij de verkoop van een goederensteen.  6/ Kapitein:  Actie: De spelers moeten om beurt goederen aan de schepen leveren. Een speler kan telkens enkel goederen leveren van één soort. Op het einde van deze fase mag je slechts 1 goederensteen overhouden (uitzondering: pakhuizen). Als laatste handeling lost de kapitein alle volle schepen.  Privilege: De kapitein krijgt bij een levering één extra punt.  7/ Goudzoeker:  Actie: Geen  Privilege: De goudzoeker neemt 1 dubloen van de bank.  Einde van het spel :  Het spel eindigt aan het einde van de ronde waarin aan minstens 1 van de 3 voorwaarden wordt voldaan: 1. een speler bouwt zijn 12e stadsveld. 2. er kunnen niet voldoende kolonisten op het kolonistenschip worden gelegd (burgemeesterfase). 3. alle puntenfiches zijn op.  Belangrijke regels:  + De speler mag niet weigeren een rol te kiezen. Hij mag echter wel een rol kiezen, die hij vervolgens helemaal niet kan of wil gebruiken. + Geld en goederen moeten steeds zichtbaar zijn. + Maïs wordt direct van op de plantage gewonnen, het heeft geen productiegebouw nodig.  Burgemeesterfase: + De speler mag tijdens deze fase steeds zijn kolonisten herverdelen. + Als een kolonist(en) niet tewerk gesteld kan worden, dan gaat hij naar San Juan. In de volgende burgemeesterfase kan je hem terug inzetten. + Geen enkele speler mag vrijwillig kolonisten plaatsen in San Juan.  Bouwmeesterfase: + Je mag maar 1 gebouw bouwen in je beurt . + Elke bezette steengroeve die je bezit, vermindert de bouwkosten met 1 dubloen. Een speler kan echter bij de gebouwen uit de eerste kolom (overzichtskaart) slecht één bezette steengroeve als vermindering laten gelden; bij de 2de kolom maximaal 2; enz...   Handelaarsfase: + Het handelshuis neemt alleen goederen van verschillende soorten op (uitzondering: magazijn)   Opzichtersfase: + Is een betreffende goederensoort niet meer voorradig, dan krijgen de spelers niets.  Kapiteinsfase: + Elk schip accepteert slechts één soort goederen. Een schip aanvaardt geen goederen die al op een ander schip aanwezig zijn. + De kapiteinsfase blijft gelden totdat er niemand meer kan leveren. Het kan dus zijn dat je meermaals aan de beurt bent. + Je moet zoveel goederen leveren als je kan, je mag niets achterhouden.  + Voor elke goederensteen dat je levert, krijg je 1 punt (puntenfiche).

comment: 2-4  Voorbereiding:  Elke speler kiest een clan en clansheet. Neem de clan’s leider figuur en 8 warrior figuren en plaats ze in de plastic basissen in jouw kleur. Neem je corresponderend schip figuur. Plaats je figuren in je reserve op je clansheet.  Plaats alle monsters naast het bord.  Zet je clan’s glory marker op de 0 van de glory track.  Plaats je clan tokens op de juiste plaats op je clansheet: 6 rage, 3 axes & 4 horns. Plaats je laatste clantoken op de 6e plek van de rage track.   Plaats de valhalla sheet en de age track sheet naast het speelbord.  Plaats de pillage tokens met de groene rand in de provincie Yggdrasil in het midden van het bord, met de beloning faceup. Schud de andere pillage tokens en plaats ze random faceup op de 8 overblijvende provincies rond Yggdrasil.  Schud de 8 ragnarok tokens en plaats er 1 op elk van de 3 ragnarok plaatsen van de age track, met de tekst faceup.  Plaats het doom token op de provincie die overeenstemt met de provincie die op het ragnarok token van de first age track staat.  Afhankelijk van het aantal spelers, neem x aantal ragnarok tokens en plaats ze met de vernietigde zijde naar boven op de juiste provincies.  5 spelers: geen vernietigde provincies 4 spelers: 1 provincie vernietigd 3 spelers: 2 provincies vernietigd 2 spelers: 3 provincies vernietigd  Een provincie met een ragnarok token is onbestaand. Hierop kunnen geen figuren worden geplaatst.  Sorteer de kaarten op hun rugzijde en maak 3 decks: 1, 2 en 3.   5 spelers: voeg de 5+ kaarten toe 4 spelers: verwijder geen kaarten 3 spelers: verwijder alle 4+ kaarten 2 spelers: verwijder alle 3+ en 4+ kaarten.  Plaats het saga token op de eerste plek van de first age op de story track.  Geef de startspeler het startspelertoken. Dit token schuift op het einde van elke age door naar de linkse speler.  Elke provincie (gebied) heeft 3 tot 5 dorpen. In elk dorp kan 1 figuur staan. In Yggdrasil kunnen oneindig veel figuren staan.  Er zijn 4 fjorden, telkens tussen twee provincies aan de buitenrand. Elke fjord ondersteunt de 2 provincies die hieraan grenzen. Elk effect dat de provincie beïnvloedt, zal ook de ondersteunende fjord beïnvloeden. In elk fjord kunnen oneindig veel schepen staan.  Speelbeurt:  Het spel duurt 3 ages. Elke age bestaat uit 6 fasen. Verplaats de saga token op de age track. Wanneer de laatste fase van een age is afgelopen, verplaats je de saga token naar de eerste fase van de volgende age tot het spel eindigt aan het einde van de derde age.  1/ God’s gifts:  Geef elke speler 8 kaarten. Elke speler kiest een kaart en geeft de overige kaarten aan de linkse speler. Herhaal dit tot elke speler 6 kaarten heeft. Leg de 2 overgebleven kaarten af.  Spel met 2 spelers: kies steeds 2 kaarten tot elke speler 6 kaarten heeft. Leg de 2 overgebleven kaarten af.  Kaarten van vorige ages worden bewaard op de clansheet.  2/ Acties:  Tijdens je beurt kies je 1 enkele actie. Als je actie rage kost, betaal je de kost door het token op je rage track te verplaatsen. Als je niet voldoende rage hebt om te betalen voor een actie, dan kan je die actie niet meer doen. Als je rage op 0 staat, dan kan je geen enkele actie meer doen (zelfs geen gratis acties).  De actiefase eindigt meteen wanneer alle spelers op 0 rage staan of als alle provincies zijn gepillaged.  A/ Invade:  Kies een figuur uit je reserve en betaal evenveel rage als de STR van de figuur. Plaats de figuur op een leeg dorp in om het even welke buitenprovincie (niet Yggdrasil). Een schip moet in een fjord worden geplaatst.  Invading met je leider kost geen rage!  Als je evenveel figuren op het speelbord hebt staan als het getal op je Horns stat, dan mag je geen figuren meer in het spel brengen.  B/ March:  Betaal 1 rage en kies 1 provincie (geen fjord). Verplaats om het even hoeveel figuren van 1 provincie naar lege dorpen in 1 andere provincie. De provincies hoeven niet aangrenzend te zijn.   C/ Upgrade:  Je clansheet heeft plaats voor 8 upgrades:  1 voor elke warrior, leider en schip 2 voor monsters 3 voor je clan  Kies een upgrade kaart uit je hand en betaal evenveel rage als de STR van je kaart. Plaats de kaart op de juiste plek op je clan sheet. Als er geen plaats meer is, leg je de oude kaart af en vervang je ze door de nieuwe kaart.  Troop upgrades: Wanneer je een leider, warrior of schip opwaardeert en je hebt het corresponderende figuur in je reserve, dan mag je deze figuur meteen in het spel brengen (invade) zonder rage te betalen.  Monster upgrades: Wanneer je een monster opwaardeert, neem je het corresponderende figuur en plaats je jouw basiskleur eronder. Daarna mag je het monster figuur meteen in het spel brengen (invade) zonder rage te betalen.  D/ Quest:  Speel een quest kaart facedown op je clan sheet. Dit kost geen rage. Je mag zoveel quests spelen als je wil, zolang je rage niet op 0 staat.  E/ Pillage:  Kies een provincie waar minstens 1 van je figuren instaat (of in een ondersteunende fjord) en die deze rond nog niet succesvol is gepillaged. (pillage token toont de beloning side up).   Pillage kost geen rage.   Pillage bestaat uit 3 stappen.  Stap 1: kondig het gevecht aan.  Elke andere speler (van links naar rechts) kan ervoor kiezen om in het gevecht te stappen door 1 of meer van hun figuren van een aangrenzende provincie te verplaatsen naar een leeg dorp van de betreffende provincie. Dit kost geen rage. Schepen kunnen niet verplaatsen. In Yggdrasil kunnen oneindig veel figuren worden geplaatst.  Wanneer er geen vijandelijke figuren in de provincie staan of er zijn geen ondersteunende fjords van andere spelers, dan vindt er geen gevecht plaats. Je neemt de beloning en draait de pillage token naar zijn pillaged zijde. In dit geval verdien je geen glorie door het gevecht te winnen.  Stap 2: speel kaarten.  Elke speler speelt tezelfdertijd 1 kaart uit zijn hand:  Je toont een rode Battle kaart: de +STR bonus wordt toegevoegd aan de totale STR van al je figuren die deelnemen aan het gevecht + alle speciale eigenschappen op de kaart hebben effect.  Je toont een zwarte upgrade of een groene quest kaart: het voegt geen STR toe en het heeft geen effect.  Stap 3: de speler met de meeste STR wint het gevecht.  Bij gelijkspel verliezen alle spelers.   De winnaar van het gevecht verliest al zijn uitgespeelde kaarten. De verliezer van het gevecht mag al zijn uitgespeelde kaarten terug op handen nemen.   Alle verliezende spelers moeten al hun figuren in die provincie vernietigen (inclusief de ondersteunende fjords) en verplaatsen naar de Valhalla sheet.  Enkel de speler die de pillage heeft gestart, maakt kans op de beloning van het pillage token (draai het token daarna naar de pillaged zijde). Als de speler die de pillage heeft gestart, verliest, dan blijft de pillage beloning liggen.   De winnaar van het gevecht wint sowieso glorie gelijk aan hun axes stat, ongeacht of hij de pillage heeft gestart of niet.  3/ De spelers mogen 1 kaart houden voor de volgende age en leggen alle andere handkaarten af. In de derde age moeten alle handkaarten worden afgelegd.  4/ Questfase:  Elke speler draait al zijn quest kaarten om. Als de voorwaarden op je kaart zijn voldaan, dan verdien je glorie (zie questkaart) en mag je 1 van je stats met 1 stap verhogen.  5/ Ragnarok:  Vernietig de verdoemde provincie en vernietig alle figuren in de provincie en de ondersteunende fjords. Deze figuren en fjords gaan naar valhalla. Ontvang het aantal glorie dat op de age track staat voor elke figuur die werd vernietigd. Verplaats het doomtoken naar de volgende verdoemde provincie.   6/ Bevrijd Valhalla:  Alle figuren van valhalla gaan terug naar de reserves van de betreffende spelers.   Het einde van een age:  Draai alle pillage tokens terug naar de zijde met de beloning. Geef de startspelertoken door naar de linkse speler. Verplaats het sage token naar de eerste fase van de volgende age.  Het spel eindigt aan het einde van age 3.  Voor elke clan stat dat op de 4e of 5e stap staat, verdien je +10 glorie. Voor elke clan stat dat op de laatste stap staat, verdien je +20 glorie.  De speler met de meeste glorie wint!

Nagy szerencsémre az 5 színből és 50 lapból álló játék játszható a Fiasko játék lapjaival így rögtön ki is tudtam próbálni. Hihetetlen ötlet a lapokat fordítva tartatni a játékosokkal és ezzel egy okos kooperatív játékot sikerült megalkotni. Megmondhatjuk egy színből vagy számból melyik lapok konkrétan melyikek egy játékos kezében egy token felhasználásával, amit szerezni egy lap eldobásával tudunk. Harmadik akcióként pedig a játék célját valósíthatjuk meg, tűzijátékot építhetünk, de ehhez helyes lapot kell leraknunk. Tehát tulajdonképpen egy kis memóriára és jó megérzésre van szükség a játékhoz. De ahogy Joel is mondta jól játszani nem könnyű és gondolkodásra készteti a játszókat. Nagyon ötletes, nagyon egyszerű jó kis játék a Hanabi, ami akár otthon is elkészíthető. Nem véletlen Joel jó osztályzata. A pontszám akár még emelkedhet is.  [2017-02-26] Rengeteg parti van benne, mert játékosszámtól függően más a játék, a szivárvány lapok is más dimenziókat adnak a társashoz. Ettől függetlenül nem emelek a ponton.

comment: What a delightful game!  This is my favorite light Euro.  It is easily accessible to newcomers yet varied and strategic enough for frequent gamers.  Each expansion also seems to add and enrich the game.  To be fair though, the base game all alone has a few shortcomings for me: the lack of a 6th player, the incomplete feel of a total package, and too short.  Inns & Cathedrals make up the first two points while Traders and Builders takes care of the last 2 points.  I rarely play the game without at least these two expansions.  Even if I don't use all the rules, I keep all the tiles in the game.  So basic vanilla Carc probably deserves a score of an 8 for me.  Hunters & Gatherers and Ark of the Covenant are the better basic games.  But with the expansions, Carcassonne is impossible to beat.

Though this had been on my radar for years having never owned the first version, I thought it would just be a hack and slash.  To a point it kind of is, but the designers did a great job of mixing up the levels and given them their own personallity. comment: In Azul, players are drafting tiles from a central area to prepare them to add to a personal tableau. When one player finishes one row of the tableau, the game ends. Basic endgame bonuses (completed rows and columns as well as all tiles of a type covered) are applied and high score wins. Each round, the center of the table is populated with groups of four randomly selected tiles of five types. Players take all of one color from a group and the remainder in the group moves to the center to form another group that the leftover tiles from each group feeds. You can draft from the center group in the same manner you draft from the initial groups. You have to draft all of one color, which can you lead you to drafting tiles you cannot use. Tiles you cannot use are deducted from your score for the round. The tableau you are building is a 5x5 grid with each column and row consisting of 5 different tiles. From top to bottom, the prep area is 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 tiles large. At the end of a round, players move one tile from filled prep areas onto the tableau and discard the rest. Tiles added are immediately scored for columns and rows of adjacent tiles.   The game can seem overly simple at first, but once you start to understand that adjacent tile types score more points and you prioritize the endgame bonuses, a lot of considerations start to come into play. You can also choose to "hate" draft in a way to block a close competitor or force them to draft tiles they can't use and eat some points. The game is well-produced. The Bakelite tiles are nicely designed and feel good in the hand. I see why this was one of the better received games this year: easy to learn, subtle, beautiful, and satisfying.
name: Azul

comment: A Dominiontól egészen egyszerűen leesett az állam. Mindenféleképpen be akartam szerezni a játékot, de valami miatt óvakodtam attól, hogy rögtön kipróbáljuk. Azt hiszem, hogy az ilyen jellegű kártyajátékoknál megszoktam, hogy hosszabb játékidejűek, és bizony a szabályok elsajátítása is általában nem pár perc. Aztán amikor végigolvastam a szabálykönyvet, azonnal kikészítettem a paklikat, pár mondatban összefoglaltam a szabályokat Anettnek, és már el is kezdtük a játékot. ANNYIRA jó volt az első játék, hogy RÖGTÖN, ahogyan befejeztük, kezdtük is a következőt. Azért ilyen nem sokszor szokott előfordulni és nem csak a kevés idő, meg a fáradtság miatt, hanem általában egy-egy parti után nem érzem én sem, meg Anett sem, hogy abban a pillanatban ugyanazt újra szeretnénk játszani. Szerintem ez sokat elárul a Dominionról. Kártyajáték, de mégis kevés szerepe van a szerencsének, nagyon kiegyenlített. Mindenki ugyanazokkal a lapokkal indul, mindenki ugyanazokból a lapokból vásárolhat, és mindenki eldöntheti, hogy pár körön belül milyen lesz a paklijának az összetétele. Zseniális.  A dobozban pedig eléggé szép mennyiségű lap található, ami nagyon magas újrajátszhatóságot biztosít. Ez a második játék Donald X. Vaccarino szerzeményei közül, amivel játszottam (a másik a Kingdom Builder volt), de mind a kettő megalkotásánál fontos szempont lehetett, hogy nagyon sokszor lehessen velük játszani úgy, hogy mindig hozzá lehessen tenni valami újat (és most nem a kiegészítőkről beszélek, mert maga az alapjáték ilyen).

comment: Very impressed with this on first play and looking forward to playing again.  Longish rules may make it appear more complicated than it really is; though they can be forgiven their length as they make pretty much everything crystal clear and the iconography on the board does a very good job of reminding you what each of the actions etc. do.  Getting past that first impression though it's clear that the relatively straightforward rules provide the basis for an involved game which delivers on the promise of the excellent presentation (an attractive Mayan setting featuring temples and - of course - the gears) and which really rewards thoughtfull play without causing too much brainburn.  First play was, perhaps inevitably, slowish but I can see it speeding up a lot in future now the basics have been absorbed - you should be able to plan ahead for most turns once the gears have turned; which should make a big difference next time.    Altogether an excellent first impression, though I'm holding back on an even higher mark for now till that is conifmed - though I have every expectation that it will be and that my rating will increase.    As an aside can I say how wonderful it is to be living in a world where we in Scotland can play a game designed by Italians (apologies if this is incorrect - I'm going by the names), produced by a Czech company, in an English language version co-produced by a US company and acquired in Germany (at Spiel).  That's an Internationalism I'm more than happy to sign up for.

comment: 卓尔金：玛雅日历是一款普通的工人放置类游戏，但是也有其独特的地方，具体体现在其精妙的齿轮轮盘上。游戏版图上有六大轮盘，中心大轮盘代表着玛雅历法的一年一周期，大轮盘带动周边五个小轮盘转动，每转动一格表示一个时间单位过去，而五个小轮盘代表着玛雅文明五个不同的发展层面，而玩家的工人将往返于这些各具特点小轮盘，执行其提供的各种行动。游戏比较精美，规则也通俗易懂，但是在轮盘转动规律方面爱好者们需要一些时间去细细体会，可谓小游戏有大味道。。。可谓生命有限，一年时间中能完成多少事情？ 【关键词】齿轮轮盘，七齿六齿，玉米，粮食日，水晶头骨，农业/采矿/建筑/宗教科技，纪念碑，三大神明，奇迹轨迹，奇琴伊察，上人/下人/乞讨  【推荐度】高【文明建设发展，中重度德式爱好者

comment: Simplesmente o melhor "Worker Placement" q joguei até agora, e pelo q eu senti, talvez o melhor q eu vá jogar (e sim, eu já joguei Agricola). A princípio um pouco assustador, pela quantidade de símbolos e engrenagens, mas assim que vc começa a ler o manual e entender o jogo, percebe a simplicidade e inteligência contida alí. Os símbolos, a princípio muito variados (mais que 7 Wonders) logo começam a fazer sentido de uma forma bem intrínseca, mérito para a arte. Com um mecanismo simples, mas muito original, e que se integra perfeitamente com a temática do calendário Maya, esse é um jogo na medida certa: tempo, opções de jogada, equilíbrio, diversão e tensão. E é um jogo bem pensado mesmo para jogar com menos de 4 jogadores, até mesmo com apenas 2, o que não é comum em muitos jogos. E uma das coisas mais fundamentais: fator sorte praticamente zero! Não é perfeito, talvez não tenha tanta rejogabilidade, e facilitaria se os "Wealth Tiles", buildings e monuments fossem cartas ao invés de tiles, facilitando o embaralhamento. A pontuação em volta tb poderia ter números (não só de 5 em 5) para facilitar a leitura. Mas esses "contras" são meros detalhes técnicos, de implementação do jogo, e não tiram em nada o seu mérito gigantesco. JOGAÇO!

comment: I was ready to really love this game, but it was so dang hard that I found myself feeling bad when playing it. I've never been so beat down and defeated by a game while playing it for so long. The thing I love out disaster style co-ops (Pandemic, Flash Point, etc.) is that it seems dire, but there are moments of hope. It may be false hope and the house may crumble around you a turn later from that hotspot, or the big outbreak, but at least you had a chance. Robinson Crusoe I almost never feel like I have a chance. I really hope that with more plays we are able to unravel the mystery of how to not completely suck at this game. I do have a lot of fun with it and the theme is spot-on throughout (especially when the event cards come back to haunt you) but we've only tried the 1st scenario and its supposed to be the easiest! I enjoy a tough game and I don't think that it would be any fun to have an auto-win, but a feel bright spots during the game would be great. I hope that a future expansion would add some tools that make it a little smoother. Still highly recommended and I'd ask to play it again. Solid game and theme, just be warned that it is crazy tough.

comment: 主題:1 再也找不到比農家樂更切合遊戲規則及主題的桌遊了，本遊戲由我最欽佩的桌遊設計師烏玫瑰山所設計，遊戲中玩家扮演一戶農家，透過各種農耕方式、交易買賣、增加人手，來讓自己的農場五穀豐收、六畜興旺。每一個環節都讓你體會到當農夫的辛苦(這就有點誇張)。  美術:1 有個人風格的美術我覺得才是最好的美術，一些只依實物的繪製卡片，反倒會讓遊戲失去風格而流至平庸。農家樂就是一款又強烈個人美術風格的桌遊，讓我非常欣賞。另外各式各樣的動物米寶，讓遊戲配件更增CP值；此外風趣又幽默的卡片內容，配合卡牌能力文字描述，常常讓人發出會心一笑。  規則:1 再也找不到此絲絲相扣的遊戲規則，雖然步驟繁多，但規則只要教過一遍，配合遊戲過程，我的桌遊咖都能馬上融入遊戲中，比較麻煩的地方，大概就是職業卡及設備卡的選取，但職業卡及設備卡的加入，正是讓遊戲規則更完美的地方，讓遊戲更加多元及耐玩。  設置:0.5 本項目是一些深度遊戲的痛楚，眾多的卡片及各式各樣米寶，外加圖版及小配件，都讓本遊戲要花一些時間完成前置作業，對於時間寶貴的人來說有點小麻煩，但有愛玩久了，一切都不是問題。  路線:1 路線超多元，這也是一款成功遊戲必備的條件，此外配合眾多的卡片，都能讓本遊戲每一局都能玩出不同的策略。  互動:1 本遊戲互動超強烈，正是標準的你卡我我卡你的遊戲，每一個步驟都考驗上下家的決定，可以說是從玩家的第一步計算到最後一步，常常第一步的後續效果，都在影響著全部玩家，就是像是"蝴蝶效應"一樣，遊戲的最終結果，端看大家的第一步決定，這個遊戲讓玩家間的互動激盪出很多火花，表現真的太棒了!   個人:1 這款遊戲不管是多人玩還是一個人玩，都有著很多的樂趣，我個人非常喜歡。  朋友:0.9 玩過的都深深著迷，不過有人覺得太複雜，有點難以適應。  想玩:1 遊戲變化度十足，讓人欲罷不能，只是桌遊咖要有一點實力(對現在決策影響未來成果的敏銳度)，這樣玩起來才會感受到互相牽制卡位的痛苦感。  收藏:1 十大必收遊戲之一  總分:9.4 講評:擴充多，單人至多人遊戲都有不同的樂趣及玩法，本遊戲我單人玩的次數超過多人玩的次數，因為咖不好湊。在挑戰單人遊戲過程中，看著自己每場的分數持續衝高，真的很有成就感，也挑戰自己運用職業卡及次要發展卡的決策力，是訓練邏輯思考，未來決策的好遊戲。

comment: This is a deck-building adventure/race game.  I remember there was a lot of love for Trains when it first came out because it was a deck building game with a board.  I personally wasn't that impressed with Trains but this game takes that deck builder with a board conceit and does it much much better.  Along with improving your deck by getting skill points and using those to purchase cards you also collect movement and combat points to move around a dungeon map and fight monsters.  Many of the spaces on the map have special properties and the main goal of the game is to collect a valuable artifact and make it out of the dungeon.  The namesake comes from the fact that many actions in this game make "Clank" or more simply put, noise.  This is represented by colored cubes matching your player color which are put into a big bag and occasionally the dragon attacks by pulling cubes from the bag and the noisiest players are more likely to be attacked.  This is what I was hoping to get out of Trains, I like deck builders and I love the idea of another gameplay layer on top of it.  This plays so quickly and has a lot of variability.  I came in last place my first time playing it but I was one movement point from coming in first.  I pressed my luck to get more points and ALMOST made it out.  Those kind of butt clenching moments that could make or break you are part of what makes a great game.  I can't help but be a little disappointed by the quality.  The cards and art are fine but everything is cardboard or cubes past that.  There are so many amazing looking games that have come out over the past couple years that maybe I'm just a little spoiled.

comment: [2020-08-06] Szép jelölők, paraván, új játékvariáció. Egyértelműen más a lengyel régi kiadás felújítása, mint az eredeti játék. Egyrészt könnyebb, a szellem eggyel több lapból választ, másrészt a szintenkénti kitalálandó helyek, tárgyak, személyek száma is eggyel kevesebb. Itt csak 3 szint van, nincs is nagyon nehéz, bár ez simán megoldható itt is eggyel több lappal. Új elem a látnoki képességjelölők használata, amivel a játékosok a többiek tippjét ítélhetik meg az első fázisban. Ezt azért rakták bele, mert a végső gyilkosság kitalálása teljesen más az új kiadásban. Itt ugyanis nemcsak szimplán a fő tettest kell kitalálni, hanem a tárgy és a helyszín is számít. Pontosabban a szellem mindháromra ad pontosan egy kártyát, de összekeverve, nem tudni melyik melyikre vonatkozik. A játék során a leggyengébb látnok egy kártyából próbál tippelni, a legjobb viszont mind hármat láthatja a végső tippje leadásakor. A tippek alapján jön ki, hogy melyik történetre tippelnek és itt már nem beszélhetnek egymással. A régi játékban csak a gyilkost kellett megtippelni közösen. Illetve ott 7 nap volt az egész játékra összesen, tehát ha hamarabb végeztek a játékosok a saját történeteik kitalálásával, a végső gyilkosra akár több napon át is tippelhettek, az újban erre egyszer van esélyük. Az első két játékomban nem így játszottuk, hanem a régi variáció szerint, de jó lenne ezt is kipróbálni. comment: Istanbul uses Dorn's patented "stack of discs" also found in games like Genoa and Robber Knights. Here, you're moving around a 4 by 4 grid of tiles that you can interact with. You have to leave a disc on each tile you use, giving you a limited time before you have to go back to the Fountain to collect all of your discs. However, if you use a tile you've already used, you can pick up a disc you left there previously instead of leaving a new one, extending your run. So you're incentivized to use the same tiles over and over, but the scoring system really encourages players to use lots of different tiles. You get a ruby (victory point) for obtaining various sets of special abilities, as well as trading in your goods or money in increasingly difficult contracts--first one to a set number wins.  (2 plays)

UPDATE:  This game is about 9,000 times more fun than it has any right to be—16 cards and some cubes?  Passing notes to a princess?  [i]Really?[/i]  But the end result is a quick, light farce that really does feel like scurrying through gardens and halls, of tarrying in chambers at improper hours, all on the little cat feet of whispers and meaningful glances.  The genius of the game comes from the small set of interactions possible with the cards, making the deduction element satisfying enough for the time frame involved (read:  short & sweet). comment: I played through an entire Risk Legacy campaign and really enjoyed the Legacy part even though I really dislike Risk.  Pandemic however is a game I'm quite fond of.  Now we put those together and it is really as incredible as getting peanut butter in my chocolate.  For those not familiar the Legacy system is just a term in board games that came about from Risk Legacy.  It is a reasonably novel idea where each game played things happen and that cause permanent changes to the game.  Inside the box are compartments that are opened at specified times.  These do things from make permanent changes to the board and characters to even destroying some components or bringing completely new stuff into the game.  When you start the game it is almost identical to standard Pandemic but before the end of the first game several changes are made to everything from the board, to how the viruses act, to even what your objective is.  And just looking at the amount of stuff still hidden tells me there's even more here than there was in Risk Legacy.  Plus it's a much, much better game.  And they still put in some pretty stellar components as well.  This is a fantastic item if the idea of making permanent markings or even tearing up pieces to one of your games doesn't give you ulcers.  There is also the typical concern that after a campaign there's very little reason to continue playing it.  I have two responses to that.  The first is, at the end, even if you don't unlock anything new, you still have a neat Pandemic variant with its own crazy rules that is pretty unique to you and your group that you can play any time you want just like you would regular Pandemic.  The second is, one campaign is between 12-24 games...and it isn't going to be 12.  Since I got into designer gaming 3-4 years ago there are less than 20 games I've played more than 12 times.  So that's quite a bit of value even if you never play it again at the end of your campaign.

comment: I've played several family and "advanced" games. Even a basic family game version feels very good and as such is a great game. The cards add more AP to the game and especially the start of the game goes slowly as everyone is checking their cards. But I like to play with them as then you must react to the cards and adapt your play. It's also much more fun with cards!  Theme fits mechanics very well and I like how there are many small subgoals (get food to your family, building enclosure to animals, breeding, etc.) that keep you busy while playing. Actually the scoring feels almost unnecessary in the end as playing itself is so fun. There seems to be a enough freedom in strategies and chances for being creative with your moves even thought scoring forces you to keep everything rather balanced. Simply an awesome game.  Update (13.7.2008): After another game (this time Z-man english edition) I decided to increase my rating from 8 to 9. And this is only after playing second "family game".  Update (17.8.2008): After few games with cards (basic and complex decks) Agricola really feels a superb game. The cards add variety and you must adapt your play a bit depending on what combos you'll be able to do. Cards don't change too much the gameplay but give just the right amount of more to think about. The game is simply more fun with the cards. They actually do add element of luck into the game but this shouldn't affect games too often and in any case it isn't a negative thing to me.  Update (3.9.2008): Ten games and game just seems to get better and better each time. I'll rise my rating for Agricola to a full 10 as it is very fun to play but a brain burner at the same time and simply very, very good game. When played with cards it gives me the same feeling as playing a CCG games. There is no deck building but there is thinking the playing order of cards and combos the cards can give. I didn't realize I was missing it and now playing Agricola (along with Jambo) fills this small niche for me as I don't usually play CCG's at all. This is probably the reason why I'm rating the game so high.  Update (23.9.2009): There is definitely luck involved in how occupation / minor improvement cards are distributed. Tried yesterday with drafting and although that probably is one of the best alternatives it is quite taxing to read 3-5 times 14 cards and more so to try to remember what good combos you might be giving to others... To me good things in drafting aren't big enough to really use it.

comment: A internesting euro, masquerading as a war game.  The game begins with a card draft.  You then spend rage to take actions on the board or with cards.  Some actions don't require rage like plundering a town.    The game is incredibly deep.  On the surface, it may seem that aggressiveness will pay in a game called Blood Rage, but actually, it often comes down to timing.  The temporal element of this game is a big factor, and knowing when and where to act is important.  You can spend a lot of cards opposing someone and getting nothing for it.    The game can be swingy as well.  Odin's throne can really help someone in last place and turn the whole game around for you.    But on the whole, the game is great.  It may crack my top ten.  Fun family game as well but the kids need to be at least 12 or so to play.

comment: So.. the dice version of my all time favourite (and most played) board game/card game - Race for the Galaxy. What surprised me most was that the play time for this game is actually longer than the the game it´s based on. But this is a good thing - this allowed this game to have it´s own feet and have almost the depth the card game has. It certailny has been simplified in some areas, but then again the action selection system is much more compicated and deep. The dice luck is well mitigated with the freedom of choosing one die to do any phase you want and also thanks to various powers to manipulate dice. Components are very pretty (although engraved dice would have been nice) and artwork is just amazing. Some of the art has been reused from RftG, but not too much. Of course I still like RftG itself better (more elegant design, plays quicker while still is deeper and more complex) but currently Roll is the hotter game for me - lot to discover for me still.  Edit, after about 12 games I was not too keen to play it anymore. So replayability is a bit low (at least for me). Maybe expansion would have helped, but not too interested in that to buy it and haven´t had a chance to play anyone else´s copy yet. I would rate my current interest to play this game: 6. But to represent past interest and some great plays I had I will lower my rating from 8->7 (instead of 6).

comment: Sure it's a spin off and a variation on a theme, but it definitely feels like an improvement over Forbidden Island. For starters, it changes a simple hold-back-time race game into an exploration race game, where you must go out and find things in order to win. You can let go tiles you've already explored to the sand storm, but if things are building up on unexplored tiles, you could be in trouble as you'll have to spend actions digging things out. Luckily there's a few gear cards you can find that will save you from disaster. That is until the water for each player starts running out, which is a second type of disaster card in the deck. The water requirement forces more co-operation and discussion in order to get people together at the oasis to recover enough to keep going for long enough. Just that one extra dimension improves the co-operation aspect significantly. An enjoyable thumbs up.

comment: A surprisingly fun game.  I thought for sure I wasn't going to like this game based on comments that I had read comparing it to Munchkin. The game is very simple to pickup and yet there is enough complexity to make the game require a great deal of thought to play correctly.  You get more resources in cards than you tend to be able to keep up with using, so the actions that you take each turn matter quite a lot and you are faced with decisions that actually matter on a frequent basis.  A lot of other games I have played make me feel like the games are playing themselves and I am just carrying out the actions for the game.  Smash Up actually gave me the feeling like I was in control of the game instead of the other way around.  Theme: Awesome theme with puns all around Relevant Choices: How you play the game pretty directly effects your likelihood of winning the game. Card Art & design: Great artwork Replay: Tons of replay through the potential deck combinations. Learning Curve: Low learning curve, easy to pick up and play.  Promotion of thought: Lots of potential synergies between cards and factions providing for a good deal of planning and strategy Random Element: Card draw and faction combinations, but the random element of the game is very manageable. Box: The box comes with a ton of open spaces for adding new factions to the game through expansions.  Does require sleeves to have the factions fit snug though.

comment: A very interesting brain-burner that has some definite similarities but is distinct enough to be judged on its own worth and not as any sort of copycat or revamp.  Seriously agonizing decisions to be made due to a severe shortage of actions.  Just as in many other games--including Agricola and Through the Ages--there is simply not NEARLY enough time to do what you want, so you have to make due with what you can.  Lots of potential for min/maxing your moves, which makes me wary; that sort of game tends to lead to SEVERE AP problems, the like of which put me off of Caylus to a large extent.  But hopefully people can learn to plan their turns ahead of time--it seems like downtime could become a serious problem otherwise in a many-playered game.  Still, some really neat mechanics going on and a nice, satisfying feeling of having built an economy by the end.  It may be too long for me to want to play often, but I enjoyed my first game of it.

comment: Villámbeszámoló: Viszonylag egyszerű játék, de nagyon komplex a sok kis apróság miatt amire folyamatosan figyelni kell - nem a nyugis játékok közé fog tartozni ilyen szempontból sem. Megtanulni nem volt nehéz, de nagyon sok módosító, változó fog jelentkezni, és mindenre figyelni kell. Az első, tanuló játék egyébként kb. 2 óra volt, el is buktuk a küldit. A második kb. 40 perc alatt lement, igaz, az előkészületekkel itt már nem kellett pepecselni. Rendkívül hangulatos dologról van szó, ami részben a MoM, részben a Gyűrűk ura LCG utánérzetet adja, de azt remekül.  Két fontos tudnivaló: 1) A kampánymód remek, de rövid. Két délután alatt végigjátszható és máris kívánja az ember az új kieget... 2) ...hacsak nem fut neki újra, módosított paklival, és próbál meg még jobb eredményt elérni. Ekkor viszont már nincs, vagy minimalizálódik a meglepetés ereje, így kicsit átmegy amolyan Hanabi féle - ki tud jobb kombóval győzedelmeskedni dologba. Nem baj ez, de a kezdeti meglepetésfaktor csökkenésével nehogy a játék élvezeti értéke is romoljon.  Meglepetésként ért: A játék egyenesen utasít rá, hogy csak hangulati elemekkel kommunikáljunk. És ettől tényleg szuperebb lesz a játék, jár a keksz. De egy idő után (pláne amikor a maximális kombóval való győzelem a cél) ez ígyis-úgyis átmegy abba, hogy csak a kártyák nevét vagy a tesztmódosító számát mondjuk be.  Nagy pluszpont jár a húzózsákos dologért: nincs kocka, van más randomizáció.  A grafika 10/10, a hangulat 10/10. Az előkészület, a várhatóan számtalan kieget hozó pénzszívás miatt csak LCG kedvelőknek ajánlom, de nekik nagyon. Na jó, picit azoknak is, akik élnek-halnak az FFG-s lovecrafti világért. :)  Amire még kíváncsi vagyok: milyen 1, 3 és 4 fővel.

comment: Slotted insert holds sleeved cards!  Thank goodness, another savvy publisher!    Even though I love deck building games, this one looks bland to me...tiny cubes, a meeple, a board that doesn't grab my attention.  As the rules were explained, I thought this is just a copycat Ascension with so many similarities, and then I thought too, Adventurers Pyramid of Horus when players try to make it out of the pyramid, after finding hidden treasurers and backpacks to carry more.  And like Shogun, cubes go in, and blind, some come out to deliver damage.  Hmmm.  Boring.  Nothing new.  But.....I changed my mind!  Even though I found the "Clank" coming randomly out of the bag made the game quite unpredictable, and difficult to follow a plan, & unfair!!!---it also made the game quite fun, especially when rooting for the demise of others!    The outstanding board design with the movement thereon, is the gem and new element in this game.  The board offers many options with different avenues for movement, so even with a thwarted game plan(s), numerous other choices still make victory possible.  The board is 2-sided, offering variety.  Many cards have a unique concept... bonuses, but slapping you with the evil Clank as well.  Despite the fact I find the components lacking, and the game so reminiscent of other games, and planning so chaotic, I really like this game.    My impression boils down to, it's fun.  Played  2 games now, and one objection to this game, not enough cards or ways to cull junk from hand.

comment: 規則: *選擇劇本建置版圖，然後放置對應單位在對應位置，放置獎盃或目標標記在對應位置 *每人拿一個牌價並各選一個陣營，遊戲建議玩兩場，兩個陣營個玩一次，獎章分數高的贏 *經命令牌庫洗勻，根據劇本發起始張數，兩邊各拿四顆骰，根據劇本設置起始玩家 *遊戲根據劇本先贏到4~6個獎盃的獲勝，通常是消滅的敵方單位為一個獎盃放置對應位置，遊戲輪流進行直到有人獲勝，每個玩家回合有五個階段 1.出一張命令卡，卡片會指定哪個區域跟哪種單位你可以移動或攻擊 2.命令單位 根據命令卡決定符合規則的單位 3.移動單位 選取的單位可以移動，每個單位移動一次，不能通過有單位的格也不能停在同格，同格的要一起移動不能合併或分開 >步兵 移動兩格或是一格後攻擊，特種步兵可移動兩格後攻擊 >坦克 移動最多三格後攻擊 >砲兵 移動一格或是攻擊 4.戰鬥 選擇的單位可以進行戰鬥，不管該格有剩多少兵戰鬥力都一樣，只能攻擊一個目標一次，有相鄰單位時一定要優先攻擊之，遠距攻擊時要在攻擊距離內，且有視線，地形會加減骰 *視野為將兩個目標中心連線，如果有障礙物(友軍不算)就沒視野，兩格都有也會檔掉 >步兵 距離1/2/3格分別丟3/2/1顆骰 >坦克 三格內目標都丟三骰 >砲兵 1~2/3~4/5~6格丟3/2/1顆骰，無須視野 *骰結果對應兵種代表移除對方一個單位，手榴彈全都算，如果移除最後一個單位後則將他放在你的獎杯處，旗幟有幾個對方單位要退幾格 *撤退時無視地形，無法撤退則在少一個單位 *近戰步兵或坦克如果消滅對手或是迫使對手撤退可站領該格，坦克成功占領時可在額外攻擊一次，可在占領但不能攻擊第三次 5.抽一張命令卡

comment: Every time I play this game I'm amazed by the simple, but deep mechanics. The only random factors include choosing the player order (literally where you sit at the table) and the selection of the plantations that will be available. A masterfully balanced, role/action selection scheme drives the game. Bribes increase the value of roles that are not selected in any given round to encourage players to take advantage of them in following rounds. Multiple game end possibilities (out of colonists, out of victory points, or out of building space) lead to a game that never ends in quite the same way and usually tends to end just as a few people are really gathering momentum. Perfect.

comment: Tsuro is an extremely accessible game that combines area enclosure with a bit of "screw you." Each turn, a player will place a tile from his/her hand of three. This tile will be placed directly in front of his/her dragon piece. The dragon must then follow the newly created path as far as possible. The goal is to stay alive as long as possible by not following a path that sends your dragon into another dragon or off the board.   In practice, you will need to strategize about when to place your tougher pieces (the ones with similar sides and thus less options). You may find it more worthwhile to kill an opponents dragon even if it puts your dragon in a less useful position. It's ideal if you can close a section off for just your dragon to use, because as the board fills up, there is no escape from death. This creates a very nice tension between wanting to stay out of the middle where there are bound to be lots of dragons, but also to stay away from the sides which are death if you run into them.  It scales surprisingly well with 2-8 players, though with more players there is definitely more chaos. You can lose some control by virtue of the fact that 7 tiles will be placed before you get another turn. That said, dragons die very quickly with that many players, so when the smoke clears, the end game is often very exciting. It's a very light game, but it plays quickly and I'm happy to play it as a filler before/after a heavier game.

comment: One of those games which is simply fun - no doubt experience will help with completing the first stage shipbuiding task under the time pressure but for the second stage you pretty much just have to sit back and laugh as your puny spaceships are smashed to bits by irresistable galactic forces.  Great fun - the comparisons to factory fun and space dealer comes from the need to build your spaceship from the common stock of components - you turn over a tile then either play it on your board or put it in the common area where anyone can take it - and the fact that the first person finished not only gets a bonus but turns over a timer which puts a limit on how long the others have to finish.  Then the real fun part is heading off into space to see how well built your ship is - i.e. how well it stands up to meteor storms and space pirates etc. - that is when large chunks start to float off - to hoots of laughter from your opponents - there are other ways to score on the voyage but the main score comes at the end for finishing positions, any cargo you've picked up and a bonus for the best built ship - or rather best remaining bit of the ships that started - then pay for your repairs and head off on voyages 2 & 3 - on increasingly bigger ships.  Very different games but slightly reminiscent of Railway Rivals in that the first part of the game is spent building your railway/spaceship and the second is spent testing how well it stands up to the demands of space travel.  And in both games the dice can occassionally be cruel to you no matter how well you built in stage one - to the delight of your opponents.

comment: Collection: My Draft Cube: https://www.cubetutor.com/visualspoiler/1413  A well-crafted game. Nicely illustrated. Ridiculously expensive. Even to play casually with a group of friends and a bunch of random cards can get a bit pricey. This game avoids erratas and confusion much better than most CCG's especially given the sheer amount of cards in the system. The best things about this game are the ubiquity (making it easy to find events and opponents), generally easy to grasp rules, and the ease of deckbuilding. Unlike many other CCGs, it doesn't take a ton of cards to build a decent deck. With fewer than 1000 cards, you can easily build 8-10 fun and different decks.   Mechanically speaking, the distinguishing characteristic is how few cards you get each turn. Hand management and resource management are paramount here. It is much more tense and unforgiving than some other CCGs are.  Over time, I have come to appreciate more and more how much this is not just a game, but a system. A relatively simple rule set creates so many different ways to play that there is something for everyone. I think this is by far the most well-designed and most-playtested game in modern times. It's a testament to what devoted gamers can do with a limitless budget and full team of creative people. So much focus is put into making this game be something for everyone, that it can hardly help but succeed. There is something here for you, and you do a disservice to yourself by not playing.

comment: King of Tokyo is a light, beer-and-pretzels style game with a quick playing time and a healthy dose of luck. It also scales wonderfully from 2-6 players, though I think it's just plain more fun with more monsters - ah, I mean, players.  The premise of the game is basically the same as [thing=17835][/thing]. That is to say, it's not JUST Godzilla or King Kong, it's ALL THE MONSTERS and they are going to kill each other, not just the planet. The cardboard stand-ups of the monsters are high-quality and have great cartoony illustrations. It has a bunch of custom dice and some special power cards which are really what make the game shine.  Just as in Yahtzee or [thing=37380]Roll Through the Ages[/thing], you take a fistful of dice and get three rolls, keeping whatever you want from the previous roll and re-rolling the rest. The goal is to either kill all the other monsters or get 20 points. The dice have various combinations that get you points, healing, attacks on other monsters or energy. Energy is the currency of the game and is used to buy special cards.  As you would expect from Richard Garfield, these cards all break the game in various ways, changing the rules just for your monster so he has a leg up on the other critters. There are tons of these cards; it will probably take 4-5 games (depending on the number of players) to see them all, even if you set aside the ones you already used.   If I had to describe this game in one word it would be "addicting". I can't think of another game that creates more of a feeling of "just one more game" than this one.

The the Strategy is very deep but there is certainly enough to challenge the group. The order in which the black cards appear together with the combination of white cards that you get make for a surprisingly different game most times. Excellent roll play and theme; superb components and a great mid weight strategy game. While it takes the most enoyable aspects of patience as a basis it develops this hugely into a more varied, strategic, co-operative and altogether satisfying game.  It's certainly not intensive stategy. However I like how some of the turns flow fast when you know what you need to do and others require more careful consideration. comment: (1 play)  The single play was with 7 players using the Pegasus Expansion and the 7th player optional rule at the end of the rule book.  I was the Cylon Leader and the game was so dramatic.  The Cylon Leader has a completely secret wild card objective, and mine was that the humans needed to win, but one of three dials had to be 2 or below, so the humans had to be beaten down before the end.  The game was coming to a rapid close, and the dials were in good shape, so I was an obvious and overt player against the humans for most of the game.  Finally, Morale was down to 2, so I made an immediate about-face, trying to help the humans escape New Caprica any way I could.  In the end, I was able to make a final move to betray my two revealed Cylon brethren, giving two of the humans a clutch win, and leaving two stragglers to be executed on New Caprica.  I managed to orchestrate a position where the Admiral could win the game along with one human counterpart, or surely lose as the two revealed Cylons were next and the situation was DIRE.  One Cylon Leader and two Humans win, while two Cylons and two Humans lose - not an outcome anyone expected.  It took over 3 hours to play, but with that much drama and betrayal, time spent was not a problem for me.  I would love to play again.

comment: What's impressive here is Matt Leacock was able to take one of his existing games and twist it enough that it truly feels new again.  In a nutshell - if you own and like Forbidden Island, there's no reason not to get the "sequel" as well.  This time around the tiles move due to a sandstorm, and pieces can get increasingly buried under the sand.  So you can't just ignore certain tiles anymore.  Also new is water rations - if anyone runs out when the sun beats down, you lose - so knowing where the wells are is crucial.  Lastly, the pieces of your ship aren't found in one place - you have to reveal the two matching tiles and then find the piece and their intersection.  So this is a winner - I definitely will want to play it regularly.  The art theme is steampunk which is cool, but it lacks the visual wonder that I thought was so great in FI.  Other than that, as usual Gamewright has top-notch components and packaging.

To each his own, but I greatly prefer Caverna.  The addition of expeditions is fantastic, and I love watching my dwarves build up their farm and dig the caverns into the mountainside. You really feel like you're invested in creating this little kingdom for them.  The component quality and artwork is first-rate, and the sheer quantity of bits makes me positively giddy. Who acts before you (specifically what type of player they are and their skill level) is often more important than your own play. I prefer San Juan.   Personally I rate this game (flaws and all) in my top 25. It doesn't make my top 10 however.  3-30-08 2-player v. Karen 67-66 Win. Factory with 4 goods (all but Coffee led to early cash) Built small office, then factory then wharf. Karen had large office and coffee for 7 dubloons per sale in the market.  5-11-08  Karen, Sean, Ang, Moi. 37,43.40, 48 Ang had 10 vp build, 30 shipping. Karen had 15 build, 18 shipping, special (Fortress?) Sean had 20 build, 16 ship, 7 special, Moi had 24 build, 17 ship, 7 special (Guild Hall)  Karen was first player. I went with (quarry grabbing building) and eventually Hacienda. My cash crop was coffee. I purchased a Factory and got into Sugar for 3$ per craftsman phase. I used my 3 quarries and Factor cash to buy a harbor,wharf and Guild Hall sequentially. The game ended in Sean's governorship (probably turn 12) I was faced with the prospect of shipping 1 barrel of corn for 3 VP or crafting, knowing I could ship 5 VP worth of coffe via the harbor in the likely event Ang picked captain, but not knowing if I'd ship any of my other goods. So I went conservative and eeked out a small win.    4.5.18 bumped from 8 to 9 based on session ratings.

comment: I initially found this game to be too chaotic for my tastes, even though I loved the variety it afforded. But the more I've played it, the more I moved to appreciation, then admiration, then outright love. More than perhaps any other game, Cosmic Encounter is all about the players playing each other, rather than the game itself. It's not terribly cutthroat in spite of this, though most of your success will likely depend on negotiating with other players. The basic structure of the game is dead simple, but the tactical implications that emerge out of player interactions and interactions between special powers make this feel far deeper than it has any right to be. A true classic and with good reason.

comment: [2012-10-23] Az első 2012-es esseni játék, ami kezem közé került. Nos úgy tűnik egyre jobban a másolásé lesz a főszerep, mert nehéz újat kitalálni. A Terra Mystica egy nagyon erős koppintása a Hansa Teutonicának. Megpróbáltak egy témát kreálni, amiben különböző fajok érvényesülését kell minél jobban menedzselnünk. Területek formálunk át és épületeket építünk, amivel felszabadulnak különböző erőforrásaink. Érdekességet a rengeteg faj és különböző képességeik jelentik. Az ilyen hátulütője mindig, hogy nehéz kiegyenlíteni a különböző képességeket, elsőre úgy tűnik itt sem sikerült. Bőven van erősebb és gyengébb faj a játékban, ami a különböző köri bónuszok miatt mindig változó mennyire jó vagy éppen rossz, de így nehéz egymáshoz mérni a játékokat és teljesítményeket. Mivel a HT-nél hosszabb így még azt sem lehet mondani rá, hogy könnyed, sőt kicsit talán gondolkodósabb is, bár az egyes fajok előnyeinek minél jobban való kihasználása könnyen vezet a követendő játék felé. Egyáltalán nem rossz játék a Terra Mystica, a Hansa T-t kedvelőknek biztos kellemes időtöltés lesz, akinek pedig a nagy előd nem ismerős biztos még kellemesebb élményben lesz része a játék során.  [2014-10-24] Pont két éve játszottam vele, így örültem, hogy előkerült. Azóta top3-as játék lett, sőt volt top2 is kis ideig. Ha nem is jó ennyire, de már én is jobbnak látom. Tényleg játszható minden faj, csak van amelyikhez több tudás szükségeltetik. Jó játék a Terra Mystica. Hibája talán az AP veszély, öten eléggé elhúzódhat. Emelek egyet a ponton. 7->8  [2015-02-14] További játékok után egyre jobban érzem a játék nagyszerűségét. Lehet, hogy a fajok nem teljesen kiegyensúlyozottak, de több játékos esetén van olyan kis szerencse benne, ami ezt kompenzálhatja. Minden faj megismeréséhez minimum 3 játék szükséges szerintem, illetve teljesen más egy adott faj kétszemélyes és ötszemélyes játékban. Emiatt óriási az újrajátszhatóság. A játék egyedüli hibája tényleg csak az AP veszélye.

comment: This is an incredible game.  In this game each of the players is terraforming Mars to make it habitable for human beings.  Once there is enough water, oxygen, and heat on the planet for human beings to survive the game ends and the player who contributed most to the effort is the winner.  The gameplay is almost entirely made up of three components.  The first, and largest, is tableau building.  The game is entirely driven by a project deck you buy cards from each round.  The cards do everything from increase the levels of water, oxygen, and heat on the planet to provide you with pets to cuddle on Mars.  The second is tile placement.  While we are developing Mars we are adding oceans, greenery, and city tiles to a map and their placement matters a lot for end game scoring.  The final component is the resource economy.  There are 6 different main resources to manage, each of them being varying degrees of important depending on the strategies you choose to pursue and many more ancillary resources can enter the game through project cards.  I absolutely love games with a lot of content and high replay value.  After one play I knew I would love this game.  And this was even the "beginner" mode where a third to a half of the "advanced" project cards were removed and we played with the same beginner corporations with no powers.  I also love games with asynchronous player powers so I'm sure I will enjoy future games more.  My first game was also with the max 5 players and the main concern I had going into the game was whether or not the max player count would crowd the map too much.  Now my main concern is that with fewer it would be too open taking away meaningful decisions and player interaction.  We did go through the entire project deck but this was also with a huge chunk of it removed.  The game itself is great but it also has serious component issues in my opinion.  The cards, player cubes, and tiles are fine and the rulebook is actually pretty well written but past that it could use some serious love.  The board is tiny and crowded, it makes an otherwise epic feeling game feel much smaller.  The player boards suffer in the same way being thin paper boards with sections for each of the resources.  Resources you collect a lot of and can easily lose your place do to an errant elbow.  And finally, the resource cubes (the same ones are used for everything which is fine since there are 6+ resources in the game) are of terrible quality.  My copy (which I got used) has supposedly only been played 3 times now and according to the previous owner the paint on these cubes was already peeling and warping when he opened it.  A quick search online reveals this is a pretty common complaint.  It's sad because such a great game deserves better care.  This has actually been a common occurrence with Stronghold Games in my opinion (although there are worse offenders, like Splotter Spellen).  They get hold of such great games but the best level the components have ever reached for me has been mediocre.  And this one certainly falls closer to "poor".

Once you've played it a few times you see the different paths to victory and can adapt your strategy based on what others are trying to do.  Like Puerto Rico, an important element to RftG is picking phases that help you more than your opponents.  You want to be "out of phase" with them so that you can develop/settle when they pick it and produce/consume when it is the most benefit to you (for example). comment: Everything, absolutely everything about this product is solid.  It's VERY easy to teach, it plays out of the box, theres next to no set up time.  The components are excellent quality, the artwork is fantastic and the insert... innovative, functional and genius.  I love worker placement games, this might be the best one yet.  The Dungeons and Dragons theme actually blends seemlessly with the gameplay making for a delightful experience.  While it lacks some of the things I love from other titles, this has CONSIDERABLY less play time.  After 2 games of it you can blast through a full game in well under an hour.  Its highly replayable as well do to the questing system (which keeps you constantly engaged throughout the entire game).  Shockingly it plays well with 2 players as well as groups.  I can't give this enough praise... the only draw back I see is that theres not an expansion to add some new mechanics (like unique player abilities for the houses) and some stuff for more serious gamers.  Perfection.    People who don't like this one or consider it a basic worker placement game are missing the point entirely.  This is a light but serious euro game... you can get anyone to play... with no set up time... out of the box in under an hour... with a theme that doesn't feel tacked on.  It's much better than any Dungeons and Dragons board game has any right being.

comment: The game plays pretty easy and fast, there's little down time. It takes a few turns before you know all the tiles, but then it's fairly straightforward. You gather goods, sell these for money and buy rubies or instead deliver them to the sultan for rubies.  The Sultan's route is a bit more complex, as you'll need blue goods (jewelry) as well, which cannot be gathered at the warehouses, but need to be won by throwing dice (7 or up gets you one or more Jewels).   People who usually are unlucky with dice can avoid this by acquiring a card that lets you buy jewely at the warehouses or a different card that allows you to change one die of throw again.  As you need to leave your assistants behind (to take care of the paper work or something), you need to plan your route carefully. Luckily, you can always return to the fountain and recall your assistants there.  The fun part is that you encounter people on your way, other Merchants, the governour, the smuggler or one of the "nephews", either your own or someone elses. The other Merchants have to be paid off before they allow you to perform the action, the governour and the smuggler allow you to buy cards or goods and the nephews can be sent to jail for a reward. You can even turn in your own kin.   All in all, Rudiger Dorn has put together another nice game. I see some resemblance to one of his earlier games Waka Waka, where the same goods (fruits, spices and silk) can be gathered and delivered for more status. We like that game as well, but this one is certainly more developed.   As this is a modular board (all the 16 tiles of the market can be set up randomly), the most efficient way of moving around varies per game, so replayability is high. There's a nice alternative play as well, where one of your assistants has a neutral colour and can therefore be taken by one of your opponents.

Some of the cards also have powers that effect the gameplay. Games are usually fairly quick, though the ability of one character to destroy cards can extend the playing time. comment: Clearly a quality game. It offers the perennial choice between taking resources or building. And between those, do you take resources that helps you stay alive (food) but can't help you build, or resources that help you build buildings. And if you build, do you build something that helps you feed (ships) or to progress your VP engine.   There's the added charm of making all buildings available to all players, if they pay a fee to the owner. It's about doing things more efficiently than the other players through your resource takes, using your own buildings more than the others (to limit fees, so it is important what you build) and getting an efficient food engine going without sacrificing tempo.   There is an issue with downtime with more players as there's a LOT of options to explore on a turn. And players on their turns may take your options so your strategy is continually changing. Causing more downtime. This lessens with experience. Which is a good thing because there's a lot to explore here and a lot to like.

comment: From HeroQuest as a kid until now, I've always loved a good dungeon crawl board game.  And I think this is as good as the genre has ever been.  One thing to be clear on before you get into this is that it doesn't have the feeling of exploration that Hero Quest or Descent 1st edition gives you.  This is a tactical fantasy miniatures game.  You know the goals as soon as the encounter is set up and it's basically a small tactical battle.  I know some people don't like 2nd Ed and the lack of exploration is the root of all their problems with the game.  The thing is, exploring rooms and killing stuff and collecting treasure gets old after a while if there isn't a strong story linking it all together.  Hero Quest (as much as I love it) and Descent 1st Ed. suffer from this sameyness.  In fact no board game has succeeded in giving a dungeon crawl feel along with a strong story- for that you need to play D&D.  Another thing 2nd has going over 1st edition is that this is so much more streamlined and easy to play than the bloated sessions of 1st Ed which basically ended up going nowhere anyway.  Anyway, enough comparisons.  This game has so many diverse scenarios and is rich with so much material, campaigns, and monsters, heroes, classes, etc.  You could play forever and never do the same thing.  And with a little imagination you can really get into the game and your character.  And there is a sense of discovery and story finding new equipment, encountering new monsters, and when each quest is set up, etc.  Combat is varied and fun with lots of special abilities but it doesn't bog down. Components are stellar.  Great game.

comment: Simple concept. Buy cards into your tableau, roll dice hoping to activate your cards. Each card type has a different way to earn money, be it you only, on anyone's turn, steal from other players, etc. So there's choices on whether to spread across the numbers or invest in a few numbers and aim for jackpot turns. There's combos you can shoot for. Every turn buy another card to add to your tableau (or save up for a better turn, but risk losing your money to other players in the meantime), so turns become more consistent and "bigger" as the game goes on. Turns are fast, there's cheer factor in the die rolling, and you can always blame the dice when you lose. The luck for me overwhelms the process and the game outstays its welcome a little, but at least it doesn't pretend to be anything but a meaty filler.

I think it takes a few plays to grok the connections between your choices and how the scoring ends up.   The key aspect of this game is that you draft cards to use as actions. Not exactly deck-building, more like hand-building. However, each action card also scores for you in one of six ways at the end of the game - so not only are you picking up actions, you are defining what you will score points for. Understanding the relationship between these when you draft your cards is the biggest challenge here and it is a good one. Mac Gerts has shown that he can successfully move away from the rondel that he made his name on!

comment: [After first game - rating 4] This game is a prototype for all dull, heavy and overly complicated Eurogames.  Victory points everywhere, half a dozend different mechanisms, no recognizable theme whatsoever.    Worker cubes, priest meeples, magic tokens, 4 different tracks for collecting majority points, 5 different buildings with different costs and income, 4 different city markers, 12 different special tiles, 7 different extra action spots, 14 different races with different special abilities, 6 different end-of-turn markers  etc. etc.  Get this, get that, turn this into that, get extra point here, get end-of-game points there.   Bottom line: there's surely a lot of work to do.  But where's the game in this mess?    --------------------------------------------------------  [Edit after the second game - rating 6] Ok, maybe a rating of 4 is too harsh.  Played it a second time this weekend and the game was slightly better.  The aspect of building next to different players (to collect magic power) in contrast to build on your own (to have more room) is interesting.   Raised rating to 6.  --------------------------------------------------------  [Edit after 4th game - rating 7.5] I must admit that my initial impression was wrong.  This is in fact a quite faszinating Eurogame. Its all about timing to grab the various scoring opportunities as they come along.  Not sure however, how good the races are balanced.  Raised rating to 7.5.  --------------------------------------------------------  [Edit after 7th game - rating 8.5] Ok, ok I've learned my lesson.  Never rate a (complex) game until you've tried it several times.  Regarding TM: I'm hooked.  What a fine game with so many interesting decisions.  A warning to new players though: beware this beast! comment: Truly a remarkable game by Stefan Feld.  While his games often have interlocking mechanisms, this one gives the player more room for independent choices.  Each turn players roll two dice, and the numbers allow them to perform actions - take a tile, place a tile, ship goods, or take workers.  Workers help alter the luck of the die roll, while the variety of tiles offer options for points.  A little tile-laying, a twist on worker placement, and a new twist on dice in board games.  There are so many ways to score points that it makes your head spin - yet there is no clear path to victory.  Plus there are a variety of player boards, offering endless variety.  Don't want to play too long?  Simply cut down the number of phases.  Lots of options and easy to dive into once you get a hang of it.  This is just a great game and I look forward to playing it again soon.
