comment: I've often said that co-op games aren't my favorite. There is a sense in which they must necessarily be either a pure puzzle, purely random, or somewhere in between. Hanabi answers that particular complaint by essentially being a puzzle, but hiding a different part of the information from each player.   This is an inspired solution, and it also serves to eliminate any of the Alpha Dog problems that can plague other co-ops. Even if you see someone do something you think is dumb, it may not be, simply because you don't have all the information.   Along those same lines, when someone plays a card that makes the team lose, it is never that player's fault. Rather, the rest of the team failed in their responsibility to give information to that player. This leads to very few "feel-bad" moments.  More than perhaps any other co-op, Hanabi rewards players who practice together and learn each others styles and conventions. It is brutally difficult to win, which makes it extremely satisfying when it happens. It's so quick-playing though, that an early loss simply leads to feelings of "let's give it another shot".   Having the players hands backwards is such a simple change, so easy to understand, but with implications that are so deep. My favorite thing to do when explaining the game is to wait to tell players that their hands are backwards until very late in the explanation. The look on their faces is priceless.   This game has tension, teamwork, accessibility, affordability, portability, and depth. Sure to be a classic for years to come.
name: Hanabi

comment: Ausgezeichnetes Spiel: elegant designed, variantenreich, starkes Thema. Wunderbare Mischung aus Engine-Builder und Rennspiel. Langfristige Planung ist ebenso wichtig wie das Erkennen kurzfristiger Gelegenheiten. Besonders gut gefallen mir die vielen Wege zum Sieg die es gibt: Städte- und Waldbau, Tierentwicklung, Weltraumereignisse und Titan, Hausbau über Stahl, Meilensteine und und und. Dazu eine aufgeräumte Regel ohne große Ausnahmen oder schrägen Sonderfällen.   Für 10/10 reicht es trotzdem nicht, denn das Material ist angesichts eines Preises von 60€ suboptimal: die Playercubes sind nicht plan und verrutschen sehr leicht, die Ressourcencubes stoßen sich recht schnell ab. Auch die Spieldauer ist mit 2.5h an der oberen Grenze.  Trotzdem: exzellentes Spiel und der beste Titel im Herbst 2016.  Nachtrag: Habe die Bewertung nach fast 20 Spielen nun doch auf 10 Punkte gehoben denn mittlerweile hat sich gezeigt, *wie* gute die Mischung aus taktisch kurzfristigen Entscheidungen und langer strategischer Linie in TM funktioniert. Die Variante mit Karten-Drafting erlaubt es wirklich, sich eine Plan zurecht zu legen und diesen dann durchzuziehen. Das Spiel zeigt dabei eine enorme Belastbarkeit hinsichtlich der unterschiedlichen Spielweisen. Ich habe mittlerweile Partien erlebt, in denen zB Spieler die massiv auf Waldbau spielten und solche die fast ohne auskamen, am Ende genau 1 Punkt auseinander waren.  Und das bei einem Spiel, das 100% ohne Catchup. Mechanismen auskommt. Grandios  Neues Fazit: Bestes anspruchsvolles Spiel 2016.

comment: When I first played Terraforming Mars, my initial thought was 'hey this is Race for the Galaxy with engine building so better'. However, I'm not sure I still feel that is the case. While I like the layer of added complexity, there is one glaring fault for me in TM, and that is the lack of card control, which in Race is far superior.   Having said that though, the economics/engine building in this game is superb, I love the awards and the board play. It's very true that this game doesn't have the depth of strategic choices as other great euros, particularly due to the limited card control, but there is enough there to at least keep me interested. Also the solitaire mode in this game is superb, unlike many games where the tacked on solo game falls flat. I prefer to play TM with 1-2 people, perhaps 3 if all players are quick and experienced, as that enhances the milestone/awards grabbing but can be too long with more players (which is odd, considering theoretically it should take the same amount of time to meet game end conditions).   I have mixed feelings about TM; while it heavily lacks in some areas for me, in others it shines. I need to try the drafting variant, but also, I can't help but wondering how this game could be improved with a Twilight Struggle type card system.

But the milestones seem maybe too important- in a three player game if one player gets 2 of them they are a likely winner.  The included corporate era expansion is neat but starting the productions at 0 slows the game significantly.  The components are a little fiddly- pushing cubes around on little tracks- and can get messed up.  So the game isn't perfect but it's so good that  it's few flaws just don't seem to matter much.

comment: I was very resistant to buying this game.  A 40-50 dollar price tag for a single play (and additional plays available at 30 bucks a pop) was just too much.  I'm not against the idea of "consumable" games.  I'm currently in the middle of a Pandemic: Legacy playthrough and finished a Risk: Legacy playthrough and look forward to Seafall.  To a certain extent games like Descent and Pathfinder Adventure Card Game, which I have also played, are also consumable where while you CAN play them again it would be far less interesting after you have once (and for that matter there is nothing stopping you from playing through Pandemic or Risk: Legacy after a campaign ends either).  This game (or more specifically the included scenario) absolutely cannot be played through again after playing it once.  It is an adventure/mystery game and knowing the answers prevents you from playing it honestly again.  Sure, one "play" can be 2-3 sessions taking up to 5 hours but I have other games that take that long for a single play.  I have also heard the argument that many people have games they've spent this much for that they haven't played more than once or at all.  I do indeed have games I have only played once or not at all yet, but if I still own it I INTEND to play it again and I CAN.  I have also heard it was a good game so I was at least interested even if I wouldn't spend my own money for it, and to that end I actually won it in a G4GG auction which while not necessarily free, I earned my geek gold by giving away games of my own, is an investment I was at least comfortable with.  Okay, end of rant, onto the game.  Like I said, it is an adventure/mystery solving game.  The players are time travelers from the future jumping into the bodies of people in the past Quantum Leap-style to prevent some time destroying disaster from happening.  You do this by exploring areas and rolling dice to conquer challenges and find clues until some end game condition happens.  This usually takes multiple "runs" so you return to changed locations over and over again with new information and items until you reach the end of the adventure.  Honest-to-god, with a completely open mind, I just DO NOT get the love for this game from the board game community.  Completely taking the restrictive pricing model out of the picture, I now own a copy of this, and while it is a fine game it is nothing special.  You go from location to location, finding items to unlock new locations, and rolling dice corresponding to character stats to pass challenges like so many other coops out there.  Granted, this game has a much more cohesive story than something like Eldritch Horror or Robinson Crusoe, but the gameplay is actually less than those other games.  Even if you are really into story over substance though, and I can get that, a really good interactive story can elevate a game with less exciting gameplay, the story isn't THAT good.  This is with the caveat that I haven't finished the Asylum scenario yet, maybe there are some marquee moments and twists coming that will really change my mind.  But I'm 2 hours and 1 session into the game, which by all accounts is on average about halfway through and nothing has really impressed me yet.  In fact, sometimes quite the opposite.  There are often decisions, sometimes major ones, you as a player can make with no information to support them.  You really just randomly guess and deal with the consequences.  One thing I will say though is the game does look great.  The stark and clean base game components which are meant to act as a framework for any scenario look amazing against the beautiful watercolor cards that make up the location panoramas.  I also really do love how the box is designed to "save" your place in the game if you have to stop in the middle of a session.  Past that though everything in this game from story to content to actual gameplay is incredibly average.  Hearing nothing but accolades for this game I wasn't convinced to support the ridiculous pricing structure of this game.  Having played it and found it incredibly mediocre really baffles me.

comment: Every phase in this game has interesting and challenging decisions. Do I go early in turn order or replenish my court? Which action do I want to take or prevent and how badly? How many cubes do I need to move to the board? Should I play heavily to the Castillo or not? Should I use the king to open up regions for placement, or block regions from other players? The specifics of each available action in the current combination makes these decisions even harder, but also more fun. Area majority games can tend to be on the dry side - place cubes, remove cubes, move cubes. I tend not to like bare-bones majority games that are not combined with special actions, such as China. But there are some - El Grande is one, Struggle of Empires is another - that use the base mechanics as a foundation for a variety of interesting choices. By the end of the path, you hope to have as many different cows as possible in your hand, which you turn in for cash and other rewards, and then start the whole process again from the beginning of the trail. Additionally, each player has a player board from which discs can be removed to reveal extra abilities, Hansa Teutonica-style. comment: Scythe is the most anticipated game of the year 2016. Fun fact: scythe is used for both farming and war. Personally for me Scythe is an alternative to Terra Mystica, both are great games.  Mechanism and Heaviness: It's basically an action-selection game with resource management and engine building. Solid mechanic. Multiple paths to victory. Very similar to The Gallerist, each turn you choose 1 out of 4 sections with 2 actions available. You can do the top-row action, or bottom-row action, or both (top-row first), or neither. In summary: move, produce, bolster power/ popularity, build structures, deploy mechs, upgrade & enlist recruits. There's no rounds or phases. It's medium heavy. It's thinky. If you like thinky Euro games like Terra Mystica, you'll like this game. Straightforward and intuitive gameplay. The depth of the game relies on the strategies players apply during the game. Almost no downtime, the turns can go very fast between players as resources are limited. Clear iconography.  Theme It's alternate-history Eastern Europa circa 1920s. Building your small empire on the map. The factions, the miniatures and encounter cards gives more thematic feeling. The encounters provide more options to get more resources, and if you spend more time to read the flavor text on the encounter cards, you get to immerse yourself into the worldbuilding, similar like Arkham Horror game. Can be retheme as Game of Thrones or Lord of the Rings if you want.  Components and Setup The components are superb and top notch, so many different shapes of tokens, different types of cards, the character and mech miniatures looks great on the board! The setup feels very much like Terra Mystica with starting resources (military, combat cards, objective cards, popularity, money) and units + buildings on personal player boards. Wooden token management on the mats like in Terra Mystica and Eclipse. There are several decks like combat, encounter, objective (just need to complete one per game) and factory cards (extra action space, gained when visited The Factory for the 1st time).   Factions and Replayability Well-balanced asymmetry faction and mech abilities like in Terra Mystica. 3 out of 4 mech abilities are to improve mechs' and character's movement, while the other 1 is to improve combat. Variability created by random pairings of faction mat and player mat for each player. Terra Mystica base game has 14 different factions, with Fire and Ice expansion has another 6 factions (10 different coloured boards), Scythe base game has 5 faction boards and 5 player boards, with 25 different combinations. With the Invaders from Afar expansion, there's gonna be 49 combinations! The replayability is high. Different faction, different starting available terrains, different strategies. You've got to adapt to your surrounding.  Actions TOP: move/ gain money (by moving, there can be combat/ encounter/ factory), bolster military power/ gain combat cards, trade resources/ gain popularity or produce on tiles (different tile different resource, resources stay on board with worker: wood, oil, metal, food or worker); BOTTOM (pay with resources): upgrade (move cube from top row to bottom row for discount), deploy mechs (special faction abilities), build structures (mine/ monument/ armory/ mill) or enlist recruits (1-time bonus and unlock action-reaction). Dual benefits of the upgrade system - increase top-row action benefit and decrease bottom-row action cost. Some small reminders: mechs share abilities with character, not workers, which include riverwalk; mech and workers can transport resources; mill is an extra territory for production; enlist ongoing bonus include activation from active player and immediate neighbours.  Combat Threat of combat is constant, but not mandatory. Deterministic combat systemu sing power dial and combat cards like in Dune/ Rex (also Game of Thrones, Forbidden Stars, Cosmic Encounters). Add numbers on power dial (up to military power to spend) and numbers on combat cards (2 - 5, depend on number of units on tile except worker). The combat resolved fast, unlike those other games. Sometimes a game can be without combat. Each faction need only to win 2 combats to put 2 achievement stars on triumph track except the Saxony. Combat will lower attacker's popularity if there is any retreating workers from the opposition faction. There are no units/ structures destroyed, only retreating to home base.  Endgame Endgame condition triggers when 1 player put 6 stars on the triumph track after fulfilling various requirements. The stars will come out very fast towards the end of the game. Unique endgame condition, very similar to console gaming with the achievement stars on triumph track. Most money win - popularity (love) reminiscent to Euphoria's morale track affect how much money collected for each stars, territories controlled (The Factory counts as 3 territories) and resources controlled. Plus random structure bonus scoring tile.     Solo Variant - Automa There are 4 levels of difficulty, Autometta for easy, Automa for normal, Automaszyna for hard and Ultimaszyna for hardcore. The Automa cards make the solo variant plays very smoothly. Mostly the Automa units would aim to reach The Factory. The solo variant is as good as The Gallerist's.   Final Thoughts Scythe is a keeper. Fans of Terra Mystica, The Gallerist, Eclipse and Game of Thrones will be at home with this game, with extra ability to play solo. Reputable designer of Viticulture and Euphoria fame. Watch Rodney's Watch It Played video before playing the game really helps you understand how the game flows.   Expansion The expansion with extra 2 factions is a must, the board just scream for epic 7-players game! With the base game, it's War of the Five Kings, with the expansion, it's gonna be Battle of the Seven Kingdoms!

comment: This is a lighter weight action selection/race game played out on a modular board.  Tiles are set up either randomly or following one of the suggested layouts in the rulebook into a grid.  Players have a stack of assistants topped by their merchant and can move 1 or two spaces orthogonally and take the action of the tile they land on.  The movement mechanics in this game are interesting.  Every tile where you take an action you have to leave an assistant behind so your number of available assistants diminishes with each hop to a new tile.  If you don't have an assistant available you don't get to take an action.  However if one of your assistants is already on the target tile, because you had been there in an earlier round, you get to take the action and your assistant back giving you more mileage.  The mechanics are really interesting in this game but I feel like the rest of it is somewhat shallow.  Most of the tiles are some variation on collecting money or goods which are used to buy rubies which are used to win the game.  The board is modular but even with different set ups all the actions you perform are similar enough that this game would probably feel very similar across many plays.  Also, due to the movement mechanics and similarities between the tiles I think players can find action loops that they can just perform over and over to get them to the end game.  This would be boring for both that player and everyone else.

comment: It works nicely, and is on the upside of a 7, and has interesting Dorn things in it. Move your stack to a spot and do its action, preferably where no one else is so you don't pay a penalty. Accumulate resource capability, accumulate resources, trade in resources for powers and cubes, earn money, trade in money and cubes for VPs. All standard stuff, but done in a nice package. I like how the board changes from game to game, requiring different approaches ... and how your approach will need to change during the game based on what the other players before you are doing, because you just can't afford to keep paying penalties always being second somewhere. That means the game has a strategic and a tactical element, making for constant decision making. Turns still clip along at a decent rate though. There's a little reservation about long term replayability given that you're accumulating the same things in the same way each game, but the race interaction probably gives it enough oomph. Plus there's some card powers/interactions that are worth exploring to see how much weight to give them. Anyway, I enjoyed it and would happily play again.

comment: I came into this game with very high expectations...which to be honest had me a little worried. Would it be able to live up to what I was hoping for?  The answer is unequivocally yes!  Almost everything about this game is awesome. The art and map really draw you into the world of Westeros. Combat isn't a luckfest like Risk, but still has some guessing and double-guessing uncertainty with the house cards. We played with lots of little slips of paper for Ravens and it was just the right amount of diplomacy and negotiation that I was hoping for, not too drawn out and yet still existent.  Fantasy Flight did a fantastic job with their tutorial video. While it was still a lot for the people learning to take in, it made my job as teacher so much easier! We would pause whenever anyone had a question and I could clarify or explain in further detail.  There were a couple things that keep this from being a 10 at this point  1) There are so many little rules that hold everything together that sometimes people got themselves in situations where they thought they could do something but they couldn't. I know in some ways that's unavoidable, but in a long game like this, there was some frustration around the table. I don't see that being a problem if we played another couple times  2) Some people got themselves into bad situations at the beginning and then were stuck for the rest of the game. Now I know that's their own fault, but it sucked for those people to play for the next 3 hours feeling hopeless  All that being said, I LOVED this game and can't wait to schedule another play of it in. I suspect my rating might go all the way to a 10 after a couple more plays, but don't want to get ahead of myself :)

comment: Finally Fryxgames produces a really excellent game, and of course it's Jacob's creation, the best designer in the family.   I like games with a lot to do where the skill is to optimize and maximize to be able to do more and more rather than games with a limited number of actions, so this game suits me well.   The engine that drives the game to an end, terraforming, is cooperation and at the same time as you actually compete for those terraforming points. I know some players that have problems with games where you can decide to end the game or not regardless of how you are doing and that wont "allow" you to end the game if you're not in the lead (Worst of all are the french online "Gang of Four" players). But in this game you're not entirely sure if you are in the lead or not, there are a lot of hidden points. That in it self might also be a problem for some players, but not me.   One of this games strengths is that there are several very different strategies to win. Some companies might be stronger than others, but what differs more is how you play them.   I have been of the opinion that draft is necessary to make this game fun, but I have realized that randomly dealing cards has its merits too. The Standard Projects come more in play when you get less cards that suit you.   When I play with my gaming group we always use drafting though. We also draft the ten first cards. This is how we start: Deal 2 or three companies each to chose from. Deal five cards, draft those clockwize. Decide which company you wanna play and display it. Deal five cards and draft counterclockwize.   I got to try the fast start with the prototype for Alliances at a convention this spring, which was really good. Everyone got going faster, which is more fun for everyone.

comment: The mechanics of this game are great.  I have the anniversary edition, which I think is worth it for 60 bucks, not for 90 or whatever the MSRP is.  It is best when playing where everyone knows what they are doing, as every choice that someone makes has a pretty big impact on someone else.  So an unknowing player can definitely gift wrap things for the player to their left pretty easily without realizing it.  I do think this is less of a problem than most people thing though, as the trick is to be able to profit from everyone's choices - you might not be the best shipper, or builder, but you can get something done no matter which one people choose.    This is another game that I have made the mistake of thinking that non-gamers will grasp easily, and it's not.  They can fight through it, but usually it's better to start with something else a little lighter.  Plus, it's a game that definitely rewards good play, and a new player will get hammered, particularly if they aren't used to any sort of game in this genre.  In terms of gameplay, I think it moves along well, and seldom do I see people pouring over a choice.  It is done in 90 minutes, as it states, even if you aren't being a taskmaster about people moving along.  I think it's best with 4-5, but you certainly increase the likelihood of getting screwed, or someone just making a bad play.  3 people is probably the best number to play to see who is the best at this game.  Bottom line - I think it is completely deserving of it's lofty place on the rankings and think it should stay there for a long time.

It just takes a long time to end (although RAW games can last less than an hour), and since it doesn't have a clear end in sight (or at least a predictable one), stalemates in trading and auctioning can drag this game out longer than it should.  Try a variant where you play under RAW, and you set a time limit - after 1 hour, whomever has the most money and property WINS!  EDIT:  Bumped this up to a 5 rating - without any playing.  This is why:  after reading a multitude of various strategies and session reports and reviews, this game seems to play more and more like a good auction-based game that is open to a lot of strategic possibilities when played under RAW.  CAVEAT:  This game earns a wretched "2" when any house rule of any kind is introduced.  This game demands to be played under RAW only - for those who have only played it using house rules (and most likely hate it), I guarantee it is the house rules that have made this game so unpalatable and so reviled on the geek.

comment: Excellent game by Stefan Feld; (for my opinion actually his best game ).  :thumbsup:  Burgen von Burgund is a fine mixture of dice rolling, worker placement, and tile laying.  I especially like the way how placing tiles trigger free actions which can trigger chain reaction of additional free actions.  This creates really positive and rewarding gaming experience.  Another thing I like is the way, dice are manipulated.  Players roll dice and can use worker tiles to modify dice values by +1 or -1.  One fine details here is, that a '6' can be turned into a '1' by "adding" +1 (and vice versa).  This greatly increases the players' felxibility and makes unfavorable dice rolls much less probable.  Burgen von Burgund works with any number of players but is best with two players because of the reduced playing time (~45 minutes), almost nonexistent downtime and more tactical gameplay.  My rating of '9' applies to the two player ganme.  With 4 players I'd rate it 7.5.

comment: I believe that DOOM is the best iteration of this system.  DOOM gets you to the good stuff (tactical combat, special abilities, fun dice resolution system) with the least amount of hassle.  The hook of Descent 2 for me is the campaign system.  In concept, it is cool that the heroes and the overlord can level up.  However, the two sides are leveling up more or less equally, so the "leveling up" really just means that everyone rolls more dice and can take more damage.  It is not like the leveling up in say, Runebound, where you have to judge when you are powerful enough to take on greater challenges.  In D2, you do a series of missions at level 1, then a series at level 2, which is similar except everyone rolls twice as many dice.   This is underwhelming to me.  However, I do like how the outcome of each encounter affects how following ones unfold.  The campaign is suitably epic, but it is a commitment of quite a few game nights.    Personally, I'd prefer to just get in and out with DOOM for the combat, play Mansions of Madness for the narrative, or Earth Reborn for a more intricate tactical experience.  D2 falls through these cracks for me, and is therefore getting Jones ruled off my shelves.  I would still very happily play D2 anytime, though.

comment: 2-7  Voorbereiding:  Elke speler krijgt een wonderbord en 3 munten. Verwijder uit de 3 kaartstapels de ongebruikte kaarten (afhankelijk van het aantal spelers). Selecteer willekeurig paarse kaarten voor de tijdperk 3 stapel en schud deze door de stapel.  Speloverzicht:  Er zijn drie tijdperken: tijdperk 1, 2 en 3. Punten worden uitgereikt aan het einde van tijdperk 3. Aan het begin van elk tijdperk krijgt elke speler een hand van 7 kaarten.  1. Kies een kaart:   Elke speler kiest en speelt een kaart gesloten, daarna draaien alle spelers simultaan de kaart open.  2. Mogelijke acties:   a/ bouw de kaart open (je kunt hetzelfde gebouw niet twee keer bouwen) b/ bouw de kaart gesloten als een Wonder (van links naar rechts) c/ leg de kaart op de aflegstapel en neem 3 geld van de bank  3. De volgende hand:   Elke speler geeft zijn handkaarten door aan de naburige speler.   Tijdperk 1 en 3: in wijzerzin. Tijdperk 2: tegenwijzerzin. De laatste kaart van elk tijdperk die alle spelers overhouden, gaat naar de aflegstapel.  Gebouwen:  Geldkosten: de kosten worden aan de bank betaald.  Gratis bouwen: het gebouw kan gratis worden gebouwd.  Grondstofkosten: de aangegeven grondstoffen worden geproduceerd door de stad van de speler en/of gekocht volgens de handelsregels.  Gratis bouwen (keten): Als een speler reeds een kaart met hetzelfde symbool heeft liggen, mag hij alle kaarten met dat symbool gratis bouwen.  Wonder:  Grondstofkosten: de aangegeven grondstoffen worden geproduceerd door de stad van de speler en/of gekocht volgens de handelsregels.   Productie: De grondstoffen van een stad worden geproduceerd door het wonderbord, de bruine kaarten, de grijze kaarten en sommige gele kaarten.   Om een gebouw of fase van een Wonder te bouwen zonder handel, moet de stad van de speler de grondstoffen produceren zoals aangegeven op de kaart van het gebouw of op het bord van het Wonder.   Grondstoffen worden niet verbruikt tijdens het bouwen. Ze kunnen elke ronde tijdens het hele spel gebruikt worden. De productie van een stad kan nooit verminderen.  Handel:  Elke speler kan alleen handelen met de twee naburige steden.  Elke gekochte grondstof kost 2 geld, te betalen aan de eigenaar (spelers kunnen nooit weigeren om grondstoffen te verkopen).  Een verkochte grondstof hindert de eigenaar niet om zelf deze grondstof in dezelfde ronde te gebruiken voor zijn eigen bouwen.   Na elk tijdperk volgt er een militair conflict. Elke speler vergelijkt het totaal aan schildsymbolen op zijn militaire gebouwen (rode kaarten) met het totaal van elk van de naburige steden:  a/ Speler heeft meer schilden dan zijn buurman: +1 fiche (in tijdperk 1), +3 fiche (in tijdperk 2) en +5 fiche (in tijdperk 3).  b/ Speler heeft minder schilden dan zijn buurman: -1 fiche  c/ Speler heeft evenveel schilden als zijn buurman: geen fiche.  Elke speler krijgt dus, afhankelijk van de situatie, 0, 1 of 2 fiches op zijn speelbord.  Na Tijdperk 3 tellen de spelers hun punten: 1/ punten op militaire fiches 2/ 1 punt voor elke 3 geld 3/ punten op het wonder 4/ punten op gele gebouwen 5/ punten op blauwe gebouwen 6/ punten op paarse gebouwen 7/ punten voor groene gebouwen

I'm sure that the complaints that some players have are quite legit, but so far, I haven't seen a single mechanic dominate too viciously to make it feel imbalanced.  Now I need to try the unique alien races! --- 7 plays later, I'm dropping the rating to an 8.  Not to imply I don't like the game still, it's just that the original excitement from the beauty of the mechanics has worn off a little and what I'm left with is a game that needs to be played pretty aggressively to be fun, and for some, that's not fun. Everyone wants to build up their little corner of the galaxy, and improve their ships, but you either have to fly in and decimate a weaker neighbour or take the disadvantage of being the aggressor against an equal. comment: Rating is for game design, quality of components, depth of play.  Is NOT commentary on tournament scene, "net decks," or individual sets or cards.  My first introduction to "real" gaming, back in 94.  Revolutionary concept.  I loved the game, played it daily, spent hours deck building every week, etc.  I blissfully ignored the money-grubbing tactics of WotC (Type 2?  You mean, I HAVE to buy new cards to play in tourneys?), played T1 games with my friends, etc.  I even bought several boxes of each set, although I only played with MAYBE 5% of the cards.  Then, WotC went one step too far, and lost a customer.  I sold my 15,000 card collection (Alpha through Urza's Saga or whatever).  Why?    FOIL CARDS.     A few years later, I acquired a few collections, and have ~25,000 cards now.  I rarely play with them, and have no intention of buying any new cards.  The gameplay, artwork, and just game design is just too good, I wanted to at least have the option of playing in the future...especially with my kids.

Might be better to allow the large scoring cubes to represent 3 points instead of 5, since there was at least one occasion in the game that I played where a player was forced to reveal that he had less than five of a particular colour, when there were no small cubes of that colour left, and he was unable to supply 'change' for a large cube. comment: Carcassonne recently shot up to become one of my favorite games after a bunch of one-on-one plays with my partner.  This is a simply fantastic game; simple and fairly easy to teach, friendly-looking and colorful, but rewarding of a lot of thought and downright cut-throat when it comes down to it. comment: 10x10 2017. Really interesting combination of dudes on a map area control with light combat, engine building/resource production, 7 different factions with special powers (when including the expansion).  There are also 7 different player mats which are pretty similar but can change your engine building strategy somewhat.  The theme of farming/war comes through very strong.  For example causing opposing workers to retreat decreases your popularity which heavily affects end game scoring so you can use you workers as a sort of shield.  Of course they're also vulnerable if they have a bunch of resources sitting there for someone to steal.  It's a neat push and pull and even though combat doesn't occur that often it does happen in pretty much every game so it's always on your mind.  The mechanism of selecting a pair of actions is really cool- hard to describe but pretty easy to get used to.  It requires some planning in the short to medium term to be efficient.  The game encourages you to pursue a bunch of different things at once so you'll need to succeed in several different facets to win.  So your strategy is always sort of "do everything (or at least 3 or 4 things) and do it efficiently" you can't just say I'm going to just do combat this time for example (unless you are the Germany faction).  I love the setting and art- in fact this is my favorite art in any board game.  The encounter cards are cool and the game tells a bit of a story if you let your imagination get into it.  One of the uncommon cases where the hype was right.  Fantastic game.

comment: Puerto Rico was, for a while, the absolute darling of the designer board game world. It introduced entirely new mechanics which have since been iterated and copied on. Innovation doesn't always mean quality, but in this case, these really good ideas also translated into an excellent finished product.  In this game, players take on the role merchants shipping goods from Puerto Rico back to the old world. Players will choose what kinds of goods to produce and ship (ones more costly to grow can be traded for more money) and will need to build factories, storehouses, and other types of buildings to manage this production. Variable Phase Order was the big innovation here, having players draft which turn phases will occur in a given round and in what order. The implications of these decisions are not always obvious to the novice, but even a new player still has a strong idea of what they want to do and how to do it.  Puerto Rico is an acquired taste, but one that is oh so worth acquiring. It takes a few plays to see just how well all the different mechanics work together rather than just seeming like a themeless mishmash. Granted, theme is a place this game suffers; it feels very dry and sometimes more like an optimization exercise than shipping goods, but after every play, I appreciate it even more. It is a lot more elegant than I initially gave it credit for, and the learning curve to do well is not as great as I first thought.

comment: A re-themed Vinci (which I like). Very nice components, and the fantasy theme that is thick as Vegemite.  The game is quick to learn and has tons of replayability, even without the myriad of expansions.   It has surprising strategic depth, especially when playing with thinkers.   What makes this game especially fun (aside from the artwork, theme, mechanics, and so on) is that is plays according to the group - if you have a fun, roleplaying type of group, it lends itself to that. As mentioned above,  if you have serious strategic gamers, it has enough depth and options to give you a challenge, especially when it comes to planning where to reinforce, who to be diplomatic with, and when to put a race into decline. With reckless players, or new players, you can experiment and simply enjoy yourself. It handles 2 players well, all the way to 6, and with the Reams expansion has modular boards and scenarios...  For the money, it's an "efficiency must" for any collection.

comment: It's nice to run into a game where the play lives up to the visual impact.  When you first look at Takenoko, it's hard not to be charmed by the hungry panda, the harried gardener, and those pastel bamboo pieces.  Luckily the gameplay is just as enjoyable.  Players take two actions (generally they must be different) which involve growing bamboo, moving around the pieces, or laying new tiles.  Eventually you try to complete objective cards that come in three types.  Once someone hits the magic number, the player with the most points on those cards wins.  It's quite simple, yet requires enough thinking to be a satisfying time for most gamers.  There's a bit of a puzzle element layered with some planning which should scratch the right itch.  And it's so CUTE.

comment: Rightfully received a ton of buzz at Essen 2016. This is just the kind of game that blends a bunch of mechanics together and does it right. There's several things to do, and each time you take your herd through to Kansas City, you have to decide carefully your sequence of actions. By building buildings to determine the actions and when you can take them, the replayability is huge. There's a bit of a set collection and managing your the herd and gathering more cattle is a cool deckbuilding mechanic. On top of all of this, you've got this Egizia-esque mechanc of how far do you go down the trail to Kansas City, knowing you can't go back your next round. The bonuses are varied, and it just seems that you're immersed for a couple of hours making tough and interesting choices.

comment: Much like [i]Monopoly[/i] it's not a [i]bad[/i] game—just hideously antiquated.  The simplicity of the rules set makes it primarily a social game, a game of pilsner, pals and potty mouth.  [b]EDITIONS OWNED ([-]7[/-] 5):[/b]  [b][boardgameversion=27857]That 1970s one with the caltrops[/boardgameversion][/b]  :star::star::halfstar::nostar::nostar: My very favorite Xmas present when I was 10 or so; played many times all by myself.  Lovingly maintained in a state of arrested decay.  Rating is for the standard Global Domination game, though it can shoot to [i]superawesome[/i] with the right people.  And beer.  [b][boardgameversion=23837]2003 Edition[/boardgameversion][/b] :star::star::star::nostar::nostar: Self-purchased for the mission cards.  Makes the base game waaay more playable.  [b][gameid=1829][/b] (big box edition, 2001) :star::star::star::halfstar::nostar: Self-purchased for science fiction theme.  Good stuff—almost an entirely different game.  [-][b][gameid=8107][/b][/-] :star::star::star::halfstar::nostar: Self-purchased because I'm a fanboy.  Pretty cool for what it is.  [-][b][gameid=15045][/b][/-]  :star::star::star::halfstar::nostar: Purchased for the kids.  (Yeah, right.)  Pretty decent 2p game.  [b][gameid=22551][/b] (2006) :star::star::star::halfstar::nostar: Purchased for me.  (The biggest kid in the house.)  Great for 3p.  [b][gameid=37198][/b] (2008) :star::star::star::star::nostar: Fantastic additions to the base engine—cities, capitals, objectives, a new card-exchange regime (turn in 2-10 stars for 2-30 troops) and a VP-based victory condition make this a completely different game.   UPDATE:  I really, really like the idea of [i]Risk[/i]—the stupid-simple conflict game of smack-talk and dice-chucking—far more than actually playing it.  It would be difficult to convince me to play the default Global Domination version of this, no matter how tempting the snacks, beer and company.  I'm much better disposed toward the improved versions—missions, [i]2210[/i], [i]LotR[/i], or one of the Star Wars ones.  Even better, the 2008 Revised Edition.  That said, I do play an awful lot of Global Domination [i]Risk[/i] in digital formats—you can tap out an entire game in less than 20 minutes.*  Stupid fun. comment: This game is great, and honestly, I feel a little bad only rating it an 8, because I think it might be better than that.  It's got exactly what I love in games:  simple, straightforward rules mixed with incredibly deep strategy.  I might be overstating both of those things, but you have two options on your turn:  pick up pawns, or put them down. That's it. And you're only putting them on one of 5 wheels.  Now, WHICH ones do you put them on?  That is the strategy.  Subtle as it is, it's super intricate.  In many ways, it's what I wish Le Havre had going for it - multiple paths to victory.  There really are just a number of ways to win this game I think, and it's going to shift depending on what opponents choose to do, and consequently, leave open.  I think this is a game where tactics come into play a lot.  Strategy is important, but a great strategy is to be adaptable and tactically versatile. comment: It's hard for me to even consider analysing, critiquing and rating such a celebrated game. Considered by many to be a 'perfect game', Chess is a giant of abstract strategy gaming; it is devoid of all luck, it is almost completely balanced (besides a slight advantage to first player) and yields a complex array of different possible moves, strategies and tactics. Entire books are dedicated to different combos of moves. And all this from a game that has been around for centuries.   I played Chess constantly as a child, went to Chess club regularly, and grew up in a family of avid Chess players. I admire the game for what it is, and enjoy playing against opponents of a similar skill level to mine.  So do I dare critique it? Well, there are some issues for me personally. Chess is not kind to new gamers. It does not invite you in like newer games are good at doing, and it can be quite long. AP abounds. The end game can become a game of drawn out 'cat and mouse', and I feel there are games that better streamline the experience.  But for all that, it is a great game. And I have probably just personally exhausted it somewhat. Considering I've been playing it as long as I have, and can still enjoy it, says a lot.

comment: This game is AMAZING! It lives up to my expectations and then some. I want to play it a couple more times before I solidify it in my rankings, but it even has a chance to become #1 of all time for me. There is so much to do in this game and so many possible routes to victory. However, this game is not as complicated to play as some reviewers have made it sound. There's just a lot to explain, but it is not complicated to do (easy to play, tough to master). I do feel that a person's opinion of deck building will have a good deal to do with your starting ranking for this game, but it's not the only thing you're doing. So, if you hate deck building, this is still not a deal breaker. The replayability is fantastic even from the start if you randomize the building sides and placement to use (for starting buildings and the player's buildings). I think my favorite part of the game is just the number of times you get to go through the trail and deliver to KC. It's a sense of accomplishment and you really feel like you are getting somewhere and doing something. It gives the same tough decisions of a euro game without that feeling like you are slogging through the game slowly for the elusive victory points.  Get it! Play it! Brilliant!

comment: This one is well known perhaps (certainly is around BGG) and I had high expectations. It certainly did not disappoint! The mechanics are very smart - move your stack, drop/pick up a disk to take the target action. Pay other players if they are already there. And to spice it up a bit, have special pieces to move around (and capture). There are 16 location boards that can be arrange in countless ways - so a level of replay-ability for sure. After that, alot of standard Euro goodness: 5 different resources, convert to money and then to rubies (the objective of the game is to get 5 rubies). It allows for a variety of plans to be made, paths to be taken - and just a touch of random luck (a few locations use dice) and a dash of confrontation (you can get in other's ways).  Anyhow, very deserving I think of the Spiel gamer's award. Very happy to have this one and will be anxious to play.

Only tell them the choices, and then once made and rolled-for, the resulting outcome—don't give away any results they didn't get.  This keeps things [i]mysterious[/i].  (It's best for the left-hand player to do this as the right-hand player may still be doing bookkeeping while finishing up their turn, and it gives everyone a rotating slot as storyteller.)[/size]  Now that we've played enough to get the rhythm of the thing I quite like it, especially the feeling of putting your own team together, via allies, and taking on different aspects of the mega-plot while coordinating with other globe-trotting groups.  You can almost see the red arrows gliding from place to place while the adventure-travel music beats a tattoo of ominous progress.  The mechanical stuff's fine, I guess—I don't really notice it, which says a lot—but so far the emergent narratives have been fantastic.  Which is all I really care about.  So, does this replace [gameid=15987]?  Not really.  They're two different beasts.  [i]Arkham[/i] is a mechanically quirky and convoluted thing (facets I find charming) about three-fisted Mythos adventures in New England, while [i]Eldritch[/i] is the cleaner, tighter, "more modern" global version. comment: Some card/hand management, deckbuilding and Caylusesque building-building. Weird combination of many mechanics but the mesh works surprisingly well. In general I like games (or very idea at least) of randomness in setup that guides how you should approach the game. GWT has two kinds of it (which buildings are available and position of start buildings). Then there is randomness of draw but actions offer mechanics to manage your hand before you need to show it at the end.   Only problem is that builders are a bit too weak to use efficiently it seems (and expansion didn't help much with this) and that some parts of the game are hardly used at all (extra scoring cards are a tad too hard to complete and therefore not worth collecting and alternative paths are often not worth using/building). I'd like to have some mechanics in expansion in order to use alternative paths easier but usually there are too many dangers so it's just not feasible.  But even with all the flaws Great Western Trail is one of best games of last few years.  Update: It's worthy of 10/10 rating. So many different mechanics and even some flaws but this game just feels right.

comment: Smash Up's theme is good nonsensical fun. Things are fighting other things. That's all you need to know. The illustrations are really quite lavish and stay away from being overly cartoony, despite the lightness of the game. The box has ample room for the inevitable expansions. From a production standpoint, this one is a winner.  The gameplay consists of fighting over various locations in the center of the board. Each location grants points to the player with the highest total strength of his cards played at said location. Once a total strength threshold is reached, these points are awarded, and the first player to a set number of points is the winner of the game. In practice, this ends up being a lot of addition and calculation, and never really feels like a real battle. The creature cards never really attack each other.   The hook of the game is that your deck consists of two different factions of creatures shuffled together, from the available 8. So you might have pirates and zombies fighting against your opponents ninjas and dinosaurs. Sometimes these combinations can be very complimentary, and other times not. The deck can be quite literally stacked against you from the start depending on how you draw. Additionally, some of the factions focus on discarding certain types of cards from play. If your opponents deck does not have that type of cards, many of your draws will be dead weight.   All of this randomness could be forgivable since it is such a quick and light game. Unfortunately, the combat itself offers very little opportunity for combos, clever card play, tough choices, or sacrifice. Hand management is almost irrelevant. For the first few games, you will be caught up laughing at the theme and artwork, but once you have seen it, there is no real fun to fall back on.

comment: Sagrada is an abstract game of building stained glass windows.  It is a puzzle game with dice drafting.  Everyone gets a unique window and you can choose from two cards that are double-sided with different difficulty levels.  In the game you get out a number of dice from the bag that is equal to 2n+1 where n is the number of players and you roll them.  The start player selects a dice and there is a snake draft.  The final dice is used as time marker. Dice can only be placed orthogonally adjacent to dice that are not the same color or number.  You have 3 different says to break those rules and can use a crystal currency (don't remember name) for paying for these.  Usually you can do this about 2 to 3 times.    You score based on the number of pips on your dice of the same color for a special color you work on.  You also have threes special ways to score that are random.  Add up your points at the end of game and the most points wins.  If you tie, most points from your bonus card wins if I remember correctly.    Its a fun game.  I like it about as well as I like Azul.  If you don't like puzzle games, you will not like this.
name: Sagrada

comment: This really may move up with further plays. I understand the hype for this - it's fantastic! I love that every card is a unique, beautifully represented bird. Turns are simple and quick, and while there game gains a bit in complexity as your previously placed birds draw your turns out, the chainage there is what make this shine. I love that once you have certain bird, it makes the action more useful to you, and you can use that to build a strategy. There's some decent interaction, too, as the set of birds is publicly available and some birds allow you to take advantage of what is happening on other's people turns. I like the round goals, as that also gives you something to focus on while you try to wrack up points. I nearly forgot to mention that resources are obtained via a shared dice pool, which adds to the decision tension as you sometimes have to decide between grabbing the resources you want because the dice have what you need versus taking the other actions to increase the birds in your preserve or obtain more eggs or cards.  What's funny is that I don't like Terraforming Mars, as I felt my options were too limited by what else is going on overall in the game in order for me to make my cards work, whereas in this game, I felt much more free to be able to have my cards work for me in order to score points. I think that perhaps the lack of having to collectively satisfy certain conditions in order to play cards frees you up in order for this game to really shine in my book.  UPDATE: This continues to get better and better with age. I love its elegance and it's accessible to newbies while still presenting an excellent challenge for veterans. Moving to a 9.5.

It is a little like 24.  I loved the show.  It was fun and at just the right time.  Would I go back and watch it again and again like other shows I like?  No probably not, but that doesn't make it any less great. El grave problema es que el juego es como un room-escape, una vez jugado el caso/mazo este ya no tiene sentido volver a ser jugado por el mismo grupo de jugadores, lo que implica que es un juego de una sesión (45€, entre 4 jugadores y 5 horas significa un coste de 2,25 €/jugador/hora, que no parece tanto, pero que sabe a poco). comment: 2  Voorbereiding :  - Rood schild in het midden van het bord - 4 militaire tokens open op het bord - 5 wetenschapstokens op het bord - Elke speler krijgt 7 geld - Selectie van de wonders: er liggen 4 willekeurige wonders, de eerste speler kiest een wonder, de tweede speler kiest twee wonders en tenslotte neemt de eerste speler het overgebleven wonder. Doe dit nogmaals, maar laat nu de tweede speler beginnen met kiezen. - Verwijder 3 kaarten uit elke tijdperk stapel, voeg 3 paarse kaarten toe aan de tijdperk 3stapel. Verwijder de overige paarse kaarten.  Handelen:  - Je kan altijd ontbrekende grondstoffen van de bank kopen. - Kost = 2 + aantal symbolen van dezelfde grondstof (bruin en grijs) bij de tegenspeler - Sommige gele kaarten zorgen ervoor dat je voor een grondstof slechts 1 munt moet betalen.  Speeloverzicht:  Leg de kaarten zoals aangeduid op het voorbeeld. Kies een kaart die vrij ligt (niet afgedekt door 1 of 2 andere kaarten).  1/ betaal de kost en bouw de kaart 2/ leg de kaart op de aflegstapel en ontvang 2 geld (+1 geld voor elke gele kaart in je stad) 3/ bouw een wonder  Als het zevende wonder is gebouwd, verdwijnt het achtste wonder uit het spel.  De speler die het er slechtst voor staat op militair gebied, kiest wie het volgende tijdperk mag beginnen.  Militair: voor elk schild verplaats je het schild een vakje dichter naar de zone van de tegenspeler. Als het schild het laatste vakje van de tegenspeler bereikt, win je onmiddellijk.  Wetenschap: elke keer als je twee groene kaarten met hetzelfde symbool verzamelt, mag je onmiddellijk een wetenschapstoken nemen. Wanneer je 6 verschillende symbolen hebt verzameld, win je het spel onmiddellijk.  Wanneer niemand wint via wetenschap of door het militaire gevecht, dan wint de speler met het meeste overwinningspunten.

comment: [2012-11-03] Az egyik legjobban sikerült idei esseni játékot próbálhattam ki. A dicséretek nem véletlenek a játék tényleg teljesen egyedi és nagyon jól működik. Féltem a szabálytól, de abszolút nem vészes. Gyakorlott játékosok körében egyáltalán kis gondot sem fog okozni, nem nehéz megérteni. A játékot akár rondellásnak is mondhatnám, de itt nem lépünk a rondellákon, hanem forgunk rajta minden körben egyet vagy esetleg kettőt, ha kezdő játékos úgy dönt. Az egyik keréken élelmet és fát, a másikon további nyersanyagokat tudunk szerezni. A harmadik kerék a fejlesztés és építés kereke, a negyedik a csere és gyarapodásé, az ötödik pedig győzelmi pontot hoz. A játék két korszakra oszlik, ezen időn belül kell munkásainkkal nyersanyagokat gyűjteni és épületeket építeni, illetve az ötödik keréken pontot szerezni. Körünkben összesen két dolgot tehetünk csak, vagy felrakunk a kerekekre a munkásainkból vagy leveszünk és akkor végrehajtjuk az éppen ott levő akciót. A játékba beleraktak egy a Caylusból ismert kegyrendszert és három templomot is, amelyen feljebb jutva kapunk különböző bónuszokat, illetve győzelmi pontot, ez szinte egy az egyben a Terra Mytica is hozta az idei évben, meglepő egyezőség. A játék a kerekek miatt szerintem egyedi, persze ezen kívül sok újat nem mutat, de úgy érzem ez elég változatosságot ad a játéknak. Egyetlen veszély a gondolkodás és a holtidő lehet a játékosok lépései között. Szerencsefaktor az egyes épületek feljövetelekor kerül csak a játékba, talán ez még belefér, bár néha lehet bosszantó is. comment: Such a great game, my second favorite of 2016 (behind the amazing Scythe).  This game is kind of hard to put into buckets based on mechanics.  It is basically a rondel game with multiple paths through the route on each pass.  Each time it is your turn you move a number of steps up to your movement speed and use the action for the space you end your movement on.  These can be many different things from hiring workers to acquiring wealth to rustling cattle.  There is also a minor deck building element.  At the end of each pass of the route you gain benefits based on the value of the cattle cards in your hand.  I think my favorite thing about the game is the sheer depth and breadth both of strategy it offers.  There are so many ways to gather points and many paths and decisions to be made at every point of the game.  Even little things like being able to choose whether or not to play objective cards in front of you or keep them in your deck offer interesting tidbits of strategy.  Playing them in front of you means you can lose points if they aren't achieved.  You can still score them while in your deck but they also serve to clutter up your hand and deck.  The components are incredibly standard to sub par.  There's really no artwork to speak of except for the worker profiles and different cows.  I never knew there were so many different kinds of cows.  Some of the actual components aren't great like the thin paper player mats and others are fine but nothing really is better than that.  But what is on offer here design wise can make you forget about the sturdiness of what you play it on.

Very simple gameplay (choose a card from your hand, play the card, do the action) but choices can be agonizing - as with many good games, it feels like everything you do is one step behind where you want to be. There can be downtime waiting for your turn, but I use that to plan, especially as things you think you want to do might go away as others take their turn and you have to quickly re-plan. comment: The game is ok enough to play, but the multiple runs in effect make it a memory game mixed with a guessing game - you're initially choosing which location to travel to next with close to zero information. Which doesn't make for a meaningful game. And you can only play each game (and each expansion scenario) once. As re-run games go, Tragedy Looper felt tighter and your involvement more meaningful, plus it has multiple scenarios to generate repeat play. After playing this and the Marcy case, really it's just a function of gathering information over enough runs to give you the information you need to know to be able to put together one perfect run to win the game. And try not to get frustrated by stumbling over each red herring waste of time. It's shown itself to be a co-op without interesting risk-based decisions, and galvanising the group dynamic along these lines is an essential element of any successful co-op. In effect it's a paragraph game that you're playing to see what happens in the story - but with the downside of having to play the same story numerous times. Also not a great feature. It's a ride game, for the experience and the memory, but there's no great satisfaction, no meaningful decisions, and not a lot of "fun". I'm playing just to see what happens really.

comment: [center][size=6][COLOR=#878787]LIFETIME GAME [microbadge=28495]⭐[microbadge=28496] "PLAY FOREVER"[/COLOR][/size]  [imageid=5283480 original][/center]  [url=https://www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/15987/arkham-horror/mygames/plays][b]Current Stats:[/b][/url] (2018-20)  7-5  [b]High Score:[/b]  22  [b]Wins:[/b]  7 (3 at the wire)   5 closed + trophies 1 six sealed 1 final battle  [b]Losses:[/b] 5 doom track/TPK final battle  [hr] [b]2005:[/b]  An RPG in a box, playable in a single evening.  It's a lot of "pull a card and read the encounter" followed by lots of dice rolling.  If either of those mechanics bother you, stay away.  If you don't mind (and I certainly don't) then this is the best of the genre.  [b]PROS[/b]  - A rich and detailed experience.  - High replay value.   - Cooperative play.  - Solo play!  - Art and production values to die for.  [b]CONS[/b]  - A sprawling rulebook with almost no summary.*  [size=7]*Later editions & big box expansions added a much-needed index.[/size]  - Little rules that are easy to miss, and change the game when you get them wrong.  (For example, we overlooked the fact that closing a gate banishes all monsters with like symbols.  This made a lot of really awful monsters hang around much longer than they would have otherwise.)  Expect to play the game incorrectly several times.  - The final battle is nothing but dice.  (Who knew Nyarlathotep could be defeated by the world's longest [i]Yahtzee[/i] game?)**  [size=7]**Final battle cards from [thing=31536]Kingsport Horror[/thing] fix this nicely.  Also, [thread=202663]this[/thread].[/size]  - It's long.  Really, really long.†  [size=7]†This is mitigated by repeat plays in close proximity; knowing how and when to push on the game to angle it toward conclusion is key.  We're at the point where we can knock it out in just a couple hours.  (For shockingly shorter games, use Yig or Rhan-Tegoth.)[/size]  [b]BOTTOM LINE[/b]  [i]Arkham Horror[/i] is thick, meaty and completely immersive.  This also means it takes a while, but that's not always a bad thing.  It fills an evening to brimming with blood, terror and good clean fun.  Recommended for players who enjoy the [rpgfamily=814]Call of Cthulhu[/rpgfamily] RPG.  UPDATE:  After several plays, the game is becoming easy—almost too easy.  With a crack team of selfless, team-playing RPGers it's a pretty simple thing to win by sealing six gates or closing all gates while having the requisite gate trophies for victory.  This drops the game to a 7, but it still gets the extra point for the whole Mythos thing (and the fact that it's easily handicapped).  UP-UPDATE:  I have realized, with much dismay, that there really is no "horror" in [i]Arkham Horror[/i].  It is extremely rare for anyone to get devoured, so much so that no one really ever worries about it at all.  Also, the characters don't "wear out" like they do in the RPG—they are not eroded by repeated contact with the mentally-corrosive Mythos.  Again, house rules will fix this (by having max sanity reduced by 1 every time you fail a Will check), but still, I shouldn't have to put the horror in Arkham...  It shoulda been there in the first place.  My rating holds at an 8 for all the kicks in the knickers we get out of the experience, but just barely.  [b]2006:[/b]  UP-UP-UPDATE:  Forget all the whining.  The expansions fix everything and take the experience to a well-deserved 10.  So, an 8 for the base game, a 10 with any expansion (especially [thing=21059]Dunwich[/thing]—goddamn Dunwich).  ALSO:  Have the First Player act as the "Interim Keeper" by drawing and reading encounter cards for all players.  Makes it way more fun when you don't know what your choice (or failure) will bring when you have to make a decision.  Allows for more storytelling, too.  [b]2011:[/b]  FINALLY:  I will always use the Injury & Madness cards from [i]Dunwich[/i] and the Epic Battle cards from [i]Kingsport[/i] in every play.  And the Relationships & Personal Stories are a pip!  PS.  Played once with 8p—NEVER AGAIN.  The sweet spot is most definitely 4p.  [b]• COMPLETE SET WITH ALL EXPANSIONS[/b] — Expansion-specific materials kept separate in their original boxes as we prefer to play with one expansion at a time to enhance the experience & prevent dilution.  Everything else is in the main game box.  (!)  Yeah, I got it all to fit.  [b]2018-20:[/b]  Bummed that we never got to play this enough, we put it back into heavy rotation, getting the rules down to the point where it's just [i]smooth[/i]—it really does shine as an RPG experience, telling great little stories with nail-biting finishes.  Playing it frequently also forced me to work out the optimal method for packing the box so setup and breakdown are a breeze—gone is the "archaeology of baggies", replaced with a layered "grab 'n go" stacking.  With everybody pitching in we can have it ready to go inside 15 minutes from lid-off to first Mythos card; breakdown is just as quick. comment: What a great deckbuilding game.  Fantasy Flight's LCG system offers a gamer various ways to approach classic CCG's such as Magic: the Gathering.  If you're happy with a simple set, then the core game offers plenty of replayability - 7 different decks in the box with customization available.  Data packs are being released which offer new cards to build upon.  Of course, the serious will collect any and all Data Packs, while the more relaxed of us will pick and choose. as for the game itself...as a previous Magic player/collector, I am impressed with this system.  As usual with a card game, card draw can kill you, but creating decks against the current meta game is a beautiful challenge I enjoy.  The system is assymetrical in that each player (one the Corp and one the Runner) plays a completely different game.  The Runner is trying to hack into the evil, greedy Corp and steal their precious Agendas while the Corp is trying to defend their assets from the evil hackers.  This results in the two players having different available actions.  The icing on the cake is the bluff/press your luck aspect of the Corp/Runner, respectively.  Do you run against that well defended server assuming the Corp has a juicy Agenda stored there or is it simply bait to lure a greedy Runner to it?  The rewards/penalties are high and is great fun to squirm with these decisions. Anyone disinterested in MtG because of the 'hard to get into' aspect should seriously consider this LCG. Have to lower this to an 8 as the game, to me, is about the surprise factor.  Once you've played a deck, you have a decent idea what's in it and that changes how you play against it, especially as the runner.

comment: What an awesome game!  There are a bunch of neat mechanics at play here, as the turn order varies and even turn length, since the sooner someone passes, the more expensive it is for everyone else, thereby cutting their turns short.  The building track seems to be at the core of the game, although I think the castle and favors add some nice tension.  UPDATE: I think the other element that is fascinating with this one is how which buildings actually provide benefits are set by the players. You can burn some actions to ensure that you get the benefit of the buildings, which is a costly tradeoff. Also, the order in which players pass affects when players pay to move the track, which is another aspect to this unique mechanic. Truly a classic.

comment: Sagrada is a filler-weight dice drafting game where each player is trying to fill in a 5x4 "stained glass window" grid with dice. Each player has a unique board telling them that certain spaces have to be filled with dice of certain colors or values. Additionally, there are public goals that give players points for having various sets of dice, and there are rule-breaker cards that players can use a limited number of times. Dice are taken in a snake draft fashion, and those dice can be placed upon a player's board adjacent (orthagonally or diagonally) to another die. However, orthagonally adjacent dice cannot share a color or value. This is an interesting puzzle, as you try to place your dice both to maximize your score as well as leave your options open in the future. As the game comes to an end, it often gets pretty tense as players are looking for more and more specific dice. I thought this game was good fun.  (2 plays)

comment: One of my all time favorite gaming experiences was completing this game with my dear friends Adam & Jamie Sequoyah. We started the game on my 40th birthday and played it out over half of the next year. Some of the most intense, disappointing, exhilarating moments we've ever had gaming together.   The game itself was solid. The narrative occasionally felt a little on rails, but the strategy felt wide open. I imagine things could unfold a variety of ways if you played it through a dozen times (the only thing hindering that would be your foreknowledge of what was going to happen). If you enjoy Pandemic, you'll love this. We were shocked by the some of the surprises inside and we had many long "discussions" (arguments!) over our strategy. We had a blast creating and developing characters. We even scored fairly well in the end and felt pretty good about our play. Overall, it was an awesome experience. Highly recommended.

But you can't look at your own cards, and other players have to sacrifice a play to give out a clue - and you only get so many of those.  Clues can only be of two types - which of your cards are a color, or which are a number.  Incredibly tough, but hard to not want another go when you've finished a play.  I'll give it a try again soon, I'm sure.  REVISED: The more we play, the more I enjoy it. comment: Doel van het spel:  Het spel eindigt als aan het begin van een ronde de beschavingskaarten niet tot 4 kunnen worden aangevuld OF als één stapel hutten is uitgeput (huidige ronde wordt nog uitgespeeld). De speler die na de eindtelling de meeste punten heeft, wint het spel.   In geval van gelijke stand: Huidige score + aantal gereedschap + stand op het voedselspoor + aantal stamleden. De speler met het hoogste totaal wint het spel.   Voorbereiding:  + Leg de voedselfiches (jachtvlakte), hout (bos), leem (leemgroeve), steen (steengroeve) en goud (rivier) op hun desbetreffende plaats.  + Iedere speler neemt in zijn kleur: 5 stamleden, 2 markeerstenen (veld “0” van het voedselspoor en het scorespoor), 12 voedsel en 1 spelerstableau. De jongste speler krijgt de startspelerfiguur.  + Sorteer de gereedschapsfiches (1/2 en 3/4) en leg ze op hun desbetreffende plaats.  + Schud de beschavingskaarten en leg 4 kaarten open op het speelbord  + Vorm een x-aantal stapels (4 bij 4SP, 3 bij 3SP en 2 bij 2SP) van 7 hutten en plaats ze op het speelbord.   Speelverloop :  1/ Stamleden op het speelbord plaatsen   Te beginnen met de startspeler en daarna met de klok mee, plaatst iedere speler één of meerdere stamleden op de cirkel(s) bij één locatie. Deze fase gaat door totdat alle spelers hun stamleden op het speelbord geplaatst hebben. Het is niet toegestaan om stamleden bij een locatie te zetten, waar je in een vorige beurt (in de huidige ronde) al stamleden hebt geplaatst. Je mag in deze fase niet passen.   2/ Acties uitvoeren   Te beginnen met de startspeler en daarna met de klok mee, voert iedere speler alle acties uit van zijn stamleden. Hij mag de volgorde van de acties willekeurig bepalen. Zijn alle acties van jouw stamleden uitgevoerd, neem ze dan terug op jouw spelerstableau. De volgende speler is nu aan de beurt.  Locatie – cirkels – actie:  Jacht – oneindig – De speler neemt voor elk stamlid op de jachtvlakte, 1 dobbelsteen. De speler telt alle geworpen ogen en mag ongebruikte gereedschapsfiches erbij optellen. De totale waarde deelt hij door 2 (naar beneden afgerond) en dat is het aantal voedsel dat de speler krijgt.  Bos – 7 – De speler deelt de totale waarde door 3 (naar beneden afgerond) en dat is het aantal hout dat de speler krijgt.  Leemgroeve – 7 – De speler deelt de totale waarde door 4 (naar beneden afgerond) en dat is het aantal leem dat de speler krijgt.  Steengroeve – 7 – De speler deelt de totale waarde door 5 (naar beneden afgerond) en dat is het aantal steen dat de speler krijgt.  Rivier – 7 – De speler deelt de totale waarde door 6 (naar beneden afgerond) en dat is het aantal goud dat de speler krijgt.  Gereedschapsmaker – 1 – De speler ontvangt 1 gereedschap. Leg of draai een fiche zodat jouw gereedschapswaarde stijgt met 1.  Beschavingskaarten – 1 per kaart – De speler neemt zijn gekozen kaart en betaalt de kosten (kader boven de kaart). Het bovenste deel van de kaart moet je direct uitvoeren (zie kaartenoverzicht).  Hutten – 1 per stapel – De speler neemt zijn gekozen hut en betaalt de grondstoffen op de hut. Verplaats je markeersteen op het scorespoor een x-aantal punten vooruit (zie hut) en leg een nieuwe hut open.  Akker – 1 – Zet jouw markeersteen op het voedselspoor 1 veld vooruit.  Bevolkingsaanwas – 2 (in 1 kleur) – plaats steeds twee stamleden  op deze plek en neem dan een extra stamlid uit de algemene voorraad. Dit stamlid mag je gebruiken in de volgende ronden.  3/ Stamleden voeden   Iedere speler neemt eerst zoveel voedsel uit de algemene voorraad als zijn markeersteen op het voedselspoor. Daarna moet iedere speler 1 voedsel afgeven voor elke stamlid op zijn spelerstableau. Als een speler niet voldoende voedsel heeft, mag hij het ontbrekende aantal betalen met grondstoffen. Kan of wil hij het benodigde voedsel niet met grondstoffen betalen, dan verliest hij direct 10 punten (je kan niet onder de “0” komen). Ook al kiest de speler om 10 punten te verliezen, hij verliest altijd zijn resterende voedsel.   Nieuwe ronde:  Schuif de de resterende beschavingskaarten naar rechts en vul terug aan tot 4. Spelers draaien hun gebruikte gereedschapsfiches terug naar hun beschikbare positie. Geef de startspelerfiguur door aan de volgende speler (links).  Eindtelling:  Groene achtergrond: kwadraat van het aantal verschillende symbolen + kwadraat van het aantal dezelfde symbolen.  Zandkleurige achtergrond: afhankelijk van de kaart krijg je punten: + aantal boeren x de stand van jouw markeersteen op het voedselspoor. + aantal gereedschapsmakers x de hoeveelheid gereedschap dat jij bezit. + aantal hutbouwers x het aantal hutten op jouw tableau. +  aantal medicijnmannen x het aantal stamleden in jouw bezit.  Totale score = huidige score + punten van beschavingskaarten + 1 punt per eenheid grondstof.  Belangrijke regels:  + Let op voor de aparte spelregels voor een spel met 2 à 3 spelers! Zie spelregels.  + Als je gebruik maakt van een gereedschapsfiche (actie jacht, bos, steengroeve, leemgroeve of rivier) dan draai je de desbetreffende fiche 90° naar rechts. Deze fiche kan je in deze ronde niet meer gebruiken.  + Er is geen limiet aan het aantal beschikbare grondstoffen.  + Als een speler de grondstoffen niet kan of wil betalen bij het kopen van beschavingskaarten of hutten, dan laat hij de kaart/hut liggen en zet hij zijn stamlid zonder gevolgen op zijn tableau.  + Een gereedschapsfiche moet in zijn geheel bij een dobbelsteenworp worden opgeteld. Het is niet mogelijk om een deel te bewaren voor een andere worp. Je mag meerdere fiches bij een worp optellen.

comment: Juego de asaltar un tren. Cada jugador lleva a un bandolero y su objetivo es robar la mayor cantidad de dinero del tren antes de que llegue a la estación. Se juega en cinco turno. En cada turno, una carta indica cuantas rondas se juegan. En cada ronda, un jugador puede jugar una carta de acción, o robar tres cartas de su mazo. Una vez que todos han jugado sus rondas, se resuelve el turno y van sucediendose las acciones en el orden que se jugaron las cartas. Es caótico totalmente y ahí precisamente reside su gracia. Algunas veces las cartas se juegan bocaabajo. Para más coña, al final de cada ronda hay un evento. Es un juego divertido y apto para todo el mundo. Bastante rápido.

comment: Another Family/party game?  Ugh.  But wait.  This one has cool art and hold the phone: Thinking is involved.  This cool little game is good fun.  We player gets dealt a hand of cards.  The cards are all interesting paintings.  The storyteller, describes one of his cards and places it face down on the table and each other player adds a card to the pile.  Then the cards are mixed up and revealed.  The storyteller wants the others to pick his card, but he gets no points if every other player picks his card, so the “story” has to be descriptive enough for most of the other players to guess the right card but not obvious enough so everybody does.    We haven’t turned this into a drinking game yet but I am sure that is on the horizon.

comment: 10x10 2016. The base game is rather ho-hum light-ish worker placement game.  It's fine but a bit uninteresting.  Tuscany, the expansion, changes the game perhaps more than any expansion I've played for any game.  There is a completely different board, a new deck of cards, and different worker powers.  It also mitigates the luck and variability of visitor power levels with a space allowing you to trade cards and other resources.  And all that makes the game much better and much more interesting.  With Tuscany it's a very good medium weight worker placement game.  I would always choose to play Tuscany if given the option.  The game is pretty tight but allows for some different wrinkles in you path to victory- especially with the optional building cards (again in Tuscany).  A tricky game to rate, so my rating is for the base game only- with Tuscany I'd give this a strong 8.
